paragraphs: The paper describes a way for a multilayer neural network to organize itself through successive stages in time. The central idea is that layers develop in sequence, with each layer receiving excitation patterns from the one before it. The hierarchy is therefore built through coordinated learning across levels.

Lateral inhibition supplies the local organizing mechanism. Activity in firing cells suppresses activity in their surroundings, helping a layer capture the patterns supplied by the preceding layer without supervision. The organization of one layer consequently shapes the patterns available for the next layer to learn, linking local interactions to the development of the hierarchy.

The presentation of patterns is coordinated with this process of self-organization. As patterns of increasing complexity are presented, higher levels capture concepts implicit in the pattern set. The approach matters because the timing of pattern presentation and the ordering of layer development are treated as parts of the same learning process. Increasingly complex representation is tied to how the successive layers organize.
summary.tldr: Successive layers self-organize through lateral inhibition and coordinated pattern presentation, allowing higher levels to capture increasingly complex concepts.

title: Time-Sequential Self-Organization of Hierarchical Neural Networks

abstract: Artificial Neural Networks can be used to predict future returns of stocks in order to take financial decisions . Should one build a separate network for each stock or share the same network for all the stocks? In this paper we also explore other alternatives, in which some layers are shared and others are not shared. When the prediction of future returns for different stocks are viewed as different tasks, sharing some parameters across stocks is a form of multi-task learning. In a series of experiments with Canadian stocks, we obtain yearly returns that are more than 14% above various benchmarks. 1

paragraphs: Predicting future returns for several stocks raises an architectural question: how much should their predictors share? This paper considers a separate neural network for each stock, a common network across stocks, and intermediate designs. It frames each stock's prediction problem as a distinct task within a broader learning system.

The intermediate architectures share some layers while keeping others specific to individual stocks. Shared parameters allow the tasks to use common learned structure, while unshared parameters preserve stock-specific modeling. This makes the allocation of shared and individual components the central design choice. In this formulation, stock selection becomes an application of multi-task learning.

In experiments with Canadian stocks, the authors report yearly returns more than 14% above various benchmarks. That is the stated outcome of their experimental series, connecting the modeling question to financial decisions based on predicted returns. The paper's methodological contribution is the exploration of partial parameter sharing as an alternative between fully separate predictors and a single shared predictor for every stock.
summary.tldr: The paper explores shared and stock-specific neural-network layers, reporting yearly returns more than 14% above various benchmarks in Canadian-stock experiments.

title: Multi-Task Learning for Stock Selection

abstract: This article presents a new result about the size of a multilayer neural network computing real outputs for exact learning of a finite set of real samples. The architecture of the network is feedforward, with one hidden layer and several outputs. Starting from a fixed training set, we consider the network as a function of its weights. We derive, for a wide family of transfer functions, a lower and an upper bound on the number of hidden units for exact learning, given the size of the dataset and the dimensions of the input and output spaces.

The architecture of the network is feedforward, with one hidden layer and several outputs. Starting from a fixed training set, we consider the network as a function of its weights. We derive, for a wide family of transfer functions, a lower and an upper bound on the number of hidden units for exact learning, given the size of the dataset and the dimensions of the input and output spaces.

paragraphs: The paper asks how many hidden units a neural network needs to fit a finite collection of real-valued samples exactly. The architecture is a feedforward network with one hidden layer and several outputs. Exact learning here concerns matching the supplied samples, making network size the central object of analysis.

The authors hold the training set fixed and treat the network as a function of its weights. This shifts attention to whether suitable parameter choices can produce all the required outputs. For a broad family of transfer functions, they derive both a lower bound and an upper bound on the necessary number of hidden units.

The bounds depend on the number of samples and the dimensions of the input and output spaces. Together, they constrain the range of network sizes relevant to exact fitting: the lower bound expresses a size requirement, while the upper bound provides a sufficient size guarantee. The contribution is an analytic characterization of representational requirements for the stated architecture, connecting dataset dimensions to hidden-layer capacity.
summary.tldr: The paper derives lower and upper bounds on hidden-layer size for exactly fitting finite real-valued datasets.

title: Size of Multilayer Networks for Exact Learning: Analytic Approach

This allows us to concentrate on the feature extraction and neuronal coding properties of these rules. paragraphs: Different learning rules can produce selective responses in a model neuron, but comparisons become difficult when the inputs or architecture also change. This paper holds both fixed: every rule uses the same single-cell architecture and natural-scene environment. That setup focuses the comparison on how the learning rule shapes feature extraction and neural coding.

The rules include skewness maximization, kurtosis maximization, quadratic BCM learning, and single-cell independent component analysis. The authors also use a structure-removal method to investigate which parts of the input distribution influence the learned receptive fields. They find that these receptive fields depend on a small portion of the distribution, giving a more specific account of what drives the resulting selectivity.

When the distribution contains directions with kurtotic structure, quadratic BCM behaves similarly to kurtosis maximization. Its modification equations are computationally simpler, however. This connects a biologically motivated learning rule with a statistical objective under a stated condition. It suggests that similar feature selectivity can arise from learning procedures with different mathematical forms and computational demands.
summary.tldr: Controlled comparisons connect quadratic BCM learning with kurtosis maximization and identify concentrated statistical influences on receptive-field formation.

title: Receptive Field Formation in Natural Scene Environments: Comparison of Single Cell Learning Rules

abstract: In this paper, the technique of stacking, previously only used for supervised learning, is applied to unsupervised learning. Specifi(cid:173) cally, it is used for non-parametric multivariate density estimation, to combine finite mixture model and kernel density estimators. Ex(cid:173) perimental results on both simulated data and real world data sets clearly demonstrate that stacked density estimation outperforms other strategies such as choosing the single best model based on cross-validation, combining with uniform weights, and even the sin(cid:173) gle best model chosen by "cheating" by looking at the data used for independent testing.

paragraphs: This paper brings stacking into unsupervised learning. Its task is multivariate density estimation: describing how probability is distributed across observations with multiple variables. Instead of choosing one density estimator, the method combines finite mixture models and kernel density estimators into a stacked estimate.

The key question is whether a learned combination can do better than selecting a single model or treating all models equally. The authors evaluate this on both simulated and real-world datasets. Their comparisons include selecting a model through cross-validation and combining models with uniform weights, two different ways to avoid learning a more tailored combination.

The reported stacked estimates outperform those alternatives and even the single best model selected using the independent test data. That last comparison is an intentionally advantaged model-selection reference. Within the reported experiments, it indicates that the benefit of combining estimators goes beyond merely identifying which individual candidate works best. The result extends stacking's usefulness from supervised prediction to estimating probability distributions.
summary.tldr: Stacking density estimators outperforms individual-model selection and uniform averaging in the reported simulated and real-data experiments.

title: Stacked Density Estimation

abstract: We seek the scene interpretation that best explains image data. For example, we may want to infer the projected velocities (scene) which best explain two consecutive image frames (image). From synthetic data , we model the relationship between image and scene patches, and between a scene patch and neighboring scene patches. Given' a new image, we propagate likelihoods in a Markov network (ignoring the effect of loops) to infer the underlying scene. This yields an efficient method to form low-level scene interpretations. We demonstrate the technique for motion analysis and estimating high resolution images from low-resolution ones.

paragraphs: The paper treats low-level vision as a search for the scene interpretation that best explains observed images. For motion analysis, the hidden scene consists of projected velocities that account for successive frames. For resolution enhancement, the task is to estimate a high-resolution image from lower-resolution observations.

The method learns two kinds of relationships from synthetic data: how image patches relate to scene patches, and how neighboring scene patches relate to one another. The first supplies local evidence about possible interpretations. The second allows the interpretation of one region to be informed by nearby regions, connecting local estimates into a broader scene.

For a new image, the system propagates likelihoods through a Markov network to infer the hidden scene. This computation ignores the effect of loops in the network, an explicit approximation in the method. The authors demonstrate efficient scene estimation for both motion and resolution enhancement, showing how learned local relationships can support different visual inference tasks within one framework.
summary.tldr: A Markov network learns relationships among image and scene patches to estimate motion and reconstruct higher-resolution images.

title: Learning to Estimate Scenes from Images

abstract: We investigate a probabilistic framework for automatic speech recognition based on the intrinsic geometric properties of curves. In particular, we analyze the setting in which two variables-one continuous (~), one discrete (s )-evolve jointly in time. We sup(cid:173) pose that the vector ~ traces out a smooth multidimensional curve and that the variable s evolves stochastically as a function of the arc length traversed along this curve. Since arc length does not depend on the rate at which a curve is traversed, this gives rise to a family of Markov processes whose predictions, Pr[sl~]' are invariant to nonlinear warpings of time. We describe the use of such models, known as Markov processes on curves (MPCs), for automatic speech recognition, where ~ are acoustic feature trajec(cid:173) tories and s are phonetic transcriptions. On two tasks-recognizing New Jersey town names and connected alpha-digits- we find that MPCs yield lower word error rates than comparably trained hidden Markov models.

paragraphs: The paper develops a speech recognition framework that models the geometry of acoustic trajectories. It considers a continuous variable tracing a smooth multidimensional curve together with a discrete variable representing a phonetic transcription. The key choice is to make the discrete process evolve according to distance traveled along the curve, measured by arc length.

Arc length depends on the curve's geometry rather than how quickly it is traversed. Consequently, the resulting Markov processes on curves produce transcription predictions that are invariant to nonlinear changes in timing. Within this formulation, traversing the same acoustic curve at a varying rate does not change the predicted relationship between the trajectory and the transcription.

The authors apply the framework to recognizing New Jersey town names and connected alpha-digits. On both tasks, these models achieve lower word error rates than comparably trained hidden Markov models. The experiments support the usefulness of the geometric approach on those tasks, while the model's timing invariance explains the particular representational property the method is designed to provide.
summary.tldr: Markov processes indexed by acoustic curve length provide timing-invariant predictions and outperform comparably trained hidden Markov models on two speech tasks.

title: Markov Processes on Curves for Automatic Speech Recognition

abstract: An important issue in neural computing concerns the description of learning dynamics with macroscopic dynamical variables. Recen(cid:173) t progress on on-line learning only addresses the often unrealistic case of an infinite training set. We introduce a new framework to model batch learning of restricted sets of examples, widely applica(cid:173) ble to any learning cost function, and fully taking into account the temporal correlations introduced by the recycling of the examples. For illustration we analyze the effects of weight decay and early stopping during the learning of teacher-generated examples.

Recen(cid:173) t progress on on-line learning only addresses the often unrealistic case of an infinite training set. We introduce a new framework to model batch learning of restricted sets of examples, widely applica(cid:173) ble to any learning cost function, and fully taking into account the temporal correlations introduced by the recycling of the examples. paragraphs: The paper studies how to describe neural-network learning through macroscopic variables: quantities that summarize the learning process rather than tracking every detail separately. It addresses a gap in analyses of online learning that assume an infinite supply of training examples. Batch learning instead repeatedly uses a restricted collection of examples.

Reusing examples introduces temporal correlations. What happens during one part of training is connected to what happens later because the same data return. The authors introduce a framework that fully accounts for these correlations and is broadly applicable across learning cost functions. Its focus is therefore the dynamics generated by repeated exposure to a finite training set.

To illustrate the framework, the paper analyzes weight decay and early stopping when examples are generated by a teacher. These applications show how the framework can be used to study interventions in the learning process. The central contribution is the analytical treatment of finite-set reuse; the abstract identifies the phenomena examined without stating that either intervention always improves learning or specifying a universal preferred stopping point.
summary.tldr: A framework for batch-learning dynamics accounts for correlations caused by reusing finite data and illustrates their role in weight decay and early stopping.

title: Statistical Dynamics of Batch Learning

abstract: We propose a model for natural images in which the probability of an im- age is proportional to the product of the probabilities of some ﬁlter out- puts. We encourage the system to ﬁnd sparse features by using a Student- t distribution to model each ﬁlter output. If the t-distribution is used to model the combined outputs of sets of neurally adjacent ﬁlters, the sys- tem learns a topographic map in which the orientation, spatial frequency and location of the ﬁlters change smoothly across the map. Even though maximum likelihood learning is intractable in our model, the product form allows a relatively efﬁcient learning procedure that works well even for highly overcomplete sets of ﬁlters. Once the model has been learned it can be used as a prior to derive the “iterated Wiener ﬁlter” for the pur- pose of denoising images.

paragraphs: The paper models natural images by assigning probability proportional to a product of probabilities for filter responses. Each response is modeled with a Student-t distribution to encourage sparse features. This constructs an image model from the behavior of several filters acting on the same image.

When the Student-t distribution models combined responses from groups of neighboring filters, the system learns a topographic organization. Filter orientation, spatial frequency, and location vary smoothly across the resulting map. The grouping therefore links statistical modeling of filter outputs with an organized arrangement of the learned features.

Exact maximum-likelihood learning is intractable for this model. However, its product structure supports a relatively efficient learning procedure that works well even with highly overcomplete filter sets. After learning, the model can serve as an image prior from which an iterated Wiener filter is derived for denoising. The contribution connects sparse feature learning, smooth organization of neighboring filters, and an image-restoration application within a single probabilistic model.
summary.tldr: Products of Student-t filter-response models learn sparse, topographically organized image features and provide a prior for denoising.

title: Learning Sparse Topographic Representations with Products of Student-t Distributions

paragraphs: The paper investigates how individual participants contribute to the pattern of turn-taking in conversation. The authors collect auditory recordings through wearable sensors from twenty-three people, with sixty-six hours per person over two weeks. Automated speech and conversation detection identifies conversations, their participants, and who is speaking at each point.

They model paired turn-taking with a Mixed-Memory Markov Model. The model combines statistics describing each person’s own transitions with cross-transitions involving the conversational partner. Its mixture parameters express the contribution of individual behavior to the pair’s joint behavior, providing an estimated measure of conversational influence.

The estimated influence correlates significantly with betweenness centrality, a separate measure of a person’s importance in a social network. This association suggests that conversational influence may predict social influence. The result connects the fine-grained timing of speech with a broader network property, while the model gives a quantitative interpretation to how the two participants shape their shared turn-taking pattern.
summary.tldr: A mixed-memory model estimates influence from conversational turn-taking, and those estimates correlate with social-network betweenness centrality.

title: Modeling Conversational Dynamics as a Mixed-Memory Markov Process

abstract: We present a conditional temporal probabilistic framework for reconstructing 3D human motion in monocular video based on descriptors encoding image silhouette observations. For computational efficiency we restrict visual inference to low-dimensional kernel induced non-linear state spaces. Our methodology (kBME) combines kernel PCA-based non-linear dimensionality reduction (kPCA) and Conditional Bayesian Mixture of Experts (BME) in order to learn complex multivalued predictors between observations and model hidden states. This is necessary for accurate, inverse, visual perception inferences, where several probable, distant 3D solutions exist due to noise or the uncertainty of monocular perspective projection. Low-dimensional models are appropriate because many visual processes exhibit strong non-linear correlations in both the image observations and the target, hidden state variables. The learned predictors are temporally combined within a conditional graphical model in order to allow a principled propagation of uncertainty. We study several predictors and empirically show that the proposed algorithm positively compares with techniques based on regression, Kernel Dependency Estimation (KDE) or PCA alone, and gives results competitive to those of high-dimensional mixture predictors at a fraction of their computational cost. We show that the method successfully reconstructs the complex 3D motion of humans in real monocular video sequences.

paragraphs: Recovering three-dimensional human motion from a single video view is ambiguous: similar silhouettes can correspond to several different poses. This paper develops a conditional probabilistic framework that explicitly accommodates multiple plausible hidden states. Its observations are descriptors of image silhouettes, and its predictions are linked over time.

The method, called kBME, combines kernel principal component analysis with a Conditional Bayesian Mixture of Experts. The first component creates low-dimensional nonlinear representations; the second learns predictors that can associate one observation with multiple possible states. Restricting inference to these spaces targets computational efficiency, motivated by strong nonlinear correlations in visual observations and hidden motion variables.

A conditional graphical model combines the predictors across time and propagates uncertainty. Empirical comparisons favor the approach over the tested regression, Kernel Dependency Estimation, and PCA-only techniques. It also produces results competitive with high-dimensional mixture predictors at a fraction of their computational cost. Demonstrations on real monocular videos show successful reconstruction of complex human motion, supporting the combination of compact representations and explicit ambiguity modeling.
summary.tldr: A compact nonlinear probabilistic tracker reconstructs 3D human motion from monocular video while retaining multiple plausible poses and propagating uncertainty over time.

title: Conditional Visual Tracking in Kernel Space

abstract: Perceptual Bistability refers to the phenomenon of spontaneously switching between two or more interpretations of an image under continuous viewing. Although switching behavior is increasingly well characterized, the origins remain elusive. We propose that perceptual switching naturally arises from the brain's search for best interpretations while performing Bayesian inference. In particular, we propose that the brain explores a posterior distribution over image interpretations at a rapid time scale via a sampling-like process and updates its interpretation when a sampled interpretation is better than the discounted value of its current interpretation. We formalize the theory, explicitly derive switching rate distributions and discuss qualitative properties of the theory including the effect of changes in the posterior distribution on switching rates. Finally, predictions of the theory are shown to be consistent with measured changes in human switching dynamics to Necker cube stimuli induced by context.

paragraphs: An unchanged image can appear to switch between different interpretations during continuous viewing. This paper proposes that such perceptual switching emerges from the brain's search for good interpretations through Bayesian inference. The aim is to explain the dynamics of these switches, rather than simply describe which interpretations an image permits.

The theory assumes a rapid sampling-like exploration of a posterior distribution over possible interpretations. A switch occurs when a sampled alternative has greater value than a discounted version of the current interpretation. This rule connects continued exploration with the persistence and eventual replacement of the interpretation currently being experienced.

The authors formalize the account, derive switching-rate distributions, and examine how changes in the posterior affect switching. Its predictions agree with measured contextual changes in human switching behavior for Necker cube stimuli. This consistency supports the theory as an account of those dynamics, while the proposed sampling process remains a theoretical explanation of how the observed behavior could arise.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian sampling-like theory explains perceptual switching and predicts contextual changes consistent with Necker cube observations.

title: Theory and Dynamics of Perceptual Bistability

abstract: We design an on-line algorithm for Principal Component Analysis. In each trial the current instance is projected onto a probabilistically chosen low dimensional subspace. The total expected quadratic approximation error equals the total quadratic approximation error of the best subspace chosen in hindsight plus some additional term that grows linearly in dimension of the subspace but logarithmically in the dimension of the instances.
originalAbstract: We design an on-line algorithm for Principal Component Analysis. In each trial the current instance is projected onto a probabilistically chosen low dimensional subspace. The total expected quadratic approximation error equals the total quadratic approximation error of the best subspace chosen in hindsight plus some additional term that grows linearly in dimension of the subspace but logarithmically in the dimension of the instances.

paragraphs: This paper designs an online algorithm for principal component analysis. On each trial, it projects the current observation onto a low-dimensional subspace chosen probabilistically. The algorithm therefore makes a sequence of randomized projection choices as observations arrive, rather than relying on a single subspace selected with access to the complete sequence.

The theoretical comparison is with the best subspace that could have been chosen in hindsight. Performance is measured by total quadratic approximation error, which evaluates the discrepancy introduced by projecting the observations. The paper relates the algorithm's expected total error to that hindsight benchmark plus an additional term.

The additional term grows linearly with the dimension of the retained subspace and logarithmically with the dimension of the original observations. This separates two distinct costs: keeping more dimensions increases the term linearly, while increasing the input dimension affects it only logarithmically. The guarantee concerns expected cumulative error for the randomized algorithm, providing a precise account of the cost of making projection decisions online.
summary.tldr: Randomized online PCA has an expected-error guarantee whose extra term grows only logarithmically with input dimension.

title: Randomized PCA Algorithms with Regret Bounds that are Logarithmic in the Dimension

abstract: We formulate the problem of bipartite graph inference as a supervised learning problem, and propose a new method to solve it from the viewpoint of distance metric learning. The method involves the learning of two mappings of the heterogeneous objects to a unified Euclidean space representing the network topology of the bipartite graph, where the graph is easy to infer. The algorithm can be formulated as an optimization problem in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space. We report encouraging results on the problem of compound-protein interaction network reconstruction from chemical structure data and genomic sequence data.
originalAbstract: We formulate the problem of bipartite graph inference as a supervised learning problem, and propose a new method to solve it from the viewpoint of distance metric learning. The method involves the learning of two mappings of the heterogeneous objects to a unified Euclidean space representing the network topology of the bipartite graph, where the graph is easy to infer. The algorithm can be formulated as an optimization problem in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space. We report encouraging results on the problem of compound-protein interaction network reconstruction from chemical structure data and genomic sequence data.

paragraphs: A bipartite graph represents links between two different types of objects. This paper treats reconstructing such links as supervised learning, using known information to learn how the two object types relate. Its central idea is to approach graph inference through distance metric learning, so the representation of objects supports predicting their connections.

The method learns two mappings, one for each kind of object, into a shared Euclidean space. That space is intended to represent the graph's network structure and make its links easier to infer. Separate mappings allow heterogeneous descriptions to enter the model while producing representations that can be compared within the same geometric setting.

The learning algorithm can be formulated as optimization in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space. The authors apply it to reconstructing compound–protein interaction networks using chemical structures and genomic sequences, and report encouraging results. This application illustrates the purpose of the two mappings: distinct forms of biological information can contribute to a common representation organized around the interactions being predicted.
summary.tldr: Two learned mappings place heterogeneous objects in a shared space to support supervised bipartite-link prediction.

title: Supervised Bipartite Graph Inference

abstract: From an information-theoretic perspective, a noisy transmission system such as a visual Brain-Computer Interface (BCI) speller could benefit from the use of error-correcting codes. However, optimizing the code solely according to the maximal minimum-Hamming-distance criterion tends to lead to an overall increase in target frequency of target stimuli, and hence a significantly reduced average target-to-target interval (TTI), leading to difficulties in classifying the individual event-related potentials (ERPs) due to overlap and refractory effects. Clearly any change to the stimulus setup must also respect the possible psychophysiological consequences. Here we report new EEG data from experiments in which we explore stimulus types and codebooks in a within-subject design, finding an interaction between the two factors. Our data demonstrate that the traditional, row-column code has particular spatial properties that lead to better performance than one would expect from its TTIs and Hamming-distances alone, but nonetheless error-correcting codes can improve performance provided the right stimulus type is used.

paragraphs: A visual brain-computer interface speller must identify intended selections from noisy brain responses. Error-correcting codes appear useful because they can make transmitted choices easier to distinguish despite errors. This paper examines why choosing a code purely for its mathematical separation can conflict with the physiology of the responses being measured.

Maximizing minimum Hamming distance tends to increase how often target stimuli appear, shortening the interval between them. Closely spaced responses can overlap, and refractory effects can make individual event-related potentials harder to classify. The authors collect EEG data in a within-subject experiment that varies both stimulus type and codebook, allowing them to examine how these design choices interact.

The results show that stimulus type changes the effect of code design. The traditional row-column code benefits from spatial properties that its target intervals and Hamming distances alone do not explain. Error-correcting codes can nevertheless improve performance with an appropriate stimulus type. The practical implication is that coding and stimulus presentation need to be designed together, with their psychophysiological interaction taken into account.
summary.tldr: Error-correcting codes can improve BCI spelling when stimulus design accommodates how closely spaced brain responses interact.

title: Effects of Stimulus Type and of Error-Correcting Code Design on BCI Speller Performance

abstract: A striking aspect of cortical neural networks is the divergence of a relatively small number of input channels from the peripheral sensory apparatus into a large number of cortical neurons, an over-complete representation strategy. Cortical neurons are then connected by a sparse network of lateral synapses. Here we propose that such architecture may increase the persistence of the representation of an incoming stimulus, or a percept. We demonstrate that for a family of networks in which the receptive field of each neuron is re-expressed by its outgoing connections, a represented percept can remain constant despite changing activity. We term this choice of connectivity REceptive FIeld REcombination (REFIRE) networks. The sparse REFIRE network may serve as a high-dimensional integrator and a biologically plausible model of the local cortical circuit.

paragraphs: Cortical circuits expand relatively few sensory input channels into activity across many neurons, producing an over-complete representation. Those neurons are connected through sparse lateral synapses. This paper proposes that the combination of expanded representation and sparse recurrent connectivity may help a percept persist after an incoming stimulus has been represented.

The authors study a family of networks in which each neuron's receptive field is re-expressed through its outgoing connections. They call this connectivity arrangement REceptive FIeld REcombination, or REFIRE. For this family, they demonstrate that the represented percept can remain unchanged even while neural activity changes. Persistence therefore concerns the information represented by the network, not a requirement that every neuron maintain constant activity.

The paper suggests that sparse REFIRE networks may act as high-dimensional integrators and may provide a biologically plausible model of local cortical circuitry. These are proposed implications of the architecture. The demonstrated result is the possibility of preserving a percept under changing activity when the specified connectivity relationship holds.
summary.tldr: REFIRE connectivity allows an over-complete recurrent network to preserve a represented percept even as its neural activity changes.

title: Over-complete representations on recurrent neural networks can support persistent percepts

abstract: Diagnosis of Alzheimer's disease (AD) at the early stage of the disease development is of great clinical importance. Current clinical assessment that relies primarily on cognitive measures proves low sensitivity and specificity. The fast growing neuroimaging techniques hold great promise. Research so far has focused on single neuroimaging modalities. However, as different modalities provide complementary measures for the same disease pathology, fusion of multi-modality data may increase the statistical power in identification of disease-related brain regions. This is especially true for early AD, at which stage the disease-related regions are most likely to be weak-effect regions that are difficult to be detected from a single modality alone. We propose a sparse composite linear discriminant analysis model (SCLDA) for identification of disease-related brain regions of early AD from multi-modality data. SCLDA uses a novel formulation that decomposes each LDA parameter into a product of a common parameter shared by all the modalities and a parameter specific to each modality, which enables joint analysis of all the modalities and borrowing strength from one another. We prove that this formulation is equivalent to a penalized likelihood with non-convex regularization, which can be solved by the DC ((difference of convex functions) programming. We show that in using the DC programming, the property of the non-convex regularization in terms of preserving weak-effect features can be nicely revealed. We perform extensive simulations to show that SCLDA outperforms existing competing algorithms on feature selection, especially on the ability for identifying weak-effect features. We apply SCLDA to the Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) and Positron Emission Tomography (PET) images of 49 AD patients and 67 normal controls (NC). Our study identifies disease-related brain regions consistent with findings in the AD literature.

paragraphs: The paper addresses the identification of brain regions associated with early Alzheimer’s disease. Signals from these regions may be weak in any single imaging modality. Because different modalities provide complementary measurements of disease pathology, analyzing them together may improve the ability to detect regions that would be difficult to identify separately.

This structure lets modalities contribute jointly while retaining their differences. The authors prove an equivalent formulation using a non-convex penalty and solve it through difference-of-convex programming, which also reveals the penalty’s ability to preserve weak-effect features.

Simulations show better feature selection than the compared algorithms, particularly for weak-effect features. The authors also analyze MRI and PET images from 49 patients with Alzheimer’s disease and 67 normal controls. The identified brain regions agree with findings in the Alzheimer’s literature. These results support the model’s use for identifying disease-related regions through combined imaging evidence.
summary.tldr: A sparse model combining imaging modalities improves weak-feature selection in simulations and identifies Alzheimer’s-related brain regions consistent with prior findings.

title: Identifying Alzheimer's Disease-Related Brain Regions from Multi-Modality Neuroimaging Data using Sparse Composite Linear Discrimination Analysis

abstract: Partially-observable Markov decision processes (POMDPs) provide a powerful model for real-world sequential decision-making problems. In recent years, point- based value iteration methods have proven to be extremely effective techniques for ﬁnding (approximately) optimal dynamic programming solutions to POMDPs when an initial set of belief states is known. However, no point-based work has provided exact point-based backups for both continuous state and observation spaces, which we tackle in this paper. Our key insight is that while there may be an inﬁnite number of possible observations, there are only a ﬁnite number of observation partitionings that are relevant for optimal decision-making when a ﬁnite, ﬁxed set of reachable belief states is known. To this end, we make two important contributions: (1) we show how previous exact symbolic dynamic pro- gramming solutions for continuous state MDPs can be generalized to continu- ous state POMDPs with discrete observations, and (2) we show how this solution can be further extended via recently developed symbolic methods to continuous state and observations to derive the minimal relevant observation partitioning for potentially correlated, multivariate observation spaces. We demonstrate proof-of- concept results on uni- and multi-variate state and observation steam plant control.

paragraphs: Partially observable Markov decision processes support sequential decisions when the true state is uncertain. Point-based methods plan using selected belief states, which describe uncertainty about that state. This paper addresses exact point-based backup operations when both states and observations are continuous, a setting where infinitely many possible observations complicate dynamic programming.

The key insight depends on having a finite, fixed set of reachable belief states. Although observations may range continuously, only finitely many observation partitionings matter for optimal decisions over that set. The authors first extend exact symbolic dynamic programming from continuous-state MDPs to POMDPs with discrete observations, then extend the approach to continuous observations.

The symbolic methods derive the minimal relevant observation partitioning, including for multivariate observation spaces with possible correlations. Proof-of-concept demonstrations use steam-plant control problems with univariate and multivariate states and observations. The contribution is exact backup computation within the stated point-based setting; the finite belief-set condition is central to making the continuous observation space manageable.
summary.tldr: Symbolic observation partitioning enables exact point-based POMDP backups for continuous states and observations given a finite, fixed reachable belief set.

title: Symbolic Dynamic Programming for Continuous State and Observation POMDPs

abstract: Multi-dimensional latent variable models can capture the many latent factors in a text corpus, such as topic, author perspective and sentiment. We introduce factorial LDA, a multi-dimensional latent variable model in which a document is influenced by K different factors, and each word token depends on a K-dimensional vector of latent variables. Our model incorporates structured word priors and learns a sparse product of factors. Experiments on research abstracts show that our model can learn latent factors such as research topic, scientific discipline, and focus (e.g. methods vs. applications.) Our modeling improvements reduce test perplexity and improve human interpretability of the discovered factors.

We introduce factorial LDA, a multi-dimensional latent variable model in which a document is influenced by K different factors, and each word token depends on a K-dimensional vector of latent variables. Our model incorporates structured word priors and learns a sparse product of factors. paragraphs: A document’s words reflect more than its topic: they can also reveal discipline, perspective, sentiment, or methodological focus. Standard single-factor topic representations can entangle those influences. Factorial LDA models several latent dimensions simultaneously so different sources of variation can be separated.

Each document is influenced by K factors, and each word token depends on a K-dimensional latent-variable assignment. Structured word priors and a sparse product of factors guide the model toward an interpretable combination. This lets a token reflect several kinds of contextual influence without requiring them to be collapsed into one topic label.

On research abstracts, the model discovers factors corresponding to research topic, scientific discipline, and methods-versus-applications focus. It improves both held-out perplexity and human interpretability. The contribution links a richer generative structure to more useful corpus organization, showing that separating latent dimensions can help prediction and explanation together.
summary.tldr: Factorial LDA separates multiple influences on documents through sparse latent-factor products, improving perplexity and interpretability.

title: Factorial LDA: Sparse Multi-Dimensional Text Models

abstract: State-space models are successfully used in many areas of science, engineering and economics to model time series and dynamical systems. We present a fully Bayesian approach to inference and learning in nonlinear nonparametric state-space models. We place a Gaussian process prior over the transition dynamics, resulting in a flexible model able to capture complex dynamical phenomena. However, to enable efficient inference, we marginalize over the dynamics of the model and instead infer directly the joint smoothing distribution through the use of specially tailored Particle Markov Chain Monte Carlo samplers. Once an approximation of the smoothing distribution is computed, the state transition predictive distribution can be formulated analytically. We make use of sparse Gaussian process models to greatly reduce the computational complexity of the approach.

paragraphs: State-space models describe changing systems through underlying states and the rules governing their evolution. This paper develops a fully Bayesian approach for nonlinear models whose transition dynamics are not restricted to a fixed parametric form. A Gaussian process prior supplies the flexibility needed to represent complex dynamical behavior.

The main inference choice is to integrate out the transition dynamics and work directly with the joint smoothing distribution, which represents uncertainty about the underlying sequence of states given the observations. Specially designed particle Markov chain Monte Carlo samplers approximate this distribution. This organizes inference around state trajectories while accounting for uncertainty in the dynamics.

After approximating the smoothing distribution, the method can express the predictive distribution for state transitions analytically. Sparse Gaussian process models further reduce computational complexity. Together, these choices connect flexible modeling, Bayesian uncertainty, and more efficient computation: the approach learns about hidden state sequences without requiring the dynamics to be explicitly retained throughout the inference procedure.
summary.tldr: Particle MCMC and marginalized Gaussian process dynamics enable Bayesian inference in flexible nonlinear state-space models.

title: Bayesian Inference and Learning in Gaussian Process State-Space Models with Particle MCMC

abstract: We investigate a spiking neuron model of multisensory integration. Multiple stimuli from different sensory modalities are encoded by a single neural circuit comprised of a multisensory bank of receptive fields in cascade with a population of biophysical spike generators. We demonstrate that stimuli of different dimensions can be faithfully multiplexed and encoded in the spike domain and derive tractable algorithms for decoding each stimulus from the common pool of spikes. We also show that the identification of multisensory processing in a single neuron is dual to the recovery of stimuli encoded with a population of multisensory neurons, and prove that only a projection of the circuit onto input stimuli can be identified. We provide an example of multisensory integration using natural audio and video and discuss the performance of the proposed decoding and identification algorithms.

Multiple stimuli from different sensory modalities are encoded by a single neural circuit comprised of a multisensory bank of receptive fields in cascade with a population of biophysical spike generators. We demonstrate that stimuli of different dimensions can be faithfully multiplexed and encoded in the spike domain and derive tractable algorithms for decoding each stimulus from the common pool of spikes. We also show that the identification of multisensory processing in a single neuron is dual to the recovery of stimuli encoded with a population of multisensory neurons, and prove that only a projection of the circuit onto input stimuli can be identified. We provide an example of multisensory integration using natural audio and video and discuss the performance of the proposed decoding and identification algorithms.

paragraphs: A neural circuit can receive several kinds of sensory input while communicating through spikes. This paper studies how a single circuit can encode multiple stimuli together and how those inputs can subsequently be recovered. Its model combines a bank of multisensory receptive fields with a population of biophysical spike generators.

The authors demonstrate that stimuli with different dimensions can be faithfully combined in a shared spike representation. They derive tractable algorithms that recover each stimulus from the common spike pool. This makes the encoding question concrete: the representation must preserve enough information to separate the different inputs during decoding.

The paper also connects decoding to identifying the sensory processing performed by a neuron. It establishes a duality between identifying a single multisensory neuron and recovering inputs encoded by a population. A proved limit is that identification reveals only the circuit's projection onto the input stimuli, constraining what those observations can establish about the circuit. An example using natural audio and video illustrates the framework, and the authors discuss decoding and identification performance.
summary.tldr: A spiking circuit model supports joint multisensory encoding and decoding while establishing a limit on identifying the underlying circuit.

title: Multisensory Encoding, Decoding, and Identification

abstract: The prominence of weakly labeled data gives rise to a growing demand for object detection methods that can cope with minimal supervision. We propose an approach that automatically identifies discriminative configurations of visual patterns that are characteristic of a given object class. We formulate the problem as a constrained submodular optimization problem and demonstrate the benefits of the discovered configurations in remedying mislocalizations and finding informative positive and negative training examples. Together, these lead to state-of-the-art weakly-supervised detection results on the challenging PASCAL VOC dataset.
originalAbstract: The prominence of weakly labeled data gives rise to a growing demand for object detection methods that can cope with minimal supervision. We propose an approach that automatically identifies discriminative configurations of visual patterns that are characteristic of a given object class. We formulate the problem as a constrained submodular optimization problem and demonstrate the benefits of the discovered configurations in remedying mislocalizations and finding informative positive and negative training examples. Together, these lead to state-of-the-art weakly-supervised detection results on the challenging PASCAL VOC dataset.

paragraphs: Object detection with weak labels requires learning useful visual evidence from limited supervision. This paper proposes automatically discovering configurations of visual patterns that distinguish an object class. The focus on configurations makes relationships among patterns part of the evidence used to recognize and locate objects.

The authors formulate discovery as a constrained submodular optimization problem. The resulting configurations serve two purposes in the detection process: helping correct mislocalizations and identifying informative positive and negative training examples. These roles connect pattern discovery to both where a detector places an object and which examples are useful for learning.

Together, these contributions produce results reported as state of the art for weakly supervised detection on PASCAL VOC. The findings support using discovered configurations as a source of guidance when detailed supervision is limited. The approach matters because it makes the learned visual structure useful beyond class discrimination alone, applying it to localization errors and training-example selection within the same overall detection task.
summary.tldr: Discovering discriminative visual-pattern configurations improves localization and training-example selection, yielding strong weakly supervised detection results on PASCAL VOC.

title: Weakly-supervised Discovery of Visual Pattern Configurations

abstract: We introduce a method to learn a hierarchy of successively more abstract representations of complex data based on optimizing an information-theoretic objective. Intuitively, the optimization searches for a set of latent factors that best explain the correlations in the data as measured by multivariate mutual information. The method is unsupervised, requires no model assumptions, and scales linearly with the number of variables which makes it an attractive approach for very high dimensional systems. We demonstrate that Correlation Explanation (CorEx) automatically discovers meaningful structure for data from diverse sources including personality tests, DNA, and human language.

paragraphs: Correlation Explanation, or CorEx, learns hidden structure by asking which latent factors best account for dependencies among observed variables. The method optimizes an information-theoretic objective based on multivariate mutual information. In plain language, it searches for representations that explain why several parts of the data vary together.

The method builds a hierarchy of increasingly abstract representations. This makes the goal broader than finding a single grouping of variables: successive representations organize the dependence structure at higher levels. Learning is unsupervised, so the structure is discovered without target labels. The abstract describes the approach as requiring no model assumptions, with its search instead guided by the information objective.

The computation scales linearly with the number of variables, which makes the approach attractive for systems with many measured dimensions. The authors demonstrate meaningful discovered structure in personality tests, DNA, and human language. These examples show the method’s applicability across different kinds of data. Its explanatory meaning here concerns statistical correlations: the latent factors organize dependencies in the observations.
summary.tldr: CorEx learns hierarchical latent representations by explaining multivariate correlations, with computation that scales linearly in the number of variables.

title: Discovering Structure in High-Dimensional Data Through Correlation Explanation

abstract: Restricted Boltzmann machines are undirected neural networks which have been shown tobe effective in many applications, including serving as initializations fortraining deep multi-layer neural networks. One of the main reasons for their success is theexistence of efficient and practical stochastic algorithms, such as contrastive divergence,for unsupervised training. We propose an alternative deterministic iterative procedure based on an improved mean field method from statistical physics known as the Thouless-Anderson-Palmer approach. We demonstrate that our algorithm provides performance equal to, and sometimes superior to, persistent contrastive divergence, while also providing a clear and easy to evaluate objective function. We believe that this strategycan be easily generalized to other models as well as to more accurate higher-order approximations, paving the way for systematic improvements in training Boltzmann machineswith hidden units.

paragraphs: Restricted Boltzmann machines are undirected neural networks used for unsupervised learning, including initialization of deeper networks. Their practical usefulness has depended partly on stochastic training procedures such as contrastive divergence. This paper develops a deterministic iterative alternative, changing how training is carried out while retaining the same model family.

The method uses the Thouless-Anderson-Palmer approach, an improved mean-field approximation from statistical physics. This supplies a basis for iterative training together with a clear objective function that is easy to evaluate. Having an accessible objective gives the procedure an explicit quantity through which its training behavior can be assessed.

The authors demonstrate performance equal to, and sometimes better than, persistent contrastive divergence. This supports deterministic mean-field training as a practical alternative in the evaluations reported. They also suggest that the strategy could extend to other models and to more accurate higher-order approximations. Those extensions are presented as a promising direction, with the demonstrated contribution being the proposed training procedure and its comparison with persistent contrastive divergence.
summary.tldr: A deterministic TAP-based training procedure matches or sometimes exceeds persistent contrastive divergence while providing an easily evaluated objective.

title: Training Restricted Boltzmann Machine via the ￼Thouless-Anderson-Palmer free energy

abstract: We propose a novel distribution that generalizes the Multinomial distribution to enable dependencies between dimensions. Our novel distribution is based on the parametric form of the Poisson MRF model [Yang et al., 2012] but is fundamentally different because of the domain restriction to a fixed-length vector like in a Multinomial where the number of trials is fixed or known. Thus, we propose the Fixed-Length Poisson MRF (LPMRF) distribution. We develop methods to estimate the likelihood and log partition function (i.e. the log normalizing constant), which was not developed for the Poisson MRF model. In addition, we propose novel mixture and topic models that use LPMRF as a base distribution and discuss the similarities and differences with previous topic models such as the recently proposed Admixture of Poisson MRFs [Inouye et al., 2014]. We show the effectiveness of our LPMRF distribution over Multinomial models by evaluating the test set perplexity on a dataset of abstracts and Wikipedia. Qualitatively, we show that the positive dependencies discovered by LPMRF are interesting and intuitive. Finally, we show that our algorithms are fast and have good scaling (code available online).

paragraphs: The paper proposes a distribution for count vectors whose total count is fixed or known, as in a multinomial model. Its aim is to enrich the multinomial with dependencies between dimensions. Called the Fixed-Length Poisson MRF, or LPMRF, it uses the parametric form of a Poisson Markov random field while restricting the domain to vectors with the specified total.

That domain restriction is central to the proposed distribution. The authors develop methods to estimate its likelihood and log partition function, the latter being the logarithm of the normalizing constant. These calculations support evaluating the probabilistic model. They also build mixture and topic models with LPMRF as their base distribution and discuss how these relate to earlier topic models.

Evaluation on abstracts and Wikipedia uses test-set perplexity to demonstrate effectiveness relative to multinomial models. Qualitative results show positive dependencies that the authors describe as intuitive and interesting. The paper also reports fast algorithms with good scaling. Together, the results support modeling relationships among counts while retaining the fixed-total structure.
summary.tldr: LPMRF extends fixed-total count modeling with dependencies between dimensions and supports mixture and topic models.

title: Fixed-Length Poisson MRF: Adding Dependencies to the Multinomial

abstract: Abstract We describe a novel optimization method for finite sums (such as empirical risk minimization problems) building on the recently introduced SAGA method. Our method achieves an accelerated convergence rate on strongly convex smooth problems. Our method has only one parameter (a step size), and is radically simpler than other accelerated methods for finite sums. Additionally it can be applied when the terms are non-smooth, yielding a method applicable in many areas where operator splitting methods would traditionally be applied.
originalAbstract: Abstract We describe a novel optimization method for finite sums (such as empirical risk minimization problems) building on the recently introduced SAGA method. Our method achieves an accelerated convergence rate on strongly convex smooth problems. Our method has only one parameter (a step size), and is radically simpler than other accelerated methods for finite sums. Additionally it can be applied when the terms are non-smooth, yielding a method applicable in many areas where operator splitting methods would traditionally be applied.

paragraphs: Many learning objectives combine a finite collection of terms into one quantity to minimize. Empirical risk minimization is an example of this form. This paper introduces an optimization method for such finite sums, building on SAGA. Its central aim is to combine accelerated convergence with a procedure that remains simple to use.

The acceleration result applies when the objective is smooth and strongly convex. These conditions are part of the guarantee: the abstract does not claim the same accelerated rate for every finite-sum objective. The method has only one parameter, its step size, and the authors describe it as substantially simpler than other accelerated approaches for finite sums.

The method can also handle objectives whose individual terms are nonsmooth. That broadens its applicability to problems often addressed using operator splitting methods. The contribution therefore has two connected parts: a convergence improvement under the stated smoothness and convexity conditions, and a simple optimization approach that also extends to a wider class of objectives.
summary.tldr: A method built on SAGA offers accelerated convergence for smooth, strongly convex finite sums with only a step-size parameter.

title: A Simple Practical Accelerated Method for Finite Sums

abstract: Clustering large datasets is a fundamental problem with a number of applications in machine learning. Data is often collected on different sites and clustering needs to be performed in a distributed manner with low communication. We would like the quality of the clustering in the distributed setting to match that in the centralized setting for which all the data resides on a single site. In this work, we study both graph and geometric clustering problems in two distributed models: (1) a point-to-point model, and (2) a model with a broadcast channel. We give protocols in both models which we show are nearly optimal by proving almost matching communication lower bounds. Our work highlights the surprising power of a broadcast channel for clustering problems; roughly speaking, to cluster n points or n vertices in a graph distributed across s servers, for a worst-case partitioning the communication complexity in a point-to-point model is n*s, while in the broadcast model it is n + s. We implement our algorithms and demonstrate this phenomenon on real life datasets, showing that our algorithms are also very efficient in practice.

Data is often collected on different sites and clustering needs to be performed in a distributed manner with low communication. We would like the quality of the clustering in the distributed setting to match that in the centralized setting for which all the data resides on a single site. In this work, we study both graph and geometric clustering problems in two distributed models: (1) a point-to-point model, and (2) a model with a broadcast channel. We give protocols in both models which we show are nearly optimal by proving almost matching communication lower bounds. Our work highlights the surprising power of a broadcast channel for clustering problems; roughly speaking, to cluster n points or n vertices in a graph distributed across s servers, for a worst-case partitioning the communication complexity in a point-to-point model is n*s, while in the broadcast model it is n + s. We implement our algorithms and demonstrate this phenomenon on real life datasets, showing that our algorithms are also very efficient in practice.

paragraphs: When data are spread across servers, clustering quality and communication cost must be considered together. The paper studies how to obtain clustering quality comparable to a centralized setting without simply gathering everything at one location. It covers both geometric data points and graphs under two communication models.

In one model, servers communicate through point-to-point connections; in the other, they have a broadcast channel. The authors provide protocols for both settings and prove communication lower bounds that nearly match their costs. These lower bounds matter because they show that substantially reducing communication further is constrained by the problem itself.

For worst-case data partitioning, the abstract summarizes the contrast as roughly n times s communication in the point-to-point model versus n plus s with broadcasting, for n points or vertices across s servers. This is a statement about the studied models and worst-case partitions. Implementations on real datasets demonstrate the broadcast advantage and show that the proposed algorithms are efficient in practice.
summary.tldr: Nearly matching upper and lower bounds show that broadcasting can sharply reduce the communication needed for distributed clustering.

title: Communication-Optimal Distributed Clustering

abstract: Often in machine learning, data are collected as a combination of multiple conditions, e.g., the voice recordings of multiple persons, each labeled with an ID. How could we build a model that captures the latent information related to these conditions and generalize to a new one with few data? We present a new model called Latent Variable Multiple Output Gaussian Processes (LVMOGP) that allows to jointly model multiple conditions for regression and generalize to a new condition with a few data points at test time. LVMOGP infers the posteriors of Gaussian processes together with a latent space representing the information about different conditions. We derive an efficient variational inference method for LVMOGP for which the computational complexity is as low as sparse Gaussian processes. We show that LVMOGP significantly outperforms related Gaussian process methods on various tasks with both synthetic and real data.

paragraphs: Supervised datasets often combine observations from several conditions, such as recordings from different people. A condition identifier tells the model which observations belong together, but does not directly describe the hidden properties that distinguish conditions. This paper asks how to learn those properties jointly and use them to handle a new condition with only a few observations.

The proposed Latent Variable Multiple Output Gaussian Process model combines regression across conditions with a learned latent space. It infers uncertainty over the Gaussian processes together with representations of the conditions. This lets the model capture information about their differences as part of the regression problem, rather than treating the identifiers alone as a complete description.

The authors derive a variational inference method whose computational complexity is as low as that of sparse Gaussian processes. They report significant improvements over related Gaussian process methods on tasks involving synthetic and real data. The contribution combines adaptation to sparsely observed new conditions with an inference procedure designed to keep the joint latent modeling computationally practical.
summary.tldr: A Gaussian process model learns latent relationships among conditions to support regression and adaptation to new conditions from few observations.

title: Efficient Modeling of Latent Information in Supervised Learning using Gaussian Processes

abstract: The $k$-means clustering algorithm is a ubiquitous tool in data mining and machine learning that shows promising performance. However, its high computational cost has hindered its applications in broad domains. Researchers have successfully addressed these obstacles with dimensionality reduction methods. Recently, [1] develop a state-of-the-art random projection (RP) method for faster $k$-means clustering. Their method delivers many improvements over other dimensionality reduction methods. For example, compared to the advanced singular value decomposition based feature extraction approach, [1] reduce the running time by a factor of $\min \{n,d\}\epsilon^2 log(d)/k$ for data matrix $X \in \mathbb{R}^{n\times d} $ with $n$ data points and $d$ features, while losing only a factor of one in approximation accuracy. Unfortunately, they still require $\mathcal{O}(\frac{ndk}{\epsilon^2log(d)})$ for matrix multiplication and this cost will be prohibitive for large values of $n$ and $d$. To break this bottleneck, we carefully build a sparse embedded $k$-means clustering algorithm which requires $\mathcal{O}(nnz(X))$ ($nnz(X)$ denotes the number of non-zeros in $X$) for fast matrix multiplication. Moreover, our proposed algorithm improves on [1]'s results for approximation accuracy by a factor of one. Our empirical studies corroborate our theoretical findings, and demonstrate that our approach is able to significantly accelerate $k$-means clustering, while achieving satisfactory clustering performance.

paragraphs: Reducing the number of features can make k-means clustering faster, but producing that reduced representation can itself be expensive. This paper targets a matrix-multiplication bottleneck in a prior random-projection approach. That bottleneck becomes costly when a dataset has both many observations and many features.

The proposed sparse embedding reduces the multiplication cost to O(nnz(X)), where nnz(X) counts the nonzero entries of the data matrix. This ties that stage's work to the amount of nonzero input rather than the full combination of data dimensions appearing in the previous bound. The paper also establishes an improved approximation-accuracy result relative to the referenced random-projection method.

Empirical studies corroborate the theoretical findings, showing substantial acceleration of k-means while retaining satisfactory clustering performance. The computational guarantee applies specifically to the embedding's matrix multiplication, so its meaning is more precise than a claim that every part of clustering takes input-linear time. The contribution addresses the cost of preparing a smaller representation as well as the quality of clustering with it.
summary.tldr: Sparse embedding speeds a key matrix-multiplication step for k-means and improves the stated approximation guarantee over prior random projection.

title: Sparse Embedded $k$-Means Clustering

abstract: Under/overestimation of state/action values are harmful for reinforcement learning agents. In this paper, we show that a state/action value estimated using the Bellman equation can be decomposed to a weighted sum of path-wise values that follow log-normal distributions. Since log-normal distributions are skewed, the distribution of estimated state/action values can also be skewed, leading to an imbalanced likelihood of under/overestimation. The degree of such imbalance can vary greatly among actions and policies within a single problem instance, making the agent prone to select actions/policies that have inferior expected return and higher likelihood of overestimation. We present a comprehensive analysis to such skewness, examine its factors and impacts through both theoretical and empirical results, and discuss the possible ways to reduce its undesirable effects.

We present a comprehensive analysis to such skewness, examine its factors and impacts through both theoretical and empirical results, and discuss the possible ways to reduce its undesirable effects.

paragraphs: Reinforcement-learning agents choose actions using estimates of future value, so systematic overestimation or underestimation can harm their decisions. This paper investigates the shape of the distributions behind those estimates. It shows that a value estimated through the Bellman equation can be expressed as a weighted sum of path-wise values that follow log-normal distributions.

Log-normal distributions are skewed, and the resulting state or action value estimates can also be skewed. Consequently, overestimation and underestimation need not be equally likely. The degree of this imbalance can differ substantially between actions and policies even within the same problem, affecting how their estimated values compare.

That variation can make an agent prone to favor an action or policy with lower expected return but a greater likelihood of overestimation. The authors analyze the causes and consequences of skewness through theoretical and empirical results, and discuss possible ways to reduce its harmful effects. The contribution highlights distributional shape as a source of misleading value comparisons, beyond simply considering the size of estimation errors.
summary.tldr: Skewed value-estimate distributions can make overestimation uneven across actions and lead reinforcement-learning agents toward inferior choices.

title: Log-normality and Skewness of Estimated State/Action Values in Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Abstraction and realization are bilateral processes that are key in deriving intelligence and creativity. In many domains, the two processes are approached through \emph{rules}: high-level principles that reveal invariances within similar yet diverse examples. Under a probabilistic setting for discrete input spaces, we focus on the rule realization problem which generates input sample distributions that follow the given rules. More ambitiously, we go beyond a mechanical realization that takes whatever is given, but instead ask for proactively selecting reasonable rules to realize. This goal is demanding in practice, since the initial rule set may not always be consistent and thus intelligent compromises are needed. We formulate both rule realization and selection as two strongly connected components within a single and symmetric bi-convex problem, and derive an efficient algorithm that works at large scale. Taking music compositional rules as the main example throughout the paper, we demonstrate our model's efficiency in not only music realization (composition) but also music interpretation and understanding (analysis).

paragraphs: High-level rules describe common principles across examples, but generating examples from rules raises a different problem. This paper studies rule realization in discrete input spaces: constructing probability distributions over samples that follow supplied rules. It also asks which rules should be realized when the initial collection contains inconsistencies.

Rule selection and realization are formulated as connected parts of one symmetric bi-convex optimization problem. This couples the choice of reasonable rules with the construction of distributions that express them. The formulation makes compromise part of the task, addressing situations where accepting every proposed rule would not produce a consistent set of requirements.

The authors derive an efficient algorithm intended to operate at large scale. Music composition rules serve as the main example, and demonstrations cover both generating music and interpreting or understanding it. These applications illustrate the two directions of the framework: realizing principles through examples and using those principles to analyze examples. The contribution brings both directions into a shared probabilistic formulation.
summary.tldr: A joint probabilistic formulation selects compatible rules and generates distributions that realize them, with applications to music composition and analysis.

title: Probabilistic Rule Realization and Selection

abstract: For the purpose of learning on graphs, we hunt for a graph feature representation that exhibit certain uniqueness, stability and sparsity properties while also being amenable to fast computation. This leads to the discovery of family of graph spectral distances (denoted as FGSD) and their based graph feature representations, which we prove to possess most of these desired properties. To both evaluate the quality of graph features produced by FGSD and demonstrate their utility, we apply them to the graph classification problem. Through extensive experiments, we show that a simple SVM based classification algorithm, driven with our powerful FGSD based graph features, significantly outperforms all the more sophisticated state-of-art algorithms on the unlabeled node datasets in terms of both accuracy and speed; it also yields very competitive results on the labeled datasets - despite the fact it does not utilize any node label information.

paragraphs: Learning from graphs requires a representation that makes their structure usable by a prediction algorithm. This paper seeks graph features with several desirable properties: uniqueness, stability, sparsity, and fast computation. These goals concern both the information the representation preserves and how practical it is to calculate and use.

The authors introduce a family of graph spectral distances, called FGSD, and build graph representations from them. They prove that the construction possesses most of the properties they seek. To assess whether these features are useful for learning, they supply them to a simple support vector machine and evaluate graph classification.

On the tested datasets without node labels, the resulting classifier significantly outperforms the compared, more sophisticated state-of-the-art algorithms in both accuracy and speed. It also obtains very competitive results on datasets with node labels, despite not using that label information. The experiments suggest that the structural information captured by FGSD can support strong classification without a complicated classifier. The theoretical claim remains that most, rather than every one, of the desired representation properties are established.
summary.tldr: FGSD builds graph features from spectral distances, enabling strong and fast graph classification with a simple support vector machine.

title: Hunt For The Unique, Stable, Sparse And Fast Feature Learning On Graphs

abstract: Deep-embedding methods aim to discover representations of a domain that make explicit the domain's class structure and thereby support few-shot learning. Disentangling methods aim to make explicit compositional or factorial structure. We combine these two active but independent lines of research and propose a new paradigm suitable for both goals. We propose and evaluate a novel loss function based on the $F$ statistic, which describes the separation of two or more distributions. By ensuring that distinct classes are well separated on a subset of embedding dimensions, we obtain embeddings that are useful for few-shot learning. By not requiring separation on all dimensions, we encourage the discovery of disentangled representations. Our embedding method matches or beats state-of-the-art, as evaluated by performance on recall@$k$ and few-shot learning tasks. Our method also obtains performance superior to a variety of alternatives on disentangling, as evaluated by two key properties of a disentangled representation: modularity and explicitness. The goal of our work is to obtain more interpretable, manipulable, and generalizable deep representations of concepts and categories.
