paragraphs: Learning representations can serve two different goals: separating categories so they are easy to recognize, and exposing the distinct factors that compose them. This paper combines these goals in a single embedding approach. It aims to support learning from few examples while encouraging representations whose components are more interpretable and independently useful.

The authors introduce a loss based on the F statistic, which measures separation among distributions. The key design is to separate classes on a subset of embedding dimensions without requiring separation everywhere. That leaves other dimensions available to express additional structure, encouraging disentanglement while retaining information useful for distinguishing classes.

In the reported evaluations, the method matches or exceeds state-of-the-art performance on recall@k and few-shot learning tasks. It also outperforms several alternatives on modularity and explicitness, the two evaluated properties of disentangled representations. These results support the proposed compatibility between useful class separation and disentanglement; the loss encourages that structure rather than establishing that every learned dimension must have a distinct meaning.
summary.tldr: An F-statistic loss separates classes on selected embedding dimensions, supporting few-shot learning while encouraging disentangled representations.

title: Learning Deep Disentangled Embeddings With the F-Statistic Loss

abstract: We here focus on the task of learning Granger causality matrices for multivariate point processes. In order to accomplish this task, our work is the first to explore the use of Wold processes. By doing so, we are able to develop asymptotically fast MCMC learning algorithms. With $N$ being the total number of events and $K$ the number of processes, our learning algorithm has a $O(N(\,\log(N)\,+\,\log(K)))$ cost per iteration. This is much faster than the $O(N^3\,K^2)$ or $O(K^3)$ for the state of the art. Our approach, called GrangerBusca, is validated on nine datasets. This is an advance in relation to most prior efforts which focus mostly on subsets of the Memetracker data. Regarding accuracy, GrangerBusca is three times more accurate (in Precision@10) than the state of the art for the commonly explored subsets Memetracker. Due to GrangerBusca's much lower training complexity, our approach is the only one able to train models for larger, full, sets of data.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to estimate Granger causality matrices for multiple streams of timestamped events. These matrices describe predictive relationships among the event processes. Its approach, GrangerBusca, uses Wold processes to represent these interactions and develops Markov chain Monte Carlo learning algorithms around that choice.

The main computational result is a per-iteration cost of O(N(log N + log K)), where N counts events and K counts processes. The abstract contrasts this with existing costs of O(N³K²) or O(K³). This reduction matters because learning interaction patterns across many event streams can otherwise become computationally prohibitive as the number of events or processes increases.

Evaluation covers nine datasets, extending beyond the Memetracker subsets emphasized in much prior work. On commonly studied Memetracker subsets, GrangerBusca reports three times the Precision@10 accuracy of the state of the art. The authors also report that its lower training complexity makes it the only compared approach able to train on larger, full datasets. These findings connect computational scaling with broader empirical coverage.
summary.tldr: GrangerBusca uses Wold processes to estimate event-stream interactions with lower training complexity and improved reported Precision@10.

title: Fast Estimation of Causal Interactions using Wold Processes

abstract: Reparameterization of variational auto-encoders with continuous random variables is an effective method for reducing the variance of their gradient estimates. In the discrete case, one can perform reparametrization using the Gumbel-Max trick, but the resulting objective relies on an $\arg \max$ operation and is non-differentiable. In contrast to previous works which resort to \emph{softmax}-based relaxations, we propose to optimize it directly by applying the \emph{direct loss minimization} approach. Our proposal extends naturally to structured discrete latent variable models when evaluating the $\arg \max$ operation is tractable. We demonstrate empirically the effectiveness of the direct loss minimization technique in variational autoencoders with both unstructured and structured discrete latent variables.

In contrast to previous works which resort to \emph{softmax}-based relaxations, we propose to optimize it directly by applying the \emph{direct loss minimization} approach. paragraphs: Variational autoencoders with discrete hidden variables face a training difficulty: choosing among discrete alternatives introduces an operation that ordinary differentiation cannot directly handle. The Gumbel-Max trick provides a way to reparameterize these variables, but its final argmax operation selects a single alternative and leaves the resulting objective nondifferentiable.

The paper proposes applying direct loss minimization to optimize this objective. Previous approaches discussed in the abstract replace the hard selection with a softmax-based relaxation. The proposed method instead addresses the objective containing the discrete choice directly, offering another route for training models whose hidden representations involve categorical decisions.

The approach also extends to structured discrete latent variables, where choices have relationships rather than being independent alternatives. This extension depends on being able to compute the required argmax tractably. Experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of direct loss minimization for both unstructured and structured discrete variational autoencoders, supporting its use across these two kinds of latent-variable models.
summary.tldr: Direct loss minimization trains discrete variational autoencoders through hard argmax choices without using softmax relaxations.

title: Direct Optimization through $\arg \max$ for Discrete Variational Auto-Encoder

abstract: A widely deployed method for reducing the training time of deep neural networks is to normalize activations at each layer. Although various normalization schemes have been proposed, they all follow a common theme: normalize across spatial dimensions and discard the extracted statistics. In this paper, we propose a novel normalization method that deviates from this theme. Our approach, which we refer to as Positional Normalization (PONO), normalizes exclusively across channels, which allows us to capture structural information of the input image in the first and second moments. Instead of disregarding this information, we inject it into later layers to preserve or transfer structural information in generative networks. We show that PONO significantly improves the performance of deep networks across a wide range of model architectures and image generation tasks.

Our approach, which we refer to as Positional Normalization (PONO), normalizes exclusively across channels, which allows us to capture structural information of the input image in the first and second moments. paragraphs: The paper revisits what happens to information extracted during activation normalization. Normalization is widely used to shorten neural-network training, but the authors observe that existing schemes normalize across spatial dimensions and discard the resulting statistics. Their proposal treats some of those statistics as useful image information.

Positional Normalization, or PONO, normalizes only across channels. This allows the first and second moments at image positions to capture structural information about the input. The method then injects that information into later layers, making the extracted statistics part of how a generative network preserves or transfers structure.

The authors report significant performance improvements across a wide range of network architectures and image-generation tasks. The conceptual contribution is to connect normalization with information preservation: statistics computed while transforming activations can also carry structure forward. PONO therefore changes both the dimensions over which normalization is performed and the subsequent use of the resulting information, with the reported experiments supporting this design across multiple generative settings.
summary.tldr: PONO normalizes across channels and reuses position-specific statistics in later layers to preserve or transfer image structure.

title: Positional Normalization

abstract: Reconstructing observed images from fMRI brain recordings is challenging. Unfortunately, acquiring sufficient ''labeled'' pairs of {Image, fMRI} (i.e., images with their corresponding fMRI responses) to span the huge space of natural images is prohibitive for many reasons. We present a novel approach which, in addition to the scarce labeled data (training pairs), allows to train fMRI-to-image reconstruction networks also on "unlabeled" data (i.e., images without fMRI recording, and fMRI recording without images). The proposed model utilizes both an Encoder network (image-to-fMRI) and a Decoder network (fMRI-to-image). Concatenating these two networks back-to-back (Encoder-Decoder & Decoder-Encoder) allows augmenting the training data with both types of unlabeled data. Importantly, it allows training on the unlabeled test-fMRI data. This self-supervision adapts the reconstruction network to the new input test-data, despite its deviation from the statistics of the scarce training data.

paragraphs: Reconstructing a viewed image from fMRI requires learning a relationship between images and brain recordings. Paired examples are scarce, and collecting enough to cover the variety of natural images is prohibitive. This paper expands the training material available to a reconstruction network by also using images without recordings and recordings without their corresponding images.

The model contains two networks with opposite directions. An encoder maps images to fMRI, while a decoder maps fMRI to images. Joining them in either order creates a round trip: image to recording and back, or recording to image and back. These compositions provide self-supervision from each kind of unpaired data.

A particularly relevant consequence is that the reconstruction model can train on the test fMRI inputs without access to their associated images. This lets it adapt to new recordings whose statistics differ from those of the small paired training set. The contribution is a way to use otherwise unpaired observations for training and adaptation in a setting where complete image-recording pairs are difficult to obtain.
summary.tldr: Paired image-to-fMRI and fMRI-to-image networks enable self-supervised training on unpaired data, including adaptation to unlabeled test recordings.

title: From voxels to pixels and back: Self-supervision in natural-image reconstruction from fMRI

abstract: Stochastic Gradient Descent or SGD is the most popular optimization algorithm for large-scale problems. SGD estimates the gradient by uniform sampling with sample size one. There have been several other works that suggest faster epoch-wise convergence by using weighted non-uniform sampling for better gradient estimates. Unfortunately, the per-iteration cost of maintaining this adaptive distribution for gradient estimation is more than calculating the full gradient itself, which we call the chicken-and-the-egg loop. As a result, the false impression of faster convergence in iterations, in reality, leads to slower convergence in time. In this paper, we break this barrier by providing the first demonstration of a scheme, Locality sensitive hashing (LSH) sampled Stochastic Gradient Descent (LGD), which leads to superior gradient estimation while keeping the sampling cost per iteration similar to that of the uniform sampling. Such an algorithm is possible due to the sampling view of LSH, which came to light recently. As a consequence of superior and fast estimation, we reduce the running time of all existing gradient descent algorithms, that relies on gradient estimates including Adam, Ada-grad, etc. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposal with experiments on linear models as well as the non-linear BERT, which is a recent popular deep learning based language representation model.

paragraphs: Stochastic optimization estimates a gradient from sampled data instead of computing it over the entire dataset. Choosing samples non-uniformly can improve those estimates, but maintaining an adaptive sampling distribution can itself be expensive. The paper highlights the resulting trap: an algorithm can need fewer iterations yet take longer overall because each iteration costs more.

The proposed method, locality-sensitive-hashing sampled gradient descent, uses a sampling interpretation of locality-sensitive hashing to select data efficiently. Its aim is to improve gradient estimation while keeping sampling costs comparable to uniform sampling. This connects the statistical benefit of choosing more useful samples with the computational requirement that selecting them remain cheap.

The authors report reductions in running time for gradient-based methods that rely on such estimates, including Adam and AdaGrad. They demonstrate the approach on linear models and BERT. The contribution is therefore about elapsed optimization time as well as estimator quality: more informative gradients are useful when their sampling overhead does not consume the time they save.
summary.tldr: Hash-based sampling improves stochastic gradient estimates at sampling costs comparable to uniform selection, reducing reported optimization time.

title: Fast and Accurate Stochastic Gradient Estimation

abstract: Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) contain local pooling to effectively downsize feature maps for increasing computation efficiency as well as robustness to input variations. The local pooling methods are generally formulated in a form of convex combination of local neuron activations for retaining the characteristics of an input feature map in a manner similar to image downscaling. In this paper, to improve performance of CNNs, we propose a novel local pooling method based on the Gaussian-based probabilistic model over local neuron activations for flexibly pooling (extracting) features, in contrast to the previous model restricting the output within the convex hull of local neurons. In the proposed method, the local neuron activations are aggregated into the statistics of mean and standard deviation in a Gaussian distribution, and then on the basis of those statistics, we construct the probabilistic model suitable for the pooling in accordance with the knowledge about local pooling in CNNs. Through the probabilistic model equipped with trainable parameters, the proposed method naturally integrates two schemes of adaptively training the pooling form based on input feature maps and stochastically performing the pooling throughout the end-to-end learning. The experimental results on image classification demonstrate that the proposed method favorably improves performance of various CNNs in comparison with the other pooling methods.

This paper proposes a probabilistic pooling mechanism with greater flexibility in how it extracts a local feature.

The method summarizes local activations using their mean and standard deviation, then builds a Gaussian-based probabilistic model from those statistics. Trainable parameters allow the pooling behavior to adapt to input feature maps. The same formulation also supports stochastic pooling during end-to-end training, bringing adaptation and randomness together in one mechanism.

Image classification experiments show improved performance across various convolutional networks compared with other pooling methods. The contribution is therefore a change to a recurring local operation within the network, with empirical benefits across the evaluated architectures. Its underlying idea is that local statistics can support a richer pooling rule than a constrained combination of activations, while allowing that rule to be learned as part of the overall task.
summary.tldr: A trainable Gaussian-based pooling rule combines adaptive feature extraction with stochastic pooling and improves evaluated CNN classification performance.

title: Gaussian-Based Pooling for Convolutional Neural Networks

abstract: Advancements in deep generative models such as generative adversarial networks and variational autoencoders have resulted in the ability to generate realistic images that are visually indistinguishable from real images which raises concerns about their potential malicious usage. In this paper, we present an analysis of the high-frequency Fourier modes of real and deep network generated images and show that deep network generated images share an observable, systematic shortcoming in replicating the attributes of these high-frequency modes. Using this, we propose a novel detection method based on the frequency spectrum of the images which is able to achieve an accuracy of up to 99.2% in classifying real and deep network generated images from various GAN and VAE architectures on a dataset of 5000 images with as few as 8 training examples. Furthermore, we show the impact of image transformations such as compression, cropping, and resolution reduction on the classification accuracy and suggest a method for modifying the high-frequency attributes of deep network generated images to mimic real images.

This paper examines high-frequency Fourier components, which describe rapidly changing image patterns. The authors find a systematic discrepancy in how the studied deep generative models reproduce these components, revealing information that visual realism alone can obscure.

They use this discrepancy to build a detector based on an image’s frequency spectrum. On a dataset of 5,000 images from various GAN and VAE architectures, the method reaches classification accuracy of up to 99.2% with as few as eight training examples. These figures describe the reported experimental setting and show that the observed spectral signal can be useful even with very little training data.

The study also examines how compression, cropping, and reduced resolution affect classification accuracy. Finally, it suggests a way to modify generated images’ high-frequency properties to resemble those of real images. The work therefore connects a measurable generation shortcoming to detection, while also investigating transformations and modifications that matter when interpreting that detection signal.
summary.tldr: Systematic high-frequency spectral differences enable strong detection of generated images in the reported experiments, even with very few training examples.

title: Fourier Spectrum Discrepancies in Deep Network Generated Images

abstract: Graph based semi-supervised learning is the problem of learning a labeling function for the graph nodes given a few example nodes, often called seeds, usually under the assumption that the graph’s edges indicate similarity of labels. This is closely related to the local graph clustering or community detection problem of finding a cluster or community of nodes around a given seed. For this problem, we propose a novel generalization of random walk, diffusion, or smooth function methods in the literature to a convex p-norm cut function. The need for our p-norm methods is that, in our study of existing methods, we find those principled methods based on eigenvector, spectral, random walk, or linear system often have difficulty capturing the correct boundary of a target label or target cluster. In contrast, 1-norm or maxflow-mincut based methods capture the boundary, but cannot grow from small seed set; hybrid procedures that use both have many hard to set parameters. In this paper, we propose a generalization of the objective function behind these methods involving p-norms. To solve the p-norm cut problem we give a strongly local algorithm -- one whose runtime depends on the size of the output rather than the size of the graph. Our method can be thought as a nonlinear generalization of the Anderson-Chung-Lang push procedure to approximate a personalized PageRank vector efficiently. Our procedure is general and can solve other types of nonlinear objective functions, such as p-norm variants of Huber losses. We provide a theoretical analysis of finding planted target clusters with our method and show that the p-norm cut functions improve on the standard Cheeger inequalities for random walk and spectral methods. Finally, we demonstrate the speed and accuracy of our new method in synthetic and real world datasets.

They also extend the procedure to other nonlinear objectives, including p-norm variants of Huber losses. Synthetic and real-data experiments demonstrate speed and accuracy, supporting both the objective's boundary-finding role and the algorithm's local computation.
summary.tldr: Convex p-norm cuts support seed-based graph learning with improved clustering guarantees and computation that scales with the output size.

title: Strongly local p-norm-cut algorithms for semi-supervised learning and local graph clustering

abstract: The notion of implicit bias, or implicit regularization, has been suggested as a means to explain the surprising generalization ability of modern-days overparameterized learning algorithms. This notion refers to the tendency of the optimization algorithm towards a certain structured solution that often generalizes well. Recently, several papers have studied implicit regularization and were able to identify this phenomenon in various scenarios. We revisit this paradigm in arguably the simplest non-trivial setup, and study the implicit bias of Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) in the context of Stochastic Convex Optimization. As a first step, we provide a simple construction that rules out the existence of a \emph{distribution-independent} implicit regularizer that governs the generalization ability of SGD. We then demonstrate a learning problem that rules out a very general class of \emph{distribution-dependent} implicit regularizers from explaining generalization, which includes strongly convex regularizers as well as non-degenerate norm-based regularizations. Certain aspects of our constructions point out to significant difficulties in providing a comprehensive explanation of an algorithm's generalization performance by solely arguing about its implicit regularization properties.

paragraphs: Implicit regularization is the idea that an optimization algorithm tends to select structured solutions that generalize well, even without an explicit penalty enforcing that structure. This paper examines how far that explanation can go for stochastic gradient descent. It works in stochastic convex optimization, a relatively simple setting in which to test claims about optimization and generalization.

The authors first construct an example ruling out a distribution-independent implicit regularizer that governs SGD’s generalization. They then give another learning problem that rules out a broad class of explanations even when the regularizer may depend on the data distribution. This class includes strongly convex regularizers and non-degenerate regularization based on norms.

These constructions challenge the adequacy of explaining generalization solely through a preferred solution structure. Their scope matters: the paper excludes particular broad forms of regularizer-based explanation, rather than showing that implicit bias never exists or never helps. The results reveal substantial obstacles to making implicit regularization a comprehensive account of an algorithm’s generalization performance.
summary.tldr: Counterexamples show that broad classes of implicit regularizers cannot fully explain SGD’s generalization in stochastic convex optimization.

title: Can Implicit Bias Explain Generalization? Stochastic Convex Optimization as a Case Study

abstract: We provide new statistical guarantees for transfer learning via representation learning--when transfer is achieved by learning a feature representation shared across different tasks. This enables learning on new tasks using far less data than is required to learn them in isolation. Formally, we consider $t+1$ tasks parameterized by functions of the form $f_j \circ h$ in a general function class $F \circ H$, where each $f_j$ is a task-specific function in $F$ and $h$ is the shared representation in $H$. Letting $C(\cdot)$ denote the complexity measure of the function class, we show that for diverse training tasks (1) the sample complexity needed to learn the shared representation across the first $t$ training tasks scales as $C(H) + t C(F)$, despite no explicit access to a signal from the feature representation and (2) with an accurate estimate of the representation, the sample complexity needed to learn a new task scales only with $C(F)$. Our results depend upon a new general notion of task diversity--applicable to models with general tasks, features, and losses--as well as a novel chain rule for Gaussian complexities. Finally, we exhibit the utility of our general framework in several models of importance in the literature.

paragraphs: Transfer learning can reduce the data needed for a new task by reusing features learned from earlier tasks. This paper provides statistical guarantees for that idea when each task combines a shared representation with a task-specific function. It asks when training across several tasks can identify a representation that makes subsequent learning cheaper.

For diverse training tasks, the sample complexity of learning the shared representation across t tasks scales as C(H) plus t times C(F). Here, C(H) measures representation-class complexity and C(F) measures task-specific function complexity. The representation does not need to be directly observed. Once it has been estimated accurately, learning a new task requires sample complexity scaling only with C(F).

The guarantees depend on a new general notion of task diversity and a chain rule for Gaussian complexities. The authors demonstrate the framework’s usefulness in several models. The central implication is conditional: sufficiently diverse tasks can spread the cost of learning shared features across training tasks, leaving a smaller task-specific learning burden for a new task.
summary.tldr: Statistical guarantees show how diverse training tasks can support reusable representations that reduce new-task sample complexity.

title: On the Theory of Transfer Learning: The Importance of Task Diversity

abstract: While much attention has been given to the problem of estimating the effect of discrete interventions from observational data, relatively little work has been done in the setting of continuous-valued interventions, such as treatments associated with a dosage parameter. In this paper, we tackle this problem by building on a modification of the generative adversarial networks (GANs) framework. Our model, SCIGAN, is flexible and capable of simultaneously estimating counterfactual outcomes for several different continuous interventions. The key idea is to use a significantly modified GAN model to learn to generate counterfactual outcomes, which can then be used to learn an inference model, using standard supervised methods, capable of estimating these counterfactuals for a new sample. To address the challenges presented by shifting to continuous interventions, we propose a novel architecture for our discriminator - we build a hierarchical discriminator that leverages the structure of the continuous intervention setting. Moreover, we provide theoretical results to support our use of the GAN framework and of the hierarchical discriminator. In the experiments section, we introduce a new semi-synthetic data simulation for use in the continuous intervention setting and demonstrate improvements over the existing benchmark models.

paragraphs: An intervention can vary continuously, as when a treatment has an adjustable dosage. Estimating its effect therefore requires more than comparing a few discrete treatment choices. This paper introduces SCIGAN, a modified generative adversarial framework for estimating counterfactual outcomes across several different continuous interventions using observational data.

SCIGAN first learns to generate counterfactual outcomes. Those generated outcomes then support training an inference model through standard supervised learning, enabling predictions for new samples. A central architectural contribution is a hierarchical discriminator designed around the structure of continuous interventions. The discriminator adapts the adversarial learning process to the setting the model needs to handle.

The authors provide theoretical results supporting both the GAN formulation and the hierarchical discriminator. They also introduce a semi-synthetic data simulation for continuous interventions and report improvements over existing benchmark models. The contribution is a route from generated counterfactual outcomes to a reusable prediction model, together with theoretical support and experimental evidence in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: SCIGAN uses a modified GAN and hierarchical discriminator to estimate counterfactual outcomes for multiple continuously varying interventions.

title: Estimating the Effects of Continuous-valued Interventions using Generative Adversarial Networks

abstract: Tackling overestimation in $Q$-learning is an important problem that has been extensively studied in single-agent reinforcement learning, but has received comparatively little attention in the multi-agent setting. In this work, we empirically demonstrate that QMIX, a popular $Q$-learning algorithm for cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL), suffers from a more severe overestimation in practice than previously acknowledged, and is not mitigated by existing approaches. We rectify this with a novel regularization-based update scheme that penalizes large joint action-values that deviate from a baseline and demonstrate its effectiveness in stabilizing learning. Furthermore, we propose to employ a softmax operator, which we efficiently approximate in a novel way in the multi-agent setting, to further reduce the potential overestimation bias. Our approach, Regularized Softmax (RES) Deep Multi-Agent $Q$-Learning, is general and can be applied to any $Q$-learning based MARL algorithm. We demonstrate that, when applied to QMIX, RES avoids severe overestimation and significantly improves performance, yielding state-of-the-art results in a variety of cooperative multi-agent tasks, including the challenging StarCraft II micromanagement benchmarks.

The authors empirically find that QMIX suffers from more severe overestimation than previously recognized. Together, these components form Regularized Softmax Deep Multi-Agent Q-Learning, or RES.

The reported evaluation applies it to QMIX, where it avoids severe overestimation and significantly improves performance. Results reach the state of the art across several cooperative tasks, including StarCraft II micromanagement. The evidence links improved value estimation to stronger learning performance in these tested cooperative environments.
summary.tldr: RES combines value regularization with an efficiently approximated softmax operator to reduce QMIX overestimation and improve cooperative multi-agent performance.

title: Regularized Softmax Deep Multi-Agent Q-Learning

abstract: We develop methods for forming prediction sets in an online setting where the data generating distribution is allowed to vary over time in an unknown fashion. Our framework builds on ideas from conformal inference to provide a general wrapper that can be combined with any black box method that produces point predictions of the unseen label or estimated quantiles of its distribution. While previous conformal inference methods rely on the assumption that the data are exchangeable, our adaptive approach provably achieves the desired coverage frequency over long-time intervals irrespective of the true data generating process. We accomplish this by modelling the distribution shift as a learning problem in a single parameter whose optimal value is varying over time and must be continuously re-estimated. We test our method, adaptive conformal inference, on two real world datasets and find that its predictions are robust to visible and significant distribution shifts.

paragraphs: Prediction sets express uncertainty by giving a collection of plausible outcomes instead of a single guess. This paper studies how to produce these sets as observations arrive over time, even when the process generating the data changes in unknown ways. The challenge is to keep their coverage frequency near a chosen target.

The proposed adaptive conformal inference method wraps around an existing predictor. That predictor can supply either a point prediction or estimated quantiles, so the approach does not require a particular prediction architecture. Its central move is to treat adaptation as learning one parameter whose best value changes over time and must be continually re-estimated.

The theoretical result concerns coverage across long time intervals: the method achieves the desired frequency regardless of the underlying data-generating process. This differs from guaranteeing coverage separately at every moment. Unlike earlier conformal approaches described in the abstract, it does not rely on exchangeability. Tests on two real-world datasets also show robustness to substantial, visible distribution changes.
summary.tldr: Adaptive conformal inference continually adjusts prediction sets to achieve target coverage over long intervals despite unknown distribution shifts.

title: Adaptive Conformal Inference Under Distribution Shift

abstract: Invariance to a broad array of image corruptions, such as warping, noise, or color shifts, is an important aspect of building robust models in computer vision. Recently, several new data augmentations have been proposed that significantly improve performance on ImageNet-C, a benchmark of such corruptions. However, there is still a lack of basic understanding on the relationship between data augmentations and test-time corruptions. To this end, we develop a feature space for image transforms, and then use a new measure in this space between augmentations and corruptions called the Minimal Sample Distance to demonstrate there is a strong correlation between similarity and performance. We then investigate recent data augmentations and observe a significant degradation in corruption robustness when the test-time corruptions are sampled to be perceptually dissimilar from ImageNet-C in this feature space. Our results suggest that test error can be improved by training on perceptually similar augmentations, and data augmentations may not generalize well beyond the existing benchmark. We hope our results and tools will allow for more robust progress towards improving robustness to image corruptions. We provide code at https://github.com/facebookresearch/augmentation-corruption.

paragraphs: Training with augmented images can improve robustness to noise, warping, and colour changes. However, strong results on a corruption benchmark do not by themselves explain which new corruptions a model will handle. This paper investigates how the similarity between training augmentations and test-time corruptions relates to the robustness gains observed.

The authors construct a feature space for image transformations and introduce Minimal Sample Distance to measure relationships between augmentations and corruptions within it. They find a strong correlation between transformation similarity and performance. This provides a way to examine whether an augmentation’s apparent robustness benefit is associated with resemblance to the transformations used for evaluation.

They then evaluate recent augmentations on corruptions selected to be perceptually dissimilar from ImageNet-C in that feature space and observe substantial robustness degradation. The results suggest that perceptually similar training augmentations can improve test error, while benefits may transfer poorly beyond the existing benchmark. The contribution is both a measurement tool and evidence that corruption similarity matters when interpreting robustness improvements.
summary.tldr: Robustness gains correlate with augmentation–corruption similarity and can weaken substantially on perceptually different corruptions.

title: On Interaction Between Augmentations and Corruptions in Natural Corruption Robustness

abstract: Large sparse linear systems of equations are ubiquitous in science and engineering, such as those arising from discretizations of partial differential equations. Algebraic multigrid (AMG) methods are one of the most common methods of solving such linear systems, with an extensive body of underlying mathematical theory. A system of linear equations defines a graph on the set of unknowns and each level of a multigrid solver requires the selection of an appropriate coarse graph along with restriction and interpolation operators that map to and from the coarse representation. The efficiency of the multigrid solver depends critically on this selection and many selection methods have been developed over the years. Recently, it has been demonstrated that it is possible to directly learn the AMG interpolation and restriction operators, given a coarse graph selection. In this paper, we consider the complementary problem of learning to coarsen graphs for a multigrid solver, a necessary step in developing fully learnable AMG methods. We propose a method using a reinforcement learning (RL) agent based on graph neural networks (GNNs), which can learn to perform graph coarsening on small planar training graphs and then be applied to unstructured large planar graphs, assuming bounded node degree. We demonstrate that this method can produce better coarse graphs than existing algorithms, even as the graph size increases and other properties of the graph are varied. We also propose an efficient inference procedure for performing graph coarsening that results in linear time complexity in graph size.

paragraphs: Algebraic multigrid solves large sparse linear systems using multiple levels of representation. Each level needs a suitable coarse graph and operators that transfer information between representations. Choosing that graph strongly affects solver efficiency. This paper addresses learning the coarsening step, complementing work that learns transfer operators once a coarse graph is already available.

The proposed method uses a reinforcement learning agent based on graph neural networks. It learns to coarsen small planar graphs and can then be applied to large unstructured planar graphs, assuming bounded node degree. This targets a useful form of transfer: learning the selection behavior on small instances and applying it at a larger scale.

The experiments show that the method can produce better coarse graphs than existing algorithms as graph size and other properties vary. The authors also introduce an inference procedure with time complexity linear in graph size. Together, these contributions address the quality and computational cost of learned coarsening, advancing one necessary component of a fully learnable algebraic multigrid solver.
summary.tldr: A graph-based reinforcement learning agent learns multigrid coarsening on small graphs and transfers to large planar graphs with bounded degree.

title: Optimization-Based Algebraic Multigrid Coarsening Using Reinforcement Learning

abstract: We derive nearly sharp bounds for the bidirectional GAN (BiGAN) estimation error under the Dudley distance between the latent joint distribution and the data joint distribution with appropriately specified architecture of the neural networks used in the model. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first theoretical guarantee for the bidirectional GAN learning approach. An appealing feature of our results is that they do not assume the reference and the data distributions to have the same dimensions or these distributions to have bounded support. These assumptions are commonly assumed in the existing convergence analysis of the unidirectional GANs but may not be satisfied in practice. Our results are also applicable to the Wasserstein bidirectional GAN if the target distribution is assumed to have a bounded support. To prove these results, we construct neural network functions that push forward an empirical distribution to another arbitrary empirical distribution on a possibly different-dimensional space. We also develop a novel decomposition of the integral probability metric for the error analysis of bidirectional GANs. These basic theoretical results are of independent interest and can be applied to other related learning problems.

paragraphs: This paper provides finite-sample theoretical guarantees for bidirectional generative adversarial networks. It bounds estimation error by comparing the latent and data joint distributions using Dudley distance. With appropriately specified neural network architectures, the resulting bounds are nearly sharp, giving a quantitative account of the learning approach's accuracy.

A notable feature is that the analysis does not require the reference and data distributions to have equal dimensions or bounded support. Removing those assumptions broadens the settings covered by the guarantee. The authors also extend the results to Wasserstein bidirectional GANs, but that extension does require the target distribution to have bounded support.

The proofs introduce neural network constructions that map one empirical distribution to an arbitrary other empirical distribution, potentially in a space of different dimension. They also develop a decomposition of an integral probability metric for analyzing error. These tools explain how the guarantees are obtained and are presented as useful beyond BiGANs. The contribution is theoretical control of estimation error together with reusable methods for related learning problems.
summary.tldr: The paper derives nearly sharp finite-sample BiGAN error bounds without requiring equal distribution dimensions or bounded support for the main result.

title: Non-asymptotic Error Bounds for Bidirectional GANs

abstract: The “cold posterior effect” (CPE) in Bayesian deep learning describes the disturbing observation that the predictive performance of Bayesian neural networks can be significantly improved if the Bayes posterior is artificially sharpened using a temperature parameter T <1. The CPE is problematic in theory and practice and since the effect was identified many researchers have proposed hypotheses to explain the phenomenon. However, despite this intensive research effort the effect remains poorly understood. In this work we provide novel and nuanced evidence relevant to existing explanations for the cold posterior effect, disentangling three hypotheses: 1. The dataset curation hypothesis of Aitchison (2020): we show empirically that the CPE does not arise in a real curated data set but can be produced in a controlled experiment with varying curation strength. 2. The data augmentation hypothesis of Izmailov et al. (2021) and Fortuin et al. (2021): we show empirically that data augmentation is sufficient but not necessary for the CPE to be present. 3. The bad prior hypothesis of Wenzel et al. (2020): we use a simple experiment evaluating the relative importance of the prior and the likelihood, strongly linking the CPE to the prior. Our results demonstrate how the CPE can arise in isolation from synthetic curation, data augmentation, and bad priors. Cold posteriors observed “in the wild” are therefore unlikely to arise from a single simple cause; as a result, we do not expect a simple “fix” for cold posteriors.

paragraphs: The cold posterior effect occurs when a Bayesian neural network predicts better after its posterior is artificially sharpened using a temperature below one. This is puzzling because it changes the usual Bayesian posterior. The paper investigates three proposed explanations: dataset curation, data augmentation, and the choice of prior.

The curation results resist a simple explanation. The effect is absent in one real curated dataset, yet appears in a controlled experiment that varies curation strength. For augmentation, the experiments show that it can be sufficient to produce the effect but is not necessary: the effect can also occur without augmentation.

A separate experiment compares the influence of prior and likelihood and strongly links the effect to the prior. Taken together, the findings indicate that synthetic curation, augmentation, and problematic priors can each contribute in isolation. The authors therefore argue that cold posteriors encountered in practice are unlikely to have a single simple cause. Their evidence motivates distinguishing these mechanisms rather than expecting one universal correction.
summary.tldr: Experiments separate several contributors to the cold posterior effect and argue against a single-cause explanation or simple universal fix.

title: Disentangling the Roles of Curation, Data-Augmentation and the Prior in the Cold Posterior Effect

abstract: Performance on the most commonly used Visual Question Answering dataset (VQA v2) is starting to approach human accuracy. However, in interacting with state-of-the-art VQA models, it is clear that the problem is far from being solved. In order to stress test VQA models, we benchmark them against human-adversarial examples. Human subjects interact with a state-of-the-art VQA model, and for each image in the dataset, attempt to find a question where the model’s predicted answer is incorrect. We find that a wide range of state-of-the-art models perform poorly when evaluated on these examples. We conduct an extensive analysis of the collected adversarial examples and provide guidance on future research directions. We hope that this Adversarial VQA (AdVQA) benchmark can help drive progress in the field and advance the state of the art.

paragraphs: Visual question answering asks a model to answer questions about an image. Although results on the widely used VQA v2 dataset were approaching human accuracy, interactions with leading models still exposed mistakes. This paper investigates that mismatch by building a benchmark around questions that people deliberately create to challenge a model.

Human participants interact with a state-of-the-art visual question-answering system. For each image, they try to find a question that causes it to predict an incorrect answer. The resulting AdVQA benchmark makes model failure part of the data-collection process, turning human attempts to expose weaknesses into a structured evaluation set.

A broad range of leading models performs poorly on the collected examples. This shows that strong performance on the commonly used benchmark can coexist with substantial vulnerability to human-designed questions. The authors also analyze the adversarial examples and offer guidance for future research. The benchmark's purpose is to make those weaknesses measurable and help direct progress toward image-question answering that withstands this more demanding form of evaluation.
summary.tldr: AdVQA collects human-written questions that expose substantial weaknesses in leading visual question-answering models.

title: Human-Adversarial Visual Question Answering

abstract: Most existing neural architecture search (NAS) algorithms are dedicated to and evaluated by the downstream tasks, e.g., image classification in computer vision. However, extensive experiments have shown that, prominent neural architectures, such as ResNet in computer vision and LSTM in natural language processing, are generally good at extracting patterns from the input data and perform well on different downstream tasks. In this paper, we attempt to answer two fundamental questions related to NAS. (1) Is it necessary to use the performance of specific downstream tasks to evaluate and search for good neural architectures? (2) Can we perform NAS effectively and efficiently while being agnostic to the downstream tasks? To answer these questions, we propose a novel and generic NAS framework, termed Generic NAS (GenNAS). GenNAS does not use task-specific labels but instead adopts regression on a set of manually designed synthetic signal bases for architecture evaluation. Such a self-supervised regression task can effectively evaluate the intrinsic power of an architecture to capture and transform the input signal patterns, and allow more sufficient usage of training samples. Extensive experiments across 13 CNN search spaces and one NLP space demonstrate the remarkable efficiency of GenNAS using regression, in terms of both evaluating the neural architectures (quantified by the ranking correlation Spearman's rho between the approximated performances and the downstream task performances) and the convergence speed for training (within a few seconds). For example, on NAS-Bench-101, GenNAS achieves 0.85 rho while the existing efficient methods only achieve 0.38. We then propose an automatic task search to optimize the combination of synthetic signals using limited downstream-task-specific labels, further improving the performance of GenNAS. We also thoroughly evaluate GenNAS's generality and end-to-end NAS performance on all search spaces, which outperforms almost all existing works with significant speedup. For example, on NASBench-201, GenNAS can find near-optimal architectures within 0.3 GPU hour.

paragraphs: Neural architecture search usually evaluates candidate networks through a particular downstream task. GenNAS asks whether a more general test can assess an architecture's ability to capture and transform input patterns. It evaluates networks using regression against manually designed synthetic signals, without requiring task-specific labels for this basic evaluation.

The synthetic regression task serves as a proxy for downstream performance. Experiments cover thirteen convolutional-network search spaces and one language-processing search space. They assess both training speed and how well the proxy ranks architectures compared with their downstream results. On NAS-Bench-101, the reported ranking correlation is 0.85, compared with 0.38 for the existing efficient methods discussed in the abstract.

The paper also introduces an automatic search for combinations of synthetic signals, using a limited amount of downstream labeled data to improve performance further. End-to-end evaluations report strong results and significant speedups across the search spaces, including near-optimal architectures on NASBench-201 within 0.3 GPU hour. The findings support synthetic regression as an efficient architecture-evaluation signal.
summary.tldr: GenNAS uses synthetic-signal regression to evaluate architectures efficiently, with strong reported agreement between its rankings and downstream performance.

title: Generic Neural Architecture Search via Regression

abstract: Combinatorial Optimization (CO) has been a long-standing challenging research topic featured by its NP-hard nature. Traditionally such problems are approximately solved with heuristic algorithms which are usually fast but may sacrifice the solution quality. Currently, machine learning for combinatorial optimization (MLCO) has become a trending research topic, but most existing MLCO methods treat CO as a single-level optimization by directly learning the end-to-end solutions, which are hard to scale up and mostly limited by the capacity of ML models given the high complexity of CO. In this paper, we propose a hybrid approach to combine the best of the two worlds, in which a bi-level framework is developed with an upper-level learning method to optimize the graph (e.g. add, delete or modify edges in a graph), fused with a lower-level heuristic algorithm solving on the optimized graph. Such a bi-level approach simplifies the learning on the original hard CO and can effectively mitigate the demand for model capacity. The experiments and results on several popular CO problems like Directed Acyclic Graph scheduling, Graph Edit Distance and Hamiltonian Cycle Problem show its effectiveness over manually designed heuristics and single-level learning methods.

paragraphs: Finding good solutions to difficult graph optimization problems creates a tradeoff between speed and solution quality. Handcrafted heuristics can work quickly, while learning a complete solution directly can place heavy demands on a model. This paper proposes dividing the work between a learned component and an existing heuristic solver.

The framework has two levels. At the upper level, a learning method changes the graph, for example by adding, removing, or modifying edges. At the lower level, a heuristic solves the problem on that modified graph. Learning therefore focuses on preparing a useful graph for the solver rather than producing the entire solution itself.

This division simplifies the learning task and can reduce the model capacity it requires. Experiments cover directed acyclic graph scheduling, graph edit distance, and the Hamiltonian cycle problem. The reported results show advantages over manually designed heuristics and methods that learn solutions in a single stage, supporting the usefulness of combining learned graph modifications with established solving procedures.
summary.tldr: A two-level framework learns to modify graphs so that a heuristic solver can find better solutions.

title: A Bi-Level Framework for Learning to Solve Combinatorial Optimization on Graphs

abstract: Numerous recent works show that overparameterization implicitly reduces variance for min-norm interpolators and max-margin classifiers. These findings suggest that ridge regularization has vanishing benefits in high dimensions. We challenge this narrative by showing that, even in the absence of noise, avoiding interpolation through ridge regularization can significantly improve generalization. We prove this phenomenon for the robust risk of both linear regression and classification, and hence provide the first theoretical result on \emph{robust overfitting}.
originalAbstract: Numerous recent works show that overparameterization implicitly reduces variance for min-norm interpolators and max-margin classifiers. These findings suggest that ridge regularization has vanishing benefits in high dimensions. We challenge this narrative by showing that, even in the absence of noise, avoiding interpolation through ridge regularization can significantly improve generalization. We prove this phenomenon for the robust risk of both linear regression and classification, and hence provide the first theoretical result on \emph{robust overfitting}.

paragraphs: Interpolation means fitting the training data exactly. Research on highly overparameterized models has shown that certain interpolating solutions can implicitly reduce variance, suggesting that explicit ridge regularization may offer diminishing benefits in high dimensions. This paper examines whether that conclusion remains appropriate when the objective is robust generalization.

The authors prove that avoiding interpolation through ridge regularization can significantly improve robust risk even when the data contain no noise. They establish this phenomenon for both linear regression and classification. The absence of noise is central: the demonstrated benefit cannot be explained solely as preventing the model from fitting noisy training observations. Exact fit can itself be disadvantageous for the robust criterion studied.

The paper presents this as a theoretical result on robust overfitting. Its significance is that favorable behavior of interpolating models does not settle the question of whether regularization helps robustness. The result establishes that improvement is possible in the analyzed settings, giving a reason to assess robust risk separately when judging the value of interpolation and ridge regularization.
summary.tldr: The paper proves that ridge regularization can improve robust generalization by avoiding exact training fit, even in noiseless regression and classification.

title: Interpolation can hurt robust generalization even when there is no noise

abstract: In recent years Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) were successfully used to model the way neural activity drives task-related behavior in animals, operating under the implicit assumption that the obtained solutions are universal. Observations in both neuroscience and machine learning challenge this assumption. Animals can approach a given task with a variety of strategies, and training machine learning algorithms introduces the phenomenon of underspecification. These observations imply that every task is associated with a space of solutions. To date, the structure of this space is not understood, limiting the approach of comparing RNNs with neural data.Here, we characterize the space of solutions associated with various tasks. We first study a simple two-neuron network on a task that leads to multiple solutions. We trace the nature of the final solution back to the network’s initial connectivity and identify discrete dynamical regimes that underlie this diversity. We then examine three neuroscience-inspired tasks: Delayed discrimination, Interval discrimination, and Time reproduction. For each task, we find a rich set of solutions. One layer of variability can be found directly in the neural activity of the networks. An additional layer is uncovered by testing the trained networks' ability to extrapolate, as a perturbation to a system often reveals hidden structure. Furthermore, we relate extrapolation patterns to specific dynamical objects and effective algorithms found by the networks. We introduce a tool to derive the reduced dynamics of networks by generating a compact directed graph describing the essence of the dynamics with regards to behavioral inputs and outputs. Using this representation, we can partition the solutions to each task into a handful of types and show that neural features can partially predict them.Taken together, our results shed light on the concept of the space of solutions and its uses both in Machine learning and in Neuroscience.

paragraphs: Recurrent neural networks can reproduce animal behavior while arriving at different internal solutions. This creates a problem for neuroscience: matching a task does not establish that a network uses a unique strategy. The paper investigates the structure of these alternative solutions and how they can be compared meaningfully.

The authors begin with a two-neuron network, tracing different final solutions to initial connectivity and identifying distinct dynamical regimes. They then examine delayed discrimination, interval discrimination, and time reproduction. Each task produces a rich collection of solutions. Differences appear in neural activity, while tests of extrapolation expose additional variation that task performance alone can conceal.

To organize this diversity, the authors introduce a compact directed graph that summarizes network dynamics in relation to behavioral inputs and outputs. This representation groups solutions into a handful of types and connects extrapolation behavior to particular dynamical structures and effective algorithms. Neural features partially predict these types. The work offers a way to compare networks through their internal strategies as well as their observed task success.
summary.tldr: Compact descriptions of recurrent network dynamics reveal distinct strategies that can solve the same task yet behave differently when extrapolating.

title: Charting and Navigating the Space of Solutions for Recurrent Neural Networks

abstract: We introduce a novel anytime batched Thompson sampling policy for multi-armed bandits where the agent observes the rewards of her actions and adjusts her policy only at the end of a small number of batches. We show that this policy simultaneously achieves a problem dependent regret of order $O(\log(T))$ and a minimax regret of order $O(\sqrt{T\log(T)})$ while the number of batches can be bounded by $O(\log(T))$ independent of the problem instance over a time horizon $T$. We also prove that in expectation the instance dependent batch complexity of our policy is of order $O(\log\log(T))$. These results indicate that Thompson sampling performs competitively with recently proposed algorithms for the batched setting, which optimize the batch structure for a given time horizon $T$ and prioritize exploration in the beginning of the experiment to eliminate suboptimal actions. Unlike these algorithms, the batched Thompson sampling algorithm we propose is an anytime policy, i.e. it operates without the knowledge of the time horizon $T$, and as such it is the only anytime algorithm that achieves optimal regret with $O(\log\log(T))$ expected batch complexity. This is achieved through a dynamic batching strategy, which uses the agents estimates to adaptively increase the batch duration.

paragraphs: In a batched multi-armed bandit problem, an agent chooses actions repeatedly but receives rewards and updates its policy only at batch boundaries. The challenge is to make good choices with infrequent feedback. This paper introduces a batched Thompson sampling policy that can operate without knowing the total number of actions, or time horizon, in advance.

Its dynamic batching strategy uses the agent's current estimates to adaptively increase batch lengths. The analysis establishes problem-dependent regret of order log(T) and worst-case regret of order square root of T log(T), where regret measures the cost of choosing actions below the best available option. The number of batches is bounded by order log(T), independently of the problem instance.

A sharper, instance-dependent result bounds the expected number of batches by order log log(T). The distinction matters: this smaller bound is an expectation, rather than a universal bound on every run. Together, the findings show that an anytime policy can combine strong regret guarantees with very few feedback rounds, without designing its batch schedule around a predetermined experiment length.
summary.tldr: Adaptive batching lets Thompson sampling achieve strong regret guarantees with few expected feedback rounds and no advance knowledge of the horizon.

title: Batched Thompson Sampling

abstract: We present SegNeXt, a simple convolutional network architecture for semantic segmentation. Recent transformer-based models have dominated the field of se- mantic segmentation due to the efficiency of self-attention in encoding spatial information. In this paper, we show that convolutional attention is a more efficient and effective way to encode contextual information than the self-attention mech- anism in transformers. By re-examining the characteristics owned by successful segmentation models, we discover several key components leading to the perfor- mance improvement of segmentation models. This motivates us to design a novel convolutional attention network that uses cheap convolutional operations. Without bells and whistles, our SegNeXt significantly improves the performance of previous state-of-the-art methods on popular benchmarks, including ADE20K, Cityscapes, COCO-Stuff, Pascal VOC, Pascal Context, and iSAID. Notably, SegNeXt out- performs EfficientNet-L2 w/ NAS-FPN and achieves 90.6% mIoU on the Pascal VOC 2012 test leaderboard using only 1/10 parameters of it. On average, SegNeXt achieves about 2.0% mIoU improvements compared to the state-of-the-art methods on the ADE20K datasets with the same or fewer computations.

paragraphs: Semantic segmentation assigns categories across an image, making spatial context central to accurate predictions. This paper introduces SegNeXt, a convolutional architecture that revisits how attention can encode that context. The authors examine characteristics of successful segmentation models and use those findings to design attention around inexpensive convolutional operations.

The design tests whether convolutional attention can provide a more effective and efficient way to capture context than transformer self-attention. SegNeXt reports substantial improvements over previous leading methods on benchmarks including ADE20K, Cityscapes, COCO-Stuff, Pascal VOC, Pascal Context, and iSAID. These comparisons connect the architectural argument to segmentation performance across several datasets.

On the Pascal VOC 2012 test leaderboard, SegNeXt reaches 90.6% mean intersection over union while using one tenth the parameters of EfficientNet-L2 with NAS-FPN, which it outperforms. On ADE20K, the authors report average improvements of about 2.0% mIoU with equal or lower computation. The results support convolutional attention as a competitive way to combine contextual modeling with computational efficiency in the evaluated segmentation settings.
summary.tldr: SegNeXt uses inexpensive convolutional attention to improve segmentation accuracy and efficiency across the reported benchmarks.

title: SegNeXt: Rethinking Convolutional Attention Design for Semantic Segmentation

abstract: We introduce \textit{Nocturne}, a new 2D driving simulator for investigating multi-agent coordination under partial observability. The focus of Nocturne is to enable research into inference and theory of mind in real-world multi-agent settings without the computational overhead of computer vision and feature extraction from images. Agents in this simulator only observe an obstructed view of the scene, mimicking human visual sensing constraints. Unlike existing benchmarks that are bottlenecked by rendering human-like observations directly using a camera input, Nocturne uses efficient intersection methods to compute a vectorized set of visible features in a C++ back-end, allowing the simulator to run at $2000+$ steps-per-second. Using open-source trajectory and map data, we construct a simulator to load and replay arbitrary trajectories and scenes from real-world driving data. Using this environment, we benchmark reinforcement-learning and imitation-learning agents and demonstrate that the agents are quite far from human-level coordination ability and deviate significantly from the expert trajectories.

paragraphs: Nocturne is a two-dimensional driving simulator designed to study coordination among agents that cannot observe the entire scene. Its focus is inference about other agents and theory of mind in realistic multi-agent situations. Obstructed views preserve a key sensing constraint while avoiding the computational burden of processing camera images.

The simulator computes visible features using efficient intersection operations in a C++ back end and returns them in vectorized form. This enables more than 2,000 simulation steps per second. Open-source maps and trajectory data allow it to load and replay arbitrary scenes and trajectories from real-world driving records.

The authors benchmark reinforcement-learning and imitation-learning agents in this environment. These agents remain well below human coordination ability and depart substantially from expert trajectories. The result identifies coordination under partial observability as a challenge even when image rendering and visual feature extraction are removed from the learning problem. Nocturne offers an efficient environment for investigating that challenge using scenes grounded in real driving data.
summary.tldr: Nocturne efficiently simulates partially observed driving scenes and exposes substantial coordination gaps in reinforcement-learning and imitation-learning agents.

title: Nocturne: a scalable driving benchmark for bringing multi-agent learning one step closer to the real world

abstract: The factorization of state-action value functions for Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) is important. Existing studies are limited by their representation capability, sample efficiency, and approximation error. To address these challenges, we propose, ResQ, a MARL value function factorization method, which can find the optimal joint policy for any state-action value function through residual functions. ResQ masks some state-action value pairs from a joint state-action value function, which is transformed as the sum of a main function and a residual function. ResQ can be used with mean-value and stochastic-value RL. We theoretically show that ResQ can satisfy both the individual global max (IGM) and the distributional IGM principle without representation limitations. Through experiments on matrix games, the predator-prey, and StarCraft benchmarks, we show that ResQ can obtain better results than multiple expected/stochastic value factorization methods.

paragraphs: In multi-agent reinforcement learning, value factorization connects the value of a team’s joint action to components that support individual decisions. Existing approaches can restrict which joint value functions they represent, alongside difficulties with sample efficiency and approximation error. ResQ introduces residual functions to address these problems.

The method masks selected state-action value pairs and rewrites the joint value function as a main function plus a residual function. The authors show that this construction can find an optimal joint policy for any state-action value function. It applies both to methods using expected values and to methods representing stochastic values.

These principles connect individual maximizing choices to joint maximizing behavior, making the factorization useful for coordinated decisions. Experiments on matrix games, predator-prey, and StarCraft report better results than multiple expected-value and stochastic-value factorization methods. Thus, the paper combines a broad representational result with empirical evidence of improved performance in the evaluated tasks.
summary.tldr: ResQ uses residual value functions to support optimal joint policies without the representation restrictions of existing value factorizations.

title: ResQ: A Residual Q Function-based Approach for Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning Value Factorization

abstract: Flow networks are ubiquitous in natural and engineered systems, and in order to understand and manage these networks, one must quantify the flow of commodities across their edges. This paper considers the estimation problem of predicting unlabeled edge flows from nodal supply and demand. We propose an implicit neural network layer that incorporates two fundamental physical laws: conservation of mass, and the existence of a constitutive relationship between edge flows and nodal states (e.g., Ohm's law). Computing the edge flows from these two laws is a nonlinear inverse problem, which our layer solves efficiently with a specialized contraction mapping. Using implicit differentiation to compute the solution's gradients, our model is able to learn the constitutive relationship within a semi-supervised framework. We demonstrate that our approach can accurately predict edge flows in several experiments on AC power networks and water distribution systems.

It builds physical relationships directly into a neural network layer so that prediction reflects the structure of the flow problem.

This combines known conservation structure with a relationship inferred from data. Experiments on AC power networks and water distribution systems demonstrate accurate edge-flow predictions, supporting the approach across the two types of network considered.
summary.tldr: An implicit neural layer combines flow conservation with a learned constitutive relationship to predict unlabeled network edge flows.

title: Physics-Informed Implicit Representations of Equilibrium Network Flows

abstract: Neural approaches for combinatorial optimization (CO) equip a learning mechanism to discover powerful heuristics for solving complex real-world problems. While neural approaches capable of high-quality solutions in a single shot are emerging, state-of-the-art approaches are often unable to take full advantage of the solving time available to them. In contrast, hand-crafted heuristics perform highly effective search well and exploit the computation time given to them, but contain heuristics that are difficult to adapt to a dataset being solved. With the goal of providing a powerful search procedure to neural CO approaches, we propose simulation-guided beam search (SGBS), which examines candidate solutions within a fixed-width tree search that both a neural net-learned policy and a simulation (rollout) identify as promising. We further hybridize SGBS with efficient active search (EAS), where SGBS enhances the quality of solutions backpropagated in EAS, and EAS improves the quality of the policy used in SGBS. We evaluate our methods on well-known CO benchmarks and show that SGBS significantly improves the quality of the solutions found under reasonable runtime assumptions.

paragraphs: Neural combinatorial optimization can learn effective heuristics, but strong methods do not always make full use of the time available to solve a problem. SGBS explores a tree while retaining a fixed-width set of candidates. Both a neural policy and simulation rollouts help identify promising possibilities. This combines learned guidance with examination of candidate continuations, allowing the search to investigate options beyond the initial output of the policy.

The authors also combine SGBS with efficient active search. The two methods reinforce each other: SGBS supplies better solutions for active-search updates, while active search improves the policy guiding SGBS. Evaluations on established combinatorial optimization benchmarks show significant solution-quality improvements under reasonable runtime assumptions. The contribution is thus a search mechanism, and a complementary learning loop, for using available solving time more effectively.
summary.tldr: Simulation-guided beam search combines learned policies and rollouts to improve combinatorial solutions within practical runtime budgets.

title: Simulation-guided Beam Search for Neural Combinatorial Optimization

abstract: In this paper, we study a novel approach for data-driven decision-making under uncertainty in the presence of contextual information. Specifically, we solve this problem from a Conditional Robust Optimization (CRO) point of view. We propose an integrated framework that designs the conditional uncertainty set by jointly learning the partitions in the covariate data space and simultaneously constructing partition specific deep uncertainty sets for the random vector that perturbs the CRO problem. We also provide theoretical guarantees for the coverage of the uncertainty sets and value at risk performances obtained using the proposed CRO approach. Finally, we use the simulated and real world data to show the implementation of our approach and compare it against two non-contextual benchmark approaches to demonstrate the value of exploiting contextual information in robust optimization.

Finally, we use the simulated and real world data to show the implementation of our approach and compare it against two non-contextual benchmark approaches to demonstrate the value of exploiting contextual information in robust optimization.

paragraphs: The paper studies decisions made under uncertainty when contextual information is also available. Its central question is how that context should shape the uncertainty considered during optimization. The authors use Conditional Robust Optimization, where the set of possible disturbances depends on the information associated with a particular decision.

Their framework jointly learns a partition of the contextual data space and constructs a deep uncertainty set for each partition. In plain terms, it learns both which contexts should be grouped together and what uncertainty should be represented within each group. Learning these pieces together makes the uncertainty description responsive to context, rather than using one description across all cases.

The authors provide theoretical guarantees for uncertainty-set coverage and the resulting value-at-risk performance. These address whether the sets capture uncertain outcomes and how the optimization performs according to a risk criterion. Experiments with simulated and real-world data illustrate the method and compare it with two approaches that do not use context. The comparisons demonstrate the value of incorporating contextual information into robust decision-making.
summary.tldr: Jointly learning context groups and their uncertainty sets supports robust decisions with coverage and value-at-risk guarantees.

title: Data-Driven Conditional Robust Optimization

abstract: Sentence scoring aims at measuring the likelihood score of a sentence and is widely used in many natural language processing scenarios, like reranking, which is to select the best sentence from multiple candidates. Previous works on sentence scoring mainly adopted either causal language modeling (CLM) like GPT or masked language modeling (MLM) like BERT, which have some limitations: 1) CLM only utilizes unidirectional information for the probability estimation of a sentence without considering bidirectional context, which affects the scoring quality; 2) MLM can only estimate the probability of partial tokens at a time and thus requires multiple forward passes to estimate the probability of the whole sentence, which incurs large computation and time cost. In this paper, we propose \textit{Transcormer} -- a Transformer model with a novel \textit{sliding language modeling} (SLM) for sentence scoring. Specifically, our SLM adopts a triple-stream self-attention mechanism to estimate the probability of all tokens in a sentence with bidirectional context and only requires a single forward pass. SLM can avoid the limitations of CLM (only unidirectional context) and MLM (multiple forward passes) and inherit their advantages, and thus achieve high effectiveness and efficiency in scoring. Experimental results on multiple tasks demonstrate that our method achieves better performance than other language modelings.
