paragraphs: Sentence scoring assigns a likelihood-based score to a sentence, supporting tasks such as choosing among candidate outputs. Existing language-modeling approaches face a tradeoff. Causal models estimate probabilities using context in only one direction, while masked models use bidirectional information but require multiple forward passes to score all the tokens in a sentence.

Transcormer introduces sliding language modeling to combine bidirectional context with single-pass scoring. Its triple-stream self-attention mechanism estimates probabilities for every token during one forward pass. This makes the attention design central to both goals: using information from both sides of a token and avoiding repeated model evaluations for the complete sentence.

Experiments on multiple tasks report better performance than the other language-modeling approaches considered. The stated significance is improved scoring effectiveness together with computational efficiency. By designing the training and attention mechanism specifically for sentence scoring, Transcormer addresses the limitations that arise when causal or masked language models are used for this purpose.
summary.tldr: Transcormer uses triple-stream attention to score all sentence tokens with bidirectional context in a single forward pass.

title: Transcormer: Transformer for Sentence Scoring with Sliding Language Modeling

abstract: Considering the ever-increasing scale of data, which may contain tens of thousands of data points or complicated latent structures, the issue of scalability and algorithmic efficiency becomes of vital importance for clustering. In this paper, we propose cluster-wise amortized mixing coupling processes (AMCP), which is able to achieve efficient amortized clustering in a well-defined non-parametric Bayesian posterior. Specifically, AMCP learns clusters sequentially with the aid of the proposed intra-cluster mixing (IntraCM) and inter-cluster coupling (InterCC) strategies, which investigate the relationship between data points and reference distribution in a linear optimal transport mixing view, and coupling the unassigned set and assigned set to generate new cluster. IntraCM and InterCC avoid pairwise calculation of distances between clusters and reduce the computational complexity from quadratic to linear in the current number of clusters. Furthermore, cluster-wise sequential process is able to improve the quick adaptation ability for the next cluster generation. In this case, AMCP simultaneously learns what makes a cluster, how to group data points into clusters, and how to adaptively control the number of clusters. To illustrate the superiority of the proposed method, we perform experiments on both synthetic data and real-world data in terms of clustering performance and computational efficiency. The source code is available at https://github.com/HuafengHK/AMCP.

paragraphs: Clustering becomes computationally demanding when datasets grow large or contain complicated hidden structure. This paper proposes Amortized Mixing Coupling Processes, or AMCP, to learn how to form clusters within a defined nonparametric Bayesian posterior. The method learns clusters sequentially and can adapt the number of clusters as part of that process.

Two mechanisms guide cluster formation. Intra-cluster mixing examines relationships between data points and a reference distribution through an optimal transport mixing perspective. Inter-cluster coupling connects points that have already been assigned with those that remain unassigned to generate a new cluster. Together, these mechanisms avoid computing pairwise distances between clusters.

The stated complexity improvement is from quadratic to linear in the current number of clusters. Sequential cluster construction also helps the method adapt when generating the next cluster. AMCP therefore learns what constitutes a cluster, how points should be grouped, and how many groups to create. Experiments on synthetic and real-world data evaluate both clustering quality and computational efficiency and are presented as evidence for the method’s advantages.
summary.tldr: AMCP learns clusters sequentially while reducing cluster-related computation from quadratic to linear in the current cluster count.

title: Amortized Mixing Coupling Processes for Clustering

abstract: Stabilizing an unknown dynamical system is one of the central problems in control theory. In this paper, we study the sample complexity of the learn-to-stabilize problem in Linear Time-Invariant (LTI) systems on a single trajectory. Current state-of-the-art approaches require a sample complexity linear in $n$, the state dimension, which incurs a state norm that blows up exponentially in $n$. We propose a novel algorithm based on spectral decomposition that only needs to learn ``a small part'' of the dynamical matrix acting on its unstable subspace. We show that, under proper assumptions, our algorithm stabilizes an LTI system on a single trajectory with $O(k \log n)$ samples, where $k$ is the instability index of the system. This represents the first sub-linear sample complexity result for the stabilization of LTI systems under the regime when $k = o(n)$.

paragraphs: Learning to stabilize an unknown dynamical system requires gathering information while the system is already evolving. For linear time-invariant systems, the paper studies how many observations are needed along a single trajectory. Existing leading approaches require a number of samples linear in the state dimension, which the abstract associates with state magnitudes growing exponentially in that dimension.

The proposed algorithm uses spectral decomposition to focus learning on the unstable subspace. Instead of learning the entire dynamical matrix, it learns only the part acting on that subspace. This targets the components of the dynamics responsible for instability, making the amount of information required depend on the system's instability index as well as its overall dimension.

Under appropriate assumptions, the authors prove stabilization using O(k log n) samples, where n is the state dimension and k is the instability index. They present this as the first sublinear sample-complexity result in the stated low-instability regime. The guarantee is conditional, and its significance is that stabilization can require learning substantially less than the full system.
summary.tldr: Under suitable assumptions, learning only unstable dynamics allows stabilization from a single trajectory using O(k log n) samples.

title: On the Sample Complexity of Stabilizing LTI Systems on a Single Trajectory

abstract: Recent advances in distributed optimization and learning have shown that communication compression is one of the most effective means of reducing communication. While there have been many results for convergence rates with compressed communication, a lower bound is still missing.Analyses of algorithms with communication compression have identified two abstract properties that guarantee convergence: the unbiased property or the contractive property. They can be applied either unidirectionally (compressing messages from worker to server) or bidirectionally. In the smooth and non-convex stochastic regime, this paper establishes a lower bound for distributed algorithms whether using unbiased or contractive compressors in unidirection or bidirection. To close the gap between this lower bound and the best existing upper bound, we further propose an algorithm, NEOLITHIC, that almost reaches our lower bound (except for a logarithm factor) under mild conditions. Our results also show that using contractive compressors in bidirection can yield iterative methods that converge as fast as those using unbiased compressors unidirectionally. We report experimental results that validate our findings.

paragraphs: Communication compression reduces the cost of exchanging information in distributed learning, but convergence guarantees alone do not establish how close an algorithm is to the best achievable performance. This paper supplies lower bounds for compressed distributed optimization in the smooth, non-convex stochastic setting, providing a reference against which algorithmic guarantees can be assessed.

The analysis covers compressors with either an unbiased or a contractive property. It also treats both worker-to-server compression and compression in both communication directions. By considering these combinations within the same study, the authors compare fundamental convergence limits across different ways of reducing communication.

The proposed algorithm, NEOLITHIC, approaches the lower bound up to a logarithmic factor under mild conditions. The results also show that bidirectional contractive compression can yield iterative methods converging as fast as methods using unbiased compression only from workers to the server. Experiments support the theoretical findings. The main contribution is a combination of performance limits and an algorithm that nearly attains them, with the stated conditions and logarithmic gap retained.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes compressed distributed-learning lower bounds and introduces NEOLITHIC, which nearly matches them under mild conditions.

title: Lower Bounds and Nearly Optimal Algorithms in Distributed Learning with Communication Compression

abstract: Most of existing work on fairness assumes available demographic information in the training set. In practice, due to legal or privacy concerns, when demographic information is not available in the training set, it is crucial to find alternative objectives to ensure fairness. Existing work on fairness without demographics follows Rawlsian Max-Min fairness objectives. However, such constraints could be too strict to improve group fairness, and could lead to a great decrease in accuracy. In light of these limitations, in this paper, we propose to solve the problem from a new perspective, i.e., through knowledge distillation. Our method uses soft label from an overfitted teacher model as an alternative, and we show from preliminary experiments that soft labelling is beneficial for improving fairness. We analyze theoretically the fairness of our method, and we show that our method can be treated as an error-based reweighing. Experimental results on three datasets show that our method outperforms state-of-the-art alternatives, with notable improvements in group fairness and with relatively small decrease in accuracy.

paragraphs: Many fairness methods assume access to demographic labels during training, but privacy or legal concerns can make those labels unavailable. Existing approaches without demographics often use Rawlsian max-min objectives. The authors argue that these constraints can be too strict for improving group fairness and can substantially reduce predictive accuracy.

The paper proposes knowledge distillation as an alternative. An overfitted teacher model supplies soft labels, which express graded predictions rather than only a single assigned class. Preliminary experiments suggest that training with these labels can benefit fairness. The authors also analyze the method theoretically and interpret its effect as reweighting examples according to errors.

Experiments on three datasets show improvements over the compared state-of-the-art alternatives, with notable gains in group fairness and relatively small accuracy decreases. This evidence supports soft-label distillation as a useful approach in the studied settings where demographic information is absent from training. The reported outcome retains an accuracy tradeoff, while offering a different way to influence fairness through the training targets.
summary.tldr: Distillation from an overfitted teacher improves group fairness without training-time demographics in experiments, with relatively small accuracy losses.

title: Fairness without Demographics through Knowledge Distillation

abstract: We study the problem of PAC learning a single neuron in the presence of Massart noise. Specifically, for a known activation function $f: \mathbb{R}\to \mathbb{R}$, the learner is given access to labeled examples $(\mathbf{x}, y) \in \mathbb{R}^d \times \mathbb{R}$, where the marginal distribution of $\mathbf{x}$ is arbitrary and the corresponding label $y$ is a Massart corruption of $f(\langle \mathbf{w}, \mathbf{x} \rangle)$. The goal of the learner is to output a hypothesis $h: \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}$ with small squared loss. For a range of activation functions, including ReLUs, we establish super-polynomial Statistical Query (SQ) lower bounds for this learning problem. In more detail, we prove that no efficient SQ algorithm can approximate the optimal error within any constant factor. Our main technical contribution is a novel SQ-hard construction for learning $\{ \pm 1\}$-weight Massart halfspaces on the Boolean hypercube that is interesting on its own right.

paragraphs: This paper asks how difficult it is to learn even a single neuron when labels suffer Massart corruption. The learner knows the activation function, but must infer a predictor from examples whose inputs can follow an arbitrary distribution. The target applies that activation to a weighted combination of inputs, and prediction quality is measured by squared loss.

For a range of activation functions, including ReLU, the authors establish super-polynomial lower bounds in the Statistical Query model of learning. More specifically, no efficient algorithm within this model can approximate the optimal error within any constant factor. This identifies a strong computational barrier even though the target has only one neuron.

The central technical ingredient is a hard construction involving Massart-corrupted halfspaces on Boolean inputs with weights restricted to plus or minus one. That construction supports the broader neuron-learning lower bounds and is also presented as a contribution in its own right. The result concerns Statistical Query algorithms under arbitrary input distributions; its significance is the difficulty established within that specified learning framework.
summary.tldr: Learning a single noisy neuron can require super-polynomial Statistical Query complexity, even for constant-factor approximation of optimal error.

title: SQ Lower Bounds for Learning Single Neurons with Massart Noise

abstract: We study exact active learning of binary and multiclass classifiers with margin. Given an $n$-point set $X \subset \mathbb{R}^m$, we want to learn an unknown classifier on $X$ whose classes have finite strong convex hull margin, a new notion extending the SVM margin. In the standard active learning setting, where only label queries are allowed, learning a classifier with strong convex hull margin $\gamma$ requires in the worst case $\Omega\big(1+\frac{1}{\gamma}\big)^{\frac{m-1}{2}}$ queries. On the other hand, using the more powerful \emph{seed} queries (a variant of equivalence queries), the target classifier could be learned in $O(m \log n)$ queries via Littlestone's Halving algorithm; however, Halving is computationally inefficient. In this work we show that, by carefully combining the two types of queries, a binary classifier can be learned in time $\operatorname{poly}(n+m)$ using only $O(m^2 \log n)$ label queries and $O\big(m \log \frac{m}{\gamma}\big)$ seed queries; the result extends to $k$-class classifiers at the price of a $k!k^2$ multiplicative overhead. Similar results hold when the input points have bounded bit complexity, or when only one class has strong convex hull margin against the rest. We complement the upper bounds by showing that in the worst case any algorithm needs $\Omega\big(k m \log \frac{1}{\gamma}\big)$ seed and label queries to learn a $k$-class classifier with strong convex hull margin $\gamma$.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to recover an unknown classifier’s labels exactly on a finite collection of points while asking relatively few questions. It covers both two-class and multiclass problems. Its geometric assumption is a new separation measure called strong convex hull margin, which extends the margin used in support vector machines.

The central challenge is balancing the number of questions against the computation needed to choose them. With ordinary label queries alone, the worst-case query requirement grows sharply with dimension and inverse margin. More powerful seed queries, a variant of equivalence queries, allow Littlestone’s Halving algorithm to use O(m log n) queries, but that algorithm is computationally inefficient.

The authors show that carefully combining both query types achieves polynomial running time in the number of points n and dimension m. For binary classification, their method uses O(m² log n) label queries and O(m log(m/γ)) seed queries, where γ is the margin. This establishes that a mixture of queries can support both computational efficiency and controlled query counts.

The result extends to k classes with a k!k² multiplicative overhead. Similar guarantees hold for bounded-bit-complexity inputs or when just one class has the required margin against the others. A complementary worst-case lower bound of Ω(km log(1/γ)) on seed and label queries shows that some dependence on class count, dimension, and margin is unavoidable.
summary.tldr: Combining label and seed queries enables exact learning of classifiers under a geometric margin assumption with polynomial computation and provable query bounds.

title: Active Learning of Classifiers with Label and Seed Queries

abstract: We consider the classical multi-armed bandit problem and design simple-to-implement new policies that simultaneously enjoy two properties: worst-case optimality for the expected regret, and safety against heavy-tailed risk for the regret distribution. Recently, Fan and Glynn (2021) showed that information-theoretic optimized bandit policies as well as standard UCB policies suffer from some serious heavy-tailed risk; that is, the probability of incurring a linear regret slowly decays at a polynomial rate of $1/T$, as $T$ (the time horizon) increases. Inspired by their result, we further show that any policy that incurs an instance-dependent $O(\ln T)$ regret must incur a linear regret with probability $\Omega(\mathrm{poly}(1/T))$ and that the heavy-tailed risk actually exists for all "instance-dependent consistent" policies. Next, for the two-armed bandit setting, we provide a simple policy design that (i) has the worst-case optimality for the expected regret at order $\tilde O(\sqrt{T})$ and (ii) has the worst-case tail probability of incurring a linear regret decay at an exponential rate $\exp(-\Omega(\sqrt{T}))$. We further prove that this exponential decaying rate of the tail probability is optimal across all policies that have worst-case optimality for the expected regret. Finally, we generalize the policy design and analysis to the general setting with an arbitrary $K$ number of arms. We provide detailed characterization of the tail probability bound for any regret threshold under our policy design. Numerical experiments are conducted to illustrate the theoretical findings. Our results reveal insights on the incompatibility between consistency and light-tailed risk, whereas indicate that worst-case optimality on expected regret and light-tailed risk are compatible.

paragraphs: A bandit policy can perform well on average while retaining a substantial chance of a very poor run. This paper studies that distinction through regret: the performance lost while learning which arm to choose. Its concern is heavy-tailed regret risk, specifically the probability of regret growing linearly with the time horizon.

The authors prove that policies achieving instance-dependent logarithmic expected regret must retain a polynomially decaying probability of linear regret. They extend this negative finding to all policies in the instance-dependent consistent class. Thus, the strong instance-specific performance criterion carries a restriction on how quickly severe-outcome probabilities can disappear.

For two arms, they design a simple policy with worst-case expected regret of roughly square-root order and linear-regret probability decreasing exponentially in the square root of the horizon. They prove that tail rate is optimal among policies with worst-case-optimal expected regret, then extend the design and analysis to arbitrary arm counts. Numerical experiments illustrate the theory: worst-case average efficiency and light-tailed regret risk can coexist.
summary.tldr: New bandit policies combine worst-case-optimal expected regret with sharply reduced severe-regret risk, while theory exposes a trade-off with instance-dependent consistency.

title: A Simple and Optimal Policy Design for Online Learning with Safety against Heavy-tailed Risk

abstract: Learning in real-world multiagent tasks is challenging due to the usual partial observability of each agent. Previous efforts alleviate the partial observability by historical hidden states with Recurrent Neural Networks, however, they do not consider the multiagent characters that either the multiagent observation consists of a number of object entities or the action space shows clear entity interactions. To tackle these issues, we propose the Agent Transformer Memory (ATM) network with a transformer-based memory. First, ATM utilizes the transformer to enable the unified processing of the factored environmental entities and memory. Inspired by the human’s working memory process where a limited capacity of information temporarily held in mind can effectively guide the decision-making, ATM updates its fixed-capacity memory with the working memory updating schema. Second, as agents' each action has its particular interaction entities in the environment, ATM parses the action space to introduce this action’s semantic inductive bias by binding each action with its specified involving entity to predict the state-action value or logit. Extensive experiments on the challenging SMAC and Level-Based Foraging environments validate that ATM could boost existing multiagent RL algorithms with impressive learning acceleration and performance improvement.

paragraphs: Agents in multiagent environments often observe only part of the situation, making memory useful for decision-making. The paper argues that recurrent hidden-state approaches overlook two structural features: observations contain distinct entities, and actions often describe interactions with particular entities. Agent Transformer Memory, or ATM, builds these features into the network.

ATM uses a Transformer to process environmental entities together with a fixed-capacity memory. Its memory update scheme is inspired by working memory, maintaining a limited amount of information that can guide current choices. This provides a shared processing mechanism for information present in the current observation and information retained from earlier observations.

The network also parses actions and binds each one to the entity involved in that action when predicting its value or logit. This introduces knowledge of action meaning directly into prediction. Experiments on SMAC and Level-Based Foraging show faster learning and improved performance when ATM augments existing multiagent reinforcement learning algorithms. The results support combining structured entity processing, bounded memory, and action-specific relationships in partially observable multiagent tasks.
summary.tldr: ATM combines Transformer-based memory with action–entity relationships to improve learning in partially observable multiagent environments.

title: Transformer-based Working Memory for Multiagent Reinforcement Learning with Action Parsing

abstract: We consider the query complexity of cake cutting in the standard query model and give lower and upper bounds for computing approximately envy-free, perfect, and equitable allocations with the minimum number of cuts. The lower bounds are tight for computing contiguous envy-free allocations among $n=3$ players and for computing perfect and equitable allocations with minimum number of cuts between $n=2$ players. For $\epsilon$-envy-free allocations with contiguous pieces, we also give an upper bound of $O(n/\epsilon)$ and lower bound of $\Omega(\log(1/\epsilon))$ queries for any number $n \geq 3$ of players.We also formalize moving knife procedures and show that a large subclass of this family, which captures all the known moving knife procedures, can be simulated efficiently with arbitrarily small error in the Robertson-Webb query model.

paragraphs: Cake cutting studies how to divide a resource fairly when participants value its parts differently. This paper asks how many queries about those preferences are needed to compute approximate fair allocations. It considers envy-free, perfect, and equitable allocations while also requiring the minimum number of cuts.

The authors establish upper and lower bounds, separating what algorithms can achieve from what any algorithm must spend in the query model. Tight bounds are obtained for contiguous envy-free allocations with three players, and for perfect and equitable allocations with minimum cuts between two players. For contiguous ε-envy-free allocations with any n ≥ 3, they give an O(n/ε) upper bound and an Ω(log(1/ε)) lower bound.

The paper also formalizes moving-knife procedures, which describe allocation through continuously moving cuts. It shows that a large subclass containing all known procedures can be simulated efficiently with arbitrarily small error in the Robertson–Webb query model. This connects continuous descriptions of fair-division procedures to algorithms that obtain information through discrete queries.
summary.tldr: The paper bounds the preference queries needed for approximate fair division and efficiently simulates a broad class of moving-knife procedures.

title: The Query Complexity of Cake Cutting

abstract: The vast majority of time-series forecasting approaches require a substantial training dataset. However, many real-life forecasting applications have very little initial observations, sometimes just 40 or fewer. Thus, the applicability of most forecasting methods is restricted in data-sparse commercial applications. While there is recent work in the setting of very limited initial data (so-called `zero-shot' forecasting), its performance is inconsistent depending on the data used for pretraining. In this work, we take a different approach and devise ForecastPFN, the first zero-shot forecasting model trained purely on a novel synthetic data distribution. ForecastPFN is a prior-data fitted network, trained to approximate Bayesian inference, which can make predictions on a new time series dataset in a single forward pass. Through extensive experiments, we show that zero-shot predictions made by ForecastPFN are more accurate and faster compared to state-of-the-art forecasting methods, even when the other methods are allowed to train on hundreds of additional in-distribution data points.

paragraphs: Many forecasting applications begin with very short observation histories, sometimes 40 points or fewer. Methods that depend on substantial task-specific training data are difficult to apply in that setting. ForecastPFN addresses this problem through zero-shot forecasting: a pretrained model predicts a new series without first undergoing a separate training procedure for that dataset.

The model is trained entirely on a newly designed synthetic data distribution. As a prior-data fitted network, it learns to approximate Bayesian inference and can produce predictions for a new time-series dataset in one forward pass. This shifts the training burden into advance preparation on synthetic series, allowing the deployed predictor to work directly with the observations available.

The authors report experiments in which ForecastPFN is both more accurate and faster than state-of-the-art forecasting methods. The comparisons include cases where competing methods can train on hundreds of additional points from the target distribution. These empirical findings support synthetic pretraining as an effective route to forecasting with scarce initial data in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: ForecastPFN learns from synthetic series to deliver fast zero-shot forecasts, outperforming the compared methods in the reported experiments.

title: ForecastPFN: Synthetically-Trained Zero-Shot Forecasting

abstract: Recent progress in Quality Diversity Reinforcement Learning (QD-RL) has enabled learning a collection of behaviorally diverse, high performing policies. However, these methods typically involve storing thousands of policies, which results in high space-complexity and poor scaling to additional behaviors. Condensing the archive into a single model while retaining the performance and coverage of theoriginal collection of policies has proved challenging. In this work, we propose using diffusion models to distill the archive into a single generative model over policy parameters. We show that our method achieves a compression ratio of 13x while recovering 98% of the original rewards and 89% of the original humanoid archive coverage. Further, the conditioning mechanism of diffusion models allowsfor flexibly selecting and sequencing behaviors, including using language. Project website: https://sites.google.com/view/policydiffusion/home.

paragraphs: Quality-diversity reinforcement learning aims to produce many successful policies that behave differently. Keeping thousands of separate policies, however, consumes substantial storage and makes it harder to accommodate additional behaviors. This paper asks whether a single generative model can preserve much of an archive’s performance and behavioral range while representing it more compactly.

The proposed method distills the archive into a diffusion model that generates policy parameters. Instead of storing every policy separately, the model represents a source from which policies can be produced. This makes preserving both reward and behavioral coverage central: compressing the archive would be less useful if it retained only a narrow set of successful behaviors.

The authors report thirteenfold compression while recovering 98% of the original rewards and 89% of the original humanoid archive’s coverage. These figures show substantial retention rather than complete preservation. Conditioning the diffusion model also enables flexible selection and sequencing of behaviors, including through language. The resulting model therefore serves both as a compressed representation of the archive and as an interface for choosing behaviors.
summary.tldr: A diffusion model compresses a diverse policy archive thirteenfold while retaining most rewards and behavioral coverage and enabling conditioned behavior selection.

title: Generating Behaviorally Diverse Policies with Latent Diffusion Models

abstract: Training recurrent neural networks (RNNs) remains a challenge due to the instability of gradients across long time horizons, which can lead to exploding and vanishing gradients. Recent research has linked these problems to the values of Lyapunov exponents for the forward-dynamics, which describe the growth or shrinkage of infinitesimal perturbations. Here, we propose gradient flossing, a novel approach to tackling gradient instability by pushing Lyapunov exponents of the forward dynamics toward zero during learning. We achieve this by regularizing Lyapunov exponents through backpropagation using differentiable linear algebra. This enables us to "floss" the gradients, stabilizing them and thus improving network training. We show that gradient flossing controls not only the gradient norm but also the condition number of the long-term Jacobian, facilitating multidimensional error feedback propagation. We find that applying gradient flossing before training enhances both the success rate and convergence speed for tasks involving long time horizons.For challenging tasks, we show that gradient flossing during training can further increase the time horizon that can be bridged by backpropagation through time. Moreover, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on various RNN architectures and tasks of variable temporal complexity. Additionally, we provide a simple implementation of our gradient flossing algorithm that can be used in practice. Our results indicate that gradient flossing via regularizing Lyapunov exponents can significantly enhance the effectiveness of RNN training and mitigate the exploding and vanishing gradients problem.

paragraphs: Recurrent neural networks can struggle to learn from distant events because gradients grow excessively or shrink away across many time steps. Gradient flossing addresses this through the network's forward dynamics. It pushes Lyapunov exponents, which describe how tiny perturbations grow or contract, toward zero during learning.

The method regularizes these exponents using backpropagation through differentiable linear algebra. Its influence extends beyond controlling overall gradient size: it also controls the condition number of the long-term Jacobian. That matters because useful error signals need to propagate across multiple directions, not merely retain a reasonable total magnitude.

The authors find that applying flossing before task training improves success rates and convergence speed on long-horizon tasks. For challenging tasks, applying it during training can further extend the time span that backpropagation through time can bridge. Experiments cover different recurrent architectures and temporal complexities, and the paper provides a simple implementation. The results support regulating dynamical stability as a practical way to mitigate exploding and vanishing gradients.
summary.tldr: Gradient flossing regularizes recurrent-network dynamics to stabilize gradients and improve learning over long time horizons.

title: Gradient Flossing: Improving Gradient Descent through Dynamic Control of Jacobians

abstract: Geodesics play a critical role in many geometry processing applications. Traditional algorithms for computing geodesics on 3D mesh models are often inefficient and slow, which make them impractical for scenarios requiring extensive querying of arbitrary point-to-point geodesics. Recently, deep implicit functions have gained popularity for 3D geometry representation, yet there is still no research on neural implicit representation of geodesics. To bridge this gap, we make the first attempt to represent geodesics using implicit learning frameworks. Specifically, we propose neural geodesic field (NeuroGF), which can be learned to encode all-pairs geodesics of a given 3D mesh model, enabling to efficiently and accurately answer queries of arbitrary point-to-point geodesic distances and paths. Evaluations on common 3D object models and real-captured scene-level meshes demonstrate our exceptional performances in terms of representation accuracy and querying efficiency. Besides, NeuroGF also provides a convenient way of jointly encoding both 3D geometry and geodesics in a unified representation. Moreover, the working mode of per-model overfitting is further extended to generalizable learning frameworks that can work on various input formats such as unstructured point clouds, which also show satisfactory performances for unseen shapes and categories. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/keeganhk/NeuroGF.

paragraphs: Geodesic queries ask for distances and paths along a shape's surface. Many geometry-processing applications need large numbers of these queries between arbitrary points, which can make traditional mesh algorithms costly. NeuroGF investigates whether a learned neural representation can store this information in a form that supports efficient distance and path queries.

The proposed neural geodesic field learns an implicit representation of all-pairs geodesics for a given 3D mesh. Once learned, it can answer queries between arbitrary points on that model. The framework also offers a unified representation for both the underlying 3D geometry and its geodesics, connecting the shape description with information about travel along its surface.

Evaluations on common object models and meshes of captured scenes report strong representation accuracy and query efficiency. The authors further extend the initial approach, which fits an individual model, into generalizable learning frameworks. These accept input formats including unstructured point clouds and show satisfactory performance on unseen shapes and categories. This extension broadens the approach beyond separately learning every queried mesh.
summary.tldr: NeuroGF learns neural representations of surface distances and paths for efficient geodesic queries on 3D shapes.

title: NeuroGF: A Neural Representation for Fast Geodesic Distance and Path Queries

abstract: Despite widespread use of LLMs as conversational agents, evaluations of performance fail to capture a crucial aspect of communication: interpreting language in context---incorporating its pragmatics. Humans interpret language using beliefs and prior knowledge about the world. For example, we intuitively understand the response "I wore gloves" to the question "Did you leave fingerprints?" as meaning "No". To investigate whether LLMs have the ability to make this type of inference, known as an implicature, we design a simple task and evaluate four categories of widely used state-of-the-art models. We find that, despite only evaluating on utterances that require a binary inference (yes or no), models in three of these categories perform close to random. However, LLMs instruction-tuned at the example-level perform significantly better. These results suggest that certain fine-tuning strategies are far better at inducing pragmatic understanding in models. We present our findings as the starting point for further research into evaluating how LLMs interpret language in context and to drive the development of more pragmatic and useful models of human discourse.

paragraphs: Conversation often communicates more than the literal words state. An indirect answer can imply yes or no through context and everyday knowledge. This paper studies whether language models can resolve such implicatures, addressing an aspect of communication that ordinary performance evaluations may fail to capture.

The authors design a simple task requiring binary inferences and evaluate four categories of widely used language models. Even though the requested answer is only yes or no, models in three categories perform near chance. Models instruction-tuned at the level of individual examples perform significantly better on the task.

The contrast suggests that fine-tuning strategy matters for eliciting pragmatic understanding, rather than conversational use alone demonstrating that ability. The findings establish a concrete evaluation target: interpreting what a speaker conveys indirectly using context. The paper presents this study as a starting point for broader investigation of contextual language understanding and for developing more useful conversational models, with the evidence specifically grounded in the tested binary implicature task.
summary.tldr: A binary implicature task reveals near-chance performance in three model categories but substantially better results from example-level instruction tuning.

title: The Goldilocks of Pragmatic Understanding: Fine-Tuning Strategy Matters for Implicature Resolution by LLMs

abstract: Due to the broad range of applications of multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL), understanding the effects of adversarial attacks against MARL model is essential for the safe applications of this model. Motivated by this, we investigate the impact of adversarial attacks on MARL. In the considered setup, there is an exogenous attacker who is able to modify the rewards before the agents receive them or manipulate the actions before the environment receives them. The attacker aims to guide each agent into a target policy or maximize the cumulative rewards under some specific reward function chosen by the attacker, while minimizing the amount of the manipulation on feedback and action. We first show the limitations of the action poisoning only attacks and the reward poisoning only attacks. We then introduce a mixed attack strategy with both the action poisoning and reward poisoning. We show that the mixed attack strategy can efficiently attack MARL agents even if the attacker has no prior information about the underlying environment and the agents’ algorithms.

paragraphs: This paper studies how an outside attacker can influence multiple reinforcement-learning agents as they learn. In the considered setting, the attacker can alter rewards before agents receive them or change actions before those actions reach the environment. These access points let the attacker interfere with both feedback and behavior.

The attacker seeks either to steer each agent toward a chosen policy or to increase cumulative rewards according to an attacker-selected objective. At the same time, the attacker wants to minimize the amount of manipulation. The authors first establish limitations of attacks that modify only actions or only rewards, then introduce a strategy that combines the two channels.

They show that the combined strategy can efficiently attack the agents even without prior knowledge of the environment or the agents' learning algorithms. The result identifies a vulnerability within the stated intervention setting: restrictions affecting either channel alone do not prevent an effective mixed attack. This makes the interaction between action manipulation and reward manipulation important for understanding the safety of multi-agent learning.
summary.tldr: Combining reward and action manipulation enables efficient attacks on multi-agent learners without prior knowledge of their environment or algorithms.

title: Efficient Adversarial Attacks on Online Multi-agent Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Given a Lipschitz or smooth convex function $f:K \to \mathbb{R}^d$ for a bounded polytope $K:=${ $\theta \in \mathbb{R}^d: A\theta \leq b$}, where $A\in \mathbb{R}^{m\times d}$ and $b \in \mathbb{R}^m$, we consider the problem of sampling from the log-concave distribution $\pi(\theta) \propto e^{-f(\theta)}$ constrained to $K$. Interest in this problem derives from its applications to Bayesian inference and differential privacy. We present a generalization of the Dikin walk to this setting that requires at most $O((md + d L^2 R^2) \times md^{\omega-1} \log(\frac{w}{\delta}))$ arithmetic operations to sample from $\pi$ within error $\delta>0$ in the total variation distance from a $w$-warm start. Here $L$ is the Lipschitz constant of $f$, $K$ is contained in a ball of radius $R$ and contains a ball of smaller radius $r$, and $\omega \approx 2.37$ is the matrix-multiplication constant. This improves on the running time of prior works for a range of structured settings important for the aforementioned inference and privacy applications. Technically, we depart from previous Dikin walks by adding a soft-threshold regularizer derived from the Lipschitz or smoothness properties of $f$ to a barrier function for $K$ that allows our version of the Dikin walk to propose updates that have a high Metropolis acceptance ratio for $f$, while at the same time remaining inside the polytope $K$.

Here $L$ is the Lipschitz constant of $f$, $K$ is contained in a ball of radius $R$ and contains a ball of smaller radius $r$, and $\omega \approx 2.37$ is the matrix-multiplication constant. This improves on the running time of prior works for a range of structured settings important for the aforementioned inference and privacy applications. Technically, we depart from previous Dikin walks by adding a soft-threshold regularizer derived from the Lipschitz or smoothness properties of $f$ to a barrier function for $K$ that allows our version of the Dikin walk to propose updates that have a high Metropolis acceptance ratio for $f$, while at the same time remaining inside the polytope $K$.

paragraphs: The paper studies sampling from a log-concave distribution restricted to a bounded polytope, a region defined by linear inequalities. The density is proportional to the exponential of a negative convex function, which is assumed to be Lipschitz or smooth. Such constrained sampling problems arise in Bayesian inference and differential privacy.

The proposed algorithm generalizes the Dikin walk by combining a barrier for the feasible region with a soft-threshold regularizer derived from the function's regularity. The barrier accounts for the polytope's boundaries, while the extra regularizer accounts for the target density. Together, they support proposed moves that stay inside the region and have a high Metropolis acceptance ratio.

Starting from a warm initial distribution, the authors bound the arithmetic operations needed to reach a specified total-variation error. The bound tracks dimensions, constraints, function regularity, region size, and requested accuracy. It improves on previous running times for a range of structured settings relevant to inference and privacy. The improvement is therefore tied to problem structure and the stated initialization and regularity conditions.
summary.tldr: A regularized Dikin walk improves constrained log-concave sampling bounds in structured settings under the stated regularity and warm-start conditions.

title: Sampling from Structured Log-Concave Distributions via a Soft-Threshold Dikin Walk

abstract: We study the mean estimation problem under communication and local differential privacy constraints. While previous work has proposed order-optimal algorithms for the same problem (i.e., asymptotically optimal as we spend more bits), exact optimality (in the non-asymptotic setting) still has not been achieved. In this work, we take a step towards characterizing the exact-optimal approach in the presence of shared randomness (a random variable shared between the server and the user) and identify several conditions for exact optimality. We prove that one of the conditions is to utilize a rotationally symmetric shared random codebook. Based on this, we propose a randomization mechanism where the codebook is a randomly rotated simplex -- satisfying the properties of the exact-optimal codebook. The proposed mechanism is based on a $k$-closest encoding which we prove to be exact-optimal for the randomly rotated simplex codebook.

paragraphs: Distributed mean estimation asks a server to estimate an average from information supplied by users. Communication limits restrict how much each user can send, while local differential privacy constrains what those messages can reveal. This paper studies the exact tradeoff among communication, privacy, and estimation quality at finite communication budgets.

Earlier algorithms were optimal in their asymptotic order as the number of transmitted bits increased. The authors take a step toward exact optimality when users and the server have access to shared randomness. They identify several conditions for exact optimality and prove that one requires a rotationally symmetric shared random codebook, the collection of representations used for communication.

They then propose a mechanism whose codebook is a randomly rotated simplex, satisfying the identified codebook properties. For this codebook, they prove that a k-closest encoding is exactly optimal. The scope of this result matters: the encoding guarantee is for the randomly rotated simplex codebook, while the broader contribution advances the characterization of exact optimality under shared randomness.
summary.tldr: The paper identifies conditions for exact private mean estimation and proves a k-closest encoding optimal for a randomly rotated simplex codebook.

title: Exact Optimality of Communication-Privacy-Utility Tradeoffs in Distributed Mean Estimation

abstract: Rationalization aims to strengthen the interpretability of NLP models by extracting a subset of human-intelligible pieces of their inputting texts. Conventional works generally employ the maximum mutual information (MMI) criterion to find the rationale that is most indicative of the target label. However, this criterion can be influenced by spurious features that correlate with the causal rationale or the target label. Instead of attempting to rectify the issues of the MMI criterion, we propose a novel criterion to uncover the causal rationale, termed the Minimum Conditional Dependence (MCD) criterion, which is grounded on our finding that the non-causal features and the target label are \emph{d-separated} by the causal rationale. By minimizing the dependence between the non-selected parts of the input and the target label conditioned on the selected rationale candidate, all the causes of the label are compelled to be selected. In this study, we employ a simple and practical measure for dependence, specifically the KL-divergence, to validate our proposed MCD criterion. Empirically, we demonstrate that MCD improves the F1 score by up to 13.7% compared to previous state-of-the-art MMI-based methods.Our code is in an anonymous repository: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/MCD-CE88.

paragraphs: Text rationalization extracts understandable pieces of an input to explain a model’s prediction. A common objective selects text that carries strong information about the target label. The paper argues that this can favor spurious features, because a feature may correlate with the label or its causal explanation without being part of that explanation.

The proposed Minimum Conditional Dependence criterion asks a different question: after accounting for the selected rationale, how much dependence remains between the omitted text and the label? Its basis is the authors’ finding that the causal rationale d-separates non-causal features from the target. Under that causal relationship, minimizing the remaining dependence compels the selection of all causes of the label.

The authors use KL-divergence as a practical dependence measure to evaluate this criterion. Experiments report F1 improvements of up to 13.7% over earlier leading methods based on maximum mutual information. The contribution is an explanation objective that evaluates what relevant dependence remains outside a rationale, giving a causal motivation for how text should be selected.
summary.tldr: A causal rationale criterion selects text by minimizing the label dependence that remains in omitted text after conditioning on the rationale.

title: D-Separation for Causal Self-Explanation

abstract: Discovering causal relations from observational time series without making the stationary assumption is a significant challenge. In practice, this challenge is common in many areas, such as retail sales, transportation systems, and medical science. Here, we consider this problem for a class of non-stationary time series. The structural causal model (SCM) of this type of time series, called the semi-stationary time series, exhibits that a finite number of different causal mechanisms occur sequentially and periodically across time. This model holds considerable practical utility because it can represent periodicity, including common occurrences such as seasonality and diurnal variation. We propose a constraint-based, non-parametric algorithm for discovering causal relations in this setting. The resulting algorithm, PCMCI$_{\Omega}$, can capture the alternating and recurring changes in the causal mechanisms and then identify the underlying causal graph with conditional independence (CI) tests. We show that this algorithm is sound in identifying causal relations on discrete time series. We validate the algorithm with extensive experiments on continuous and discrete simulated data. We also apply our algorithm to a real-world climate dataset.

paragraphs: Discovering causal relationships from observational time series becomes harder when the mechanisms generating the observations change over time. This paper studies a particular form of that change: a finite collection of causal mechanisms appears in a recurring, periodic sequence. The authors call these semi-stationary time series, a setting that can represent patterns such as seasonality and daily variation.

Their algorithm, PCMCIΩ, tracks these alternating and recurring mechanisms before identifying the underlying causal graph. It uses conditional independence tests, which ask whether relationships between variables remain after accounting for other variables. The method is constraint-based and non-parametric, providing a way to search for causal structure within the specified recurring-mechanism setting.

The authors establish soundness for identifying causal relationships in discrete time series. They also evaluate the algorithm using simulated continuous and discrete data and apply it to a climate dataset. The theoretical guarantee and the experiments have different scopes: the proof concerns discrete series, while the evaluations explore a broader range of data. The central advance is accommodating structured recurring change within causal discovery.
summary.tldr: PCMCIΩ discovers causal structure in time series whose mechanisms recur periodically, with a soundness guarantee for discrete series.

title: Causal Discovery in Semi-Stationary Time Series

abstract: Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) have become an increasingly popular representation to capture high-quality appearance and shape of scenes and objects. However, learning generalizable NeRF priors over categories of scenes or objects has been challenging due to the high dimensionality of network weight space. To address the limitations of existing work on generalization, multi-view consistency and to improve quality, we propose HyP-NeRF, a latent conditioning method for learning generalizable category-level NeRF priors using hypernetworks. Rather than using hypernetworks to estimate only the weights of a NeRF, we estimate both the weights and the multi-resolution hash encodings resulting in significant quality gains. To improve quality even further, we incorporate a denoise and finetune strategy that denoises images rendered from NeRFs estimated by the hypernetwork and finetunes it while retaining multiview consistency. These improvements enable us to use HyP-NeRF as a generalizable prior for multiple downstream tasks including NeRF reconstruction from single-view or cluttered scenes and text-to-NeRF. We provide qualitative comparisons and evaluate HyP-NeRF on three tasks: generalization, compression, and retrieval, demonstrating our state-of-the-art results.

paragraphs: Neural radiance fields represent the appearance and shape of scenes or objects, but learning reusable knowledge across an entire category is difficult. One obstacle is the large space of possible network weights. HyP-NeRF uses a hypernetwork conditioned on a latent representation to learn category-level priors that can support several reconstruction and generation tasks.

The hypernetwork predicts both the NeRF’s weights and its multi-resolution hash encodings. Estimating these together produces significant quality gains compared with predicting only the weights, according to the authors. The authors provide qualitative comparisons and evaluate generalization, compression, and retrieval, reporting state-of-the-art results. The contribution combines a richer prediction target for the hypernetwork with an image-based refinement process. Together, these changes make learned category knowledge useful across multiple downstream tasks while addressing visual quality and multi-view consistency.
summary.tldr: HyP-NeRF learns reusable category-level NeRF priors by predicting weights and hash encodings, then refining rendered quality while preserving view consistency.

title: HyP-NeRF: Learning Improved NeRF Priors using a HyperNetwork

abstract: Fine-tuning language models (LMs) has yielded success on diverse downstream tasks, but as LMs grow in size, backpropagation requires a prohibitively large amount of memory. Zeroth-order (ZO) methods can in principle estimate gradients using only two forward passes but are theorized to be catastrophically slow for optimizing large models. In this work, we propose a memory-efficient zerothorder optimizer (MeZO), adapting the classical ZO-SGD method to operate in-place, thereby fine-tuning LMs with the same memory footprint as inference. For example, with a single A100 80GB GPU, MeZO can train a 30-billion parameter model, whereas fine-tuning with backpropagation can train only a 2.7B LM with the same budget. We conduct comprehensive experiments across model types (masked and autoregressive LMs), model scales (up to 66B), and downstream tasks (classification, multiple-choice, and generation). Our results demonstrate that (1) MeZO significantly outperforms in-context learning and linear probing; (2) MeZO achieves comparable performance to fine-tuning with backpropagation across multiple tasks, with up to 12× memory reduction and up to 2× GPU-hour reduction in our implementation; (3) MeZO is compatible with both full-parameter and parameter-efficient tuning techniques such as LoRA and prefix tuning; (4) MeZO can effectively optimize non-differentiable objectives (e.g., maximizing accuracy or F1). We support our empirical findings with theoretical insights, highlighting how adequate pre-training and task prompts enable MeZO to fine-tune huge models, despite classical ZO analyses suggesting otherwise.

paragraphs: Fine-tuning large language models with backpropagation can require far more memory than running them for inference. MeZO addresses this by estimating updates through forward passes and adapting a classical zeroth-order optimization method to operate in place. The result is fine-tuning with the same memory footprint as inference.

The practical difference is substantial in the reported example: one A100 with 80GB of memory supports training a 30-billion-parameter model with MeZO, compared with a 2.7-billion-parameter model using backpropagation. Experiments cover masked and autoregressive models, sizes up to 66 billion parameters, and classification, multiple-choice, and generation tasks.

MeZO outperforms in-context learning and linear probing, and matches backpropagation-based fine-tuning performance on multiple tasks. The implementation achieves reductions of up to twelvefold in memory and twofold in GPU-hours. It also supports full-parameter tuning, LoRA, prefix tuning, and objectives such as accuracy or F1 that are not differentiable. The accompanying theory highlights adequate pretraining and task prompts as factors helping explain why this approach can work despite pessimistic classical analyses.
summary.tldr: MeZO fine-tunes language models using forward passes with inference-level memory, achieving performance comparable to backpropagation on multiple tested tasks.

title: Fine-Tuning Language Models with Just Forward Passes

abstract: Neural Architecture Search (NAS) is a promising paradigm in automatic architecture engineering. Zero-shot NAS can evaluate the network without training via some specific metrics called zero-cost proxies. Though effective, the existing zero-cost proxies either invoke at least one backpropagation or depend highly on the data and labels. To alleviate the above issues, in this paper, we first reveal how the Pearson correlation matrix of the feature maps impacts the convergence rate and the generalization capacity of an over-parameterized neural network. Enlightened by the theoretical analysis, we propose a novel zero-cost proxy called $\mathsf{MeCo}$, which requires only one random data for a single forward pass. We further propose an optimization approach $\mathsf{MeCo_{opt}}$ to improve the performance of our method. We design comprehensive experiments and extensively evaluate $\mathsf{MeCo}$ on multiple popular benchmarks. $\mathsf{MeCo}$ achieves the highest correlation with the ground truth (e.g., 0.89 on NATS-Bench-TSS with CIFAR-10) among all the state-of-the-art proxies, which is also fully independent of the data and labels. Moreover, we integrate $\mathsf{MeCo}$ with the existing generation method to comprise a complete NAS. The experimental results illustrate that $\mathsf{MeCo}$-based NAS can select the architecture with the highest accuracy and a low search cost. For instance, the best network searched by $\mathsf{MeCo}$-based NAS achieves 97.31% on CIFAR-10, which is 0.04% higher than the baselines under the same settings. Our code is available at https://github.com/HamsterMimi/MeCo

paragraphs: Zero-shot neural architecture search ranks candidate networks without training each one. Existing scoring proxies can still require backpropagation or depend strongly on the chosen data and labels. This paper develops MeCo, a proxy based on the minimum eigenvalue of feature-map correlation, requiring a single forward pass with one random input.

The method is motivated by an analysis connecting the Pearson correlation matrix of feature maps to convergence rate and generalization capacity in overparameterized networks. The authors also propose MeCo_opt to improve the approach. Their evaluations examine how well the proxy’s rankings correlate with actual architecture performance across several benchmarks.

summary.tldr: MeCo ranks untrained architectures using feature correlations from one random input and one forward pass.

title: MeCo: Zero-Shot NAS with One Data and Single Forward Pass via Minimum Eigenvalue of Correlation

abstract: Blind Omnidirectional Image Quality Assessment (BOIQA) aims to objectively assess the human perceptual quality of omnidirectional images (ODIs) without relying on pristine-quality image information. It is becoming more significant with the increasing advancement of virtual reality (VR) technology. However, the quality assessment of ODIs is severely hampered by the fact that the existing BOIQA pipeline lacks the modeling of the observer's browsing process. To tackle this issue, we propose a novel multi-sequence network for BOIQA called Assessor360, which is derived from the realistic multi-assessor ODI quality assessment procedure. Specifically, we propose a generalized Recursive Probability Sampling (RPS) method for the BOIQA task, combining content and details information to generate multiple pseudo viewport sequences from a given starting point. Additionally, we design a Multi-scale Feature Aggregation (MFA) module with a Distortion-aware Block (DAB) to fuse distorted and semantic features of each viewport. We also devise Temporal Modeling Module (TMM) to learn the viewport transition in the temporal domain. Extensive experimental results demonstrate that Assessor360 outperforms state-of-the-art methods on multiple OIQA datasets. The code and models are available at https://github.com/TianheWu/Assessor360.

paragraphs: Assessing a 360-degree image requires considering how people explore it. A viewer sees a sequence of viewports rather than the entire scene at once. Assessor360 uses this observation to predict perceived image quality without access to a pristine reference image, modeling aspects of the browsing process that existing assessment pipelines overlook.

The method generates several artificial viewport sequences from a starting location. Its Recursive Probability Sampling procedure uses both scene content and visual details to choose these sequences. For each viewport, a feature aggregation module combines information about image distortions with information about what the scene contains. A temporal module then learns relationships between successive views.

This design connects local image defects with the order in which a viewer might encounter them. Multiple sequences also reflect the paper's motivation of modeling assessment by multiple observers. Experiments report better performance than state-of-the-art methods on several omnidirectional image quality datasets, supporting browsing-aware modeling as a useful component of perceptual quality prediction.
summary.tldr: Assessor360 improves reference-free quality assessment of 360-degree images by modeling multiple possible viewing sequences.

title: Assessor360: Multi-sequence Network for Blind Omnidirectional Image Quality Assessment

abstract: In Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), hierarchical pooling operators generate local summaries of the data by coarsening the graph structure and the vertex features. Considerable attention has been devoted to analyzing the expressive power of message-passing (MP) layers in GNNs, while a study on how graph pooling affects the expressiveness of a GNN is still lacking. Additionally, despite the recent advances in the design of pooling operators, there is not a principled criterion to compare them. In this work, we derive sufficient conditions for a pooling operator to fully preserve the expressive power of the MP layers before it. These conditions serve as a universal and theoretically-grounded criterion for choosing among existing pooling operators or designing new ones. Based on our theoretical findings, we analyze several existing pooling operators and identify those that fail to satisfy the expressiveness conditions. Finally, we introduce an experimental setup to verify empirically the expressive power of a GNN equipped with pooling layers, in terms of its capability to perform a graph isomorphism test.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks often pool information by replacing a graph with a smaller, coarser representation. This creates local summaries of both graph structure and vertex features. The paper asks whether that compression preserves the distinctions already captured by preceding message-passing layers, an issue less studied than the expressiveness of message passing itself.

The authors derive sufficient conditions under which a pooling operator fully preserves that preceding expressive power. These conditions provide a theoretical criterion for choosing existing pooling methods and designing new ones. Because the conditions are sufficient, satisfying them establishes preservation; failing them alone does not establish that an operator must always lose expressive power.

The paper uses the criterion to examine existing operators and identify those that do not satisfy it. It also introduces an experimental setup based on graph-isomorphism testing to assess the distinguishing ability of networks with pooling layers. Together, the theory and evaluation setup make information preservation an explicit consideration when comparing methods for compressing graph representations.
summary.tldr: The paper gives sufficient conditions for graph pooling to preserve preceding message-passing expressiveness and a setup for testing that ability.

title: The expressive power of pooling in Graph Neural Networks

abstract: Single-stage neural combinatorial optimization solvers have achieved near-optimal results on various small-scale combinatorial optimization (CO) problems without requiring expert knowledge. However, these solvers exhibit significant performance degradation when applied to large-scale CO problems. Recently, two-stage neural methods motivated by divide-and-conquer strategies have shown efficiency in addressing large-scale CO problems. Nevertheless, the performance of these methods highly relies on problem-specific heuristics in either the dividing or the conquering procedure, which limits their applicability to general CO problems. Moreover, these methods employ separate training schemes and ignore the interdependencies between the dividing and conquering strategies, often leading to sub-optimal solutions. To tackle these drawbacks, this article develops a unified neural divide-and-conquer framework (i.e., UDC) for solving general large-scale CO problems. UDC offers a Divide-Conquer-Reunion (DCR) training method to eliminate the negative impact of a sub-optimal dividing policy. Employing a high-efficiency Graph Neural Network (GNN) for global instance dividing and a fixed-length sub-path solver for conquering divided sub-problems, the proposed UDC framework demonstrates extensive applicability, achieving superior performance in 10 representative large-scale CO problems. The code is available at https://github.com/CIAM-Group/NCO_code/tree/main/single_objective/UDC-Large-scale-CO-master

paragraphs: Neural solvers can perform well on small combinatorial optimization problems yet deteriorate as problem size grows. Dividing a large instance into smaller pieces offers a route to scaling, but existing neural approaches often depend on problem-specific heuristics. They may also train division and solution procedures separately, overlooking how the quality of one affects the other.

UDC introduces a unified divide-and-conquer framework with a Divide-Conquer-Reunion training method designed to eliminate the negative impact of a suboptimal dividing policy. A graph neural network handles division of the global instance, while a fixed-length sub-path solver handles the resulting subproblems. This organization brings the interacting stages into a shared framework.

The authors report superior performance across ten representative large-scale combinatorial optimization problems. That breadth supports the framework’s applicability across multiple problem types and its aim of reducing reliance on specialized heuristics. The central contribution is to treat decomposition and subproblem solution as connected decisions, addressing the weakness of optimizing them through separate training schemes.
summary.tldr: UDC unifies problem division and subproblem solving, delivering strong results across ten large-scale combinatorial optimization problems.

title: UDC: A Unified Neural Divide-and-Conquer Framework for Large-Scale Combinatorial Optimization Problems

abstract: Spiking Transformers, which integrate Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) with Transformer architectures, have attracted significant attention due to their potential for low energy consumption and high performance. However, there remains a substantial gap in performance between SNNs and Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs). To narrow this gap, we have developed QKFormer, a direct training spiking transformer with the following features: i) _Linear complexity and high energy efficiency_, the novel spike-form Q-K attention module efficiently models the token or channel attention through binary vectors and enables the construction of larger models. ii) _Multi-scale spiking representation_, achieved by a hierarchical structure with the different numbers of tokens across blocks. iii) _Spiking Patch Embedding with Deformed Shortcut (SPEDS)_, enhances spiking information transmission and integration, thus improving overall performance. It is shown that QKFormer achieves significantly superior performance over existing state-of-the-art SNN models on various mainstream datasets. Notably, with comparable size to Spikformer (66.34 M, 74.81\%), QKFormer (64.96 M) achieves a groundbreaking top-1 accuracy of **85.65\%** on ImageNet-1k, substantially outperforming Spikformer by **10.84\%**. To our best knowledge, this is the first time that directly training SNNs have exceeded 85\% accuracy on ImageNet-1K.

QKFormer addresses this gap through changes to attention, the organization of representations, and the transmission of spiking information.

The authors identify this, to their knowledge, as the first directly trained spiking network to exceed 85% accuracy on that benchmark.
summary.tldr: QKFormer combines binary Q-K attention and hierarchical spiking representations to improve accuracy at comparable model size.

title: QKFormer: Hierarchical Spiking Transformer using Q-K Attention

abstract: Prevalent human-object interaction (HOI) detection approaches typically leverage large-scale visual-linguistic models to help recognize events involving humans and objects. Though promising, models trained via contrastive learning on text-image pairs often neglect mid/low-level visual cues and struggle at compositional reasoning. In response, we introduce DIFFUSIONHOI, a new HOI detector shedding light on text-to-image diffusion models. Unlike the aforementioned models, diffusion models excel in discerning mid/low-level visual concepts as generative models, and possess strong compositionality to handle novel concepts expressed in text inputs. Considering diffusion models usually emphasize instance objects, we first devise an inversion-based strategy to learn the expression of relation patterns between humans and objects in embedding space. These learned relation embeddings then serve as textual prompts, to steer diffusion models generate images that depict specific interactions, and extract HOI-relevant cues from images without heavy finetuning. Benefited from above, DIFFUSIONHOI achieves SOTA performance on three datasets under both regular and zero-shot setups.

The paper argues that commonly used contrastively trained vision-language models can overlook lower-level visual cues and struggle with compositional reasoning. DIFFUSIONHOI explores text-to-image diffusion models as a source of useful interaction information.

The authors motivate this choice through diffusion models’ ability to represent visual details and compose concepts described in text. However, those models tend to emphasize individual objects. To make relationships accessible, the method uses an inversion-based strategy to learn embeddings that express patterns of interaction between humans and objects.

These relation embeddings act as textual prompts, guiding the diffusion model to generate images of particular interactions and helping extract relevant cues without heavy fine-tuning. DIFFUSIONHOI achieves reported state-of-the-art performance on three datasets in both regular and zero-shot settings. The results support using learned relationship representations to adapt a generative model’s visual knowledge for interaction detection, including evaluation involving unseen interaction concepts.
summary.tldr: DIFFUSIONHOI learns relation prompts that make text-to-image diffusion models useful for human-object interaction detection.

title: Human-Object Interaction Detection Collaborated with Large Relation-driven Diffusion Models

abstract: In recent years, the merging of vast datasets with powerful computational resources has led to the emergence of large pre-trained models in the field of deep learning. However, the common practices often overgeneralize the applicability of these models, overlooking the task-specific resource constraints. To mitigate this issue, we propose \textbf{Cluster-Learngene}, which effectively clusters critical internal modules from a large ancestry model and then inherits them to initialize descendant models of elastic scales. Specifically, based on the density characteristics of attention heads, our method adaptively clusters attention heads of each layer and position-wise feed-forward networks (FFNs) in the ancestry model as the learngene. Moreover, we introduce priority weight-sharing and learnable parameter transformations that expand the learngene to initialize descendant models of elastic scales. Through extensive experimentation, we demonstrate that Cluster-Learngene not only is more efficient compared to other initialization methods but also customizes models of elastic scales according to downstream task resources.

paragraphs: A large pretrained vision model may not match the computational resources available for a downstream task. Cluster-Learngene addresses this mismatch through initialization: it extracts and organizes important internal components from a large ancestry model, then uses them to initialize descendant models at different scales.

The method adaptively groups attention heads within each layer according to their density characteristics and also clusters position-wise feed-forward networks. These selected groups form the transferable learngene. Priority weight-sharing and learnable parameter transformations then expand this material to initialize descendants of varying sizes. The approach therefore makes inheritance flexible enough to accommodate different model scales.

The authors report that extensive experiments show greater efficiency than other initialization methods and the ability to customize model size to downstream resources. The practical significance is that useful components of a large model can serve as starting material for models with different resource requirements. The stated evidence concerns this initialization and customization strategy, rather than a single universally appropriate descendant size.
summary.tldr: Cluster-Learngene groups components of a large vision transformer and reuses them to efficiently initialize models suited to different resource budgets.

title: Cluster-Learngene: Inheriting Adaptive Clusters for Vision Transformers

abstract: Humans are autotelic agents who learn by setting and pursuing their own goals. However, the precise mechanisms guiding human goal selection remain unclear. Learning progress, typically measured as the observed change in performance, can provide a valuable signal for goal selection in both humans and artificial agents. We hypothesize that human choices of goals may also be driven by _latent learning progress_, which humans can estimate through knowledge of their actions and the environment – even without experiencing immediate changes in performance. To test this hypothesis, we designed a hierarchical reinforcement learning task in which human participants (N = 175) repeatedly chose their own goals and learned goal-conditioned policies. Our behavioral and computational modeling results confirm the influence of latent learning progress on goal selection and uncover inter-individual differences, partially mediated by recognition of the task's hierarchical structure. By investigating the role of latent learning progress in human goal selection, we pave the way for more effective and personalized learning experiences as well as the advancement of more human-like autotelic machines.
