The authors use these insights to improve consistency in answering and abstaining. The contribution is an initial framework for analyzing conflicting concepts, with evidence that role instructions can alter internal representations in ways that affect observable behavior.
summary.tldr: Conflicting temporal concepts in role play can disrupt language models' accuracy and abstention, partly through changes in their internal representations.

title: Concept Incongruence: An Exploration of Time and Death in Role Playing

abstract: Bayesian inference is often hampered by large computational expense. As a generalization of belief propagation (BP), expectation propagation (EP) approximates exact Bayesian computation with efficient message passing updates. However, when an approximation family used by EP is far from exact posterior distributions, message passing may lead to poor approximation quality and suffer from divergence. To address this issue, we propose an approximate inference method, relaxed expectation propagation(REP), based on a new divergence with a l1 penalty. Minimizing this penalized divergence adaptively relaxes EP’s moment matching requirement for message passing. We apply REP to Gaussian process classification and experimental results demonstrate significant improvement of REP over EP and alpha-divergence based power EP – in terms of algorithmic stability, estimation accuracy, and predictive performance. Furthermore, we develop relaxed belief propagation(RBP), a special case of REP, to conduct inference on discrete Markov random fields (MRFs). Our results show improved estimation accuracy of RBP over BP and fractional BP when interactions between MRF nodes are strong.

paragraphs: Expectation propagation approximates Bayesian inference through efficient message passing. It can struggle when its chosen family of approximate distributions cannot closely represent the true posterior. In that situation, the approximation may be inaccurate and the iterative updates may diverge. This paper modifies the matching requirements used during those updates to address that mismatch.

The proposed method, relaxed expectation propagation, minimizes a divergence equipped with an L1 penalty. This adaptively relaxes the moment-matching condition used by standard expectation propagation. The central idea is to give the approximation procedure room to adjust how closely it enforces those statistical matches when working within a restricted distribution family.

For Gaussian process classification, experiments report significant improvements over expectation propagation and power expectation propagation in stability, estimation accuracy, and prediction. The authors also derive relaxed belief propagation as a special case for discrete Markov random fields. There, results show more accurate estimates than belief propagation and fractional belief propagation when interactions between nodes are strong. The evidence connects the relaxation to improvements in two distinct inference settings.
summary.tldr: An L1-penalized divergence relaxes message-passing moment matching, improving approximate inference in the evaluated settings.

title: Message passing with l1 penalized KL minimization

abstract: In this study, we derive algorithms for estimating mixed β-divergences. Such cost functions are useful for Nonnegative Matrix and Tensor Factorization models with a compound Poisson observation model. Compound Poisson is a particular Tweedie model, an important special case of exponential dispersion models characterized by the fact that the variance is proportional to a power function of the mean. There are several well known matrix and tensor factorization algorithms that minimize the β-divergence; these estimate the mean parameter. The probabilistic interpretation gives us more flexibility and robustness by providing us additional tunable parameters such as power and dispersion. Estimation of the power parameter is useful for choosing a suitable divergence and estimation of dispersion is useful for data driven regularization and weighting in collective/coupled factorization of heterogeneous datasets. We present three inference algorithms for both estimating the factors and the additional parameters of the compound Poisson distribution. The methods are evaluated on two applications: modeling symbolic representations for polyphonic music and lyric prediction from audio features. Our conclusion is that the compound poisson based factorization models can be useful for sparse positive data.

paragraphs: Nonnegative matrix and tensor factorization methods often use a β-divergence to measure reconstruction error. This paper treats that choice through a probabilistic compound Poisson model, within the Tweedie family. In this family, variance is proportional to a power of the mean, connecting the error measure to assumptions about how observations vary.

The authors develop three inference algorithms that estimate both the factors and additional distribution parameters. Learning the power parameter helps choose an appropriate divergence. Learning dispersion supports data-driven regularization and weighting when jointly factorizing heterogeneous datasets. The probabilistic formulation therefore makes aspects of the fitting objective adjustable from the data, alongside the mean representation.

The methods are evaluated on symbolic representations of polyphonic music and on predicting lyrics from audio features. The authors conclude that compound Poisson factorization can be useful for sparse positive data. The broader contribution is a way to learn the factors together with parameters that govern how different observations and datasets contribute to the fit.
summary.tldr: Compound Poisson factorization learns factors alongside power and dispersion parameters that guide divergence choice and data weighting.

title: Learning the beta-Divergence in Tweedie Compound Poisson Matrix Factorization Models

abstract: This paper illustrates a novel approach to the estimation of generalization error of decision tree classifiers. We set out the study of decision tree errors in the context of consistency analysis theory, which proved that the Bayes error can be achieved only if when the number of data samples thrown into each leaf node goes to infinity. For the more challenging and practical case where the sample size is finite or small, a novel sampling error term is introduced in this paper to cope with the small sample problem effectively and efficiently. Extensive experimental results show that the proposed error estimate is superior to the well known K-fold cross validation methods in terms of robustness and accuracy. Moreover it is orders of magnitudes more efficient than cross validation methods.

Extensive experimental results show that the proposed error estimate is superior to the well known K-fold cross validation methods in terms of robustness and accuracy. Moreover it is orders of magnitudes more efficient than cross validation methods.

paragraphs: The paper proposes a way to estimate a decision tree classifier’s generalization error, meaning its error on data beyond the training sample. The motivation is especially relevant when the available sample is small. In that setting, estimating future performance must account for the limited evidence supporting the tree’s individual leaves.

The authors frame the problem through consistency analysis. The theory they discuss gives a necessary condition for achieving Bayes error: the number of observations assigned to every leaf must grow without bound. This motivates attention to finite samples, where that asymptotic condition cannot describe the amount of evidence actually available. Their estimator introduces a sampling-error term to address this problem.

Extensive experiments report more accurate and robust error estimates than K-fold cross-validation, together with computational efficiency improvements of orders of magnitude. These are findings about estimating a tree’s predictive error, rather than claims that the estimator itself improves the classifier. The approach matters because it targets both the reliability and the computational expense of performance assessment.
summary.tldr: A sampling-error correction improves decision-tree error estimation over K-fold cross-validation in the reported accuracy, robustness, and efficiency comparisons.

title: Accurate Robust and Efficient Error Estimation for Decision Trees

abstract: We consider the question of how unlabeled data can be used to estimate the true accuracy of learned classifiers, and the related question of how outputs from several classifiers performing the same task can be combined based on their estimated accuracies. To answer these questions, we first present a simple graphical model that performs well in practice. We then provide two nonparametric extensions to it that improve its performance. Experiments on two real-world data sets produce accuracy estimates within a few percent of the true accuracy, using solely unlabeled data. Our models also outperform existing state-of-the-art solutions in both estimating accuracies, and combining multiple classifier outputs.

Our models also outperform existing state-of-the-art solutions in both estimating accuracies, and combining multiple classifier outputs.

paragraphs: The paper asks whether a classifier’s true accuracy can be estimated using data without known labels. It also studies a closely related problem: when several classifiers perform the same task, how should their outputs be combined using estimates of their individual accuracies? Both questions make reliability estimation central to using classifier predictions.

The authors first introduce a simple graphical model that performs well in practice. They then develop two nonparametric extensions that improve its performance. The models provide a Bayesian approach to estimating accuracy from unlabeled observations, and those estimates also support combining multiple classifier outputs. This links evaluating the classifiers to using them together.

Experiments on two real-world datasets produce accuracy estimates within a few percent of the true values using only unlabeled data. The models also outperform the existing state-of-the-art solutions considered in both accuracy estimation and output combination. These findings demonstrate useful empirical accuracy in the tested settings, without making the reported error range a guarantee for every dataset.
summary.tldr: Bayesian graphical models estimate classifier accuracy from unlabeled data and improve the combination of multiple classifiers in reported experiments.

title: Estimating Accuracy from Unlabeled Data: A Bayesian Approach

abstract: Neural networks and rational functions efficiently approximate each other. In more detail, it is shown here that for any ReLU network, there exists a rational function of degree $O(polylog(1/\epsilon))$ which is $\epsilon$-close, and similarly for any rational function there exists a ReLU network of size $O(polylog(1/\epsilon))$ which is $\epsilon$-close. By contrast, polynomials need degree $\Omega(poly(1/\epsilon))$ to approximate even a single ReLU. When converting a ReLU network to a rational function as above, the hidden constants depend exponentially on the number of layers, which is shown to be tight; in other words, a compositional representation can be beneficial even for rational functions.

paragraphs: This paper studies how efficiently ReLU networks and rational functions can approximate one another. Rational functions are ratios of polynomials, giving them a different representation from neural networks. The authors show that both representations can approximate the other with a favorable dependence on the requested error tolerance.

For approximation error ε, a ReLU network can be approximated by a rational function whose degree grows as O(polylog(1/ε)). Conversely, a rational function can be approximated by a ReLU network with size O(polylog(1/ε)). Polynomials behave differently: approximating even one ReLU requires degree growing at least as Ω(poly(1/ε)). This comparison highlights the representational advantage of allowing rational functions.

There is an important depth qualification. When converting a network into a rational function, the hidden constants depend exponentially on the number of layers, and the authors show that this dependence is tight. Thus, the favorable dependence on accuracy does not remove the effect of network depth. The result also shows why keeping a compositional representation can be beneficial even when working with rational functions.
summary.tldr: ReLU networks and rational functions approximate each other efficiently in accuracy, but converting networks incurs an unavoidable exponential dependence on depth.

title: Neural Networks and Rational Functions

abstract: Learning weights in a spiking neural network with hidden neurons, using local, stable and online rules, to control non-linear body dynamics is an open problem. Here, we employ a supervised scheme, Feedback-based Online Local Learning Of Weights (FOLLOW), to train a heterogeneous network of spiking neurons with hidden layers, to control a two-link arm so as to reproduce a desired state trajectory. We show that the network learns an inverse model of the non-linear dynamics, i.e. it infers from state trajectory as input to the network, the continuous-time command that produced the trajectory. Connection weights are adjusted via a local plasticity rule that involves pre-synaptic firing and post-synaptic feedback of the error in the inferred command. We propose a network architecture, termed differential feedforward, and show that it gives a lower test error than other feedforward and recurrent architectures. We demonstrate the performance of the inverse model to control a two-link arm along a desired trajectory.

paragraphs: Controlling a body with nonlinear dynamics requires translating a desired movement into suitable commands. This paper trains a network of spiking neurons with hidden layers to perform that translation for a two-link arm. It uses the supervised FOLLOW scheme to learn an inverse model: given a state trajectory, infer the continuous-time command that produced it.

The network adjusts its connections using a local plasticity rule. Each update involves presynaptic firing and feedback to the postsynaptic neuron about error in the inferred command. This connects the learning signal to information available around an individual connection while supporting learning in a network containing hidden neurons.

The authors introduce a differential feedforward architecture and report lower test error than the other feedforward and recurrent architectures they compare. They also demonstrate using the learned inverse model to make the two-link arm follow a desired trajectory. The findings tie a particular network design and local learning mechanism to successful nonlinear control in the studied arm system.
summary.tldr: A spiking network learns an inverse model through local error-driven updates and uses it to control a two-link arm.

title: Non-linear motor control by local learning in spiking neural networks

abstract: We present a novel cost function for semi-supervised learning of neural networks that encourages compact clustering of the latent space to facilitate separation. The key idea is to dynamically create a graph over embeddings of labeled and unlabeled samples of a training batch to capture underlying structure in feature space, and use label propagation to estimate its high and low density regions. We then devise a cost function based on Markov chains on the graph that regularizes the latent space to form a single compact cluster per class, while avoiding to disturb existing clusters during optimization. We evaluate our approach on three benchmarks and compare to state-of-the art with promising results. Our approach combines the benefits of graph-based regularization with efficient, inductive inference, does not require modifications to a network architecture, and can thus be easily applied to existing networks to enable an effective use of unlabeled data.

We then devise a cost function based on Markov chains on the graph that regularizes the latent space to form a single compact cluster per class, while avoiding to disturb existing clusters during optimization. We evaluate our approach on three benchmarks and compare to state-of-the art with promising results. Our approach combines the benefits of graph-based regularization with efficient, inductive inference, does not require modifications to a network architecture, and can thus be easily applied to existing networks to enable an effective use of unlabeled data.

paragraphs: This paper uses unlabeled examples to help organize a neural network’s internal feature space. Its training objective encourages each class to occupy a compact cluster, making classes easier to separate. The approach operates on embeddings of both labeled and unlabeled examples within each training batch.

During training, the method dynamically builds a graph over those embeddings. Label propagation estimates high- and low-density regions, and a cost function based on Markov chains over the graph encourages one compact cluster per class. The objective is also designed to avoid disrupting clusters that have already formed as optimization proceeds.

The authors evaluate the approach on three benchmarks and report promising comparisons with leading methods. The contribution combines graph-based regularization during learning with efficient inductive inference, meaning the trained network can handle new examples. Because the method does not require architectural changes, it can be applied to existing networks as a training objective for making use of unlabeled data.
summary.tldr: A graph-based training objective uses unlabeled data to encourage compact class clusters without changing the network architecture.

title: Semi-Supervised Learning via Compact Latent Space Clustering

abstract: Thompson sampling has impressive empirical performance for many multi-armed bandit problems. But current algorithms for Thompson sampling only work for the case of conjugate priors since they require to perform online Bayesian posterior inference, which is a difficult task when the prior is not conjugate. In this paper, we propose a novel algorithm for Thompson sampling which only requires to draw samples from a tractable proposal distribution. So our algorithm is efficient even when the prior is non-conjugate. To do this, we reformulate Thompson sampling as an optimization proplem via the Gumbel-Max trick. After that we construct a set of random variables and our goal is to identify the one with highest mean which is an instance of best arm identification problems. Finally, we solve it with techniques in best arm identification. Experiments show that our algorithm works well in practice.

paragraphs: Thompson sampling is effective empirically on many multi-armed bandit problems, but its implementation can require difficult online Bayesian inference. The paper focuses on non-conjugate priors, where obtaining the needed posterior samples is challenging. Its aim is to retain Thompson sampling while changing the computational problem used to select an action.

The proposed Racing Thompson algorithm only needs samples from a tractable proposal distribution. It first uses the Gumbel-Max trick to express Thompson sampling as an optimization problem. The authors then construct random variables whose means determine the desired choice, reducing the task to identifying the variable with the largest mean.

That reformulation allows techniques for best-arm identification to perform the required selection. The approach therefore connects a Bayesian action-selection problem to another bandit problem with useful solution methods. Experiments report that the algorithm works well in practice. Its stated contribution is an efficient route to Thompson sampling with non-conjugate priors, achieved by replacing demanding posterior-sampling work with proposal sampling and a best-arm identification procedure.
summary.tldr: Racing Thompson makes Thompson sampling efficient with non-conjugate priors by reformulating action selection as best-arm identification.

title: Racing Thompson: an Efficient Algorithm for Thompson Sampling with Non-conjugate Priors

abstract: We establish the first nonasymptotic error bounds for Kaplan-Meier-based nearest neighbor and kernel survival probability estimators where feature vectors reside in metric spaces. Our bounds imply rates of strong consistency for these nonparametric estimators and, up to a log factor, match an existing lower bound for conditional CDF estimation. Our proof strategy also yields nonasymptotic guarantees for nearest neighbor and kernel variants of the Nelson-Aalen cumulative hazards estimator. We experimentally compare these methods on four datasets. We find that for the kernel survival estimator, a good choice of kernel is one learned using random survival forests.

Our bounds imply rates of strong consistency for these nonparametric estimators and, up to a log factor, match an existing lower bound for conditional CDF estimation. Our proof strategy also yields nonasymptotic guarantees for nearest neighbor and kernel variants of the Nelson-Aalen cumulative hazards estimator. We experimentally compare these methods on four datasets. We find that for the kernel survival estimator, a good choice of kernel is one learned using random survival forests.

paragraphs: Survival analysis estimates the probability that an event has not yet occurred by a given time. This paper studies nearest-neighbor and kernel versions of Kaplan-Meier survival estimation, where predictions use information from similar examples. The feature vectors may live in metric spaces, so similarity is expressed through distances rather than requiring a particular coordinate representation.

The main contribution is error guarantees that apply at finite sample sizes. These bounds also imply rates of strong consistency, describing how the estimators approach the correct probabilities as data grows. Up to a logarithmic factor, the rates match an existing lower bound for conditional cumulative-distribution estimation. This connects the guarantees to a benchmark for how accurately the related estimation problem can be solved.

The proof approach also provides finite-sample guarantees for nearest-neighbor and kernel versions of the Nelson-Aalen cumulative hazards estimator. Experiments compare the methods on four datasets. For kernel survival estimation, the authors find that a kernel learned using random survival forests is a good choice, linking the theoretical analysis with an empirical way to select similarity.
summary.tldr: Finite-sample bounds establish strong consistency rates for distance-based survival estimators, with experiments supporting forest-learned kernels.

title: Nearest Neighbor and Kernel Survival Analysis: Nonasymptotic Error Bounds and Strong Consistency Rates

abstract: We consider online learning with linear models, where the algorithm predicts on sequentially revealed instances (feature vectors), and is compared against the best linear function (comparator) in hindsight. Popular algorithms in this framework, such as Online Gradient Descent (OGD), have parameters (learning rates), which ideally should be tuned based on the scales of the features and the optimal comparator, but these quantities only become available at the end of the learning process. In this paper, we resolve the tuning problem by proposing online algorithms making predictions which are invariant under arbitrary rescaling of the features. The algorithms have no parameters to tune, do not require any prior knowledge on the scale of the instances or the comparator, and achieve regret bounds matching (up to a logarithmic factor) that of OGD with optimally tuned separate learning rates per dimension, while retaining comparable runtime performance.

Performance is measured against the best linear predictor chosen afterward. A central difficulty is that effective learning rates can depend on feature scales and that eventual predictor, neither of which is known in advance.

The paper proposes algorithms that remove this tuning requirement. They need no advance information about the scale of incoming examples or the comparison predictor, and have no parameters to tune. Their predictions also remain unchanged under arbitrary rescaling of features. This connects the practical question of choosing measurement scales with the mathematical question of adapting updates during learning.

The theoretical result compares their regret with online gradient descent using optimally tuned, separate learning rates for each feature dimension. The new algorithms match that benchmark up to a logarithmic factor while retaining comparable runtime. Thus, the contribution is a way to approach a hindsight-tuned performance guarantee using decisions made entirely online.
summary.tldr: Parameter-free online linear learners make scale-invariant predictions and nearly match gradient descent with optimally tuned per-feature learning rates.

title: Adaptive Scale-Invariant Online Algorithms for Learning Linear Models

abstract: The vulnerability to adversarial attacks has been a critical issue for deep neural networks. Addressing this issue requires a reliable way to evaluate the robustness of a network. Recently, several methods have been developed to compute robustness quantification for neural networks, namely, certified lower bounds of the minimum adversarial perturbation. Such methods, however, were devised for feed-forward networks, e.g. multi-layer perceptron or convolutional networks. It remains an open problem to quantify robustness for recurrent networks, especially LSTM and GRU. For such networks, there exist additional challenges in computing the robustness quantification, such as handling the inputs at multiple steps and the interaction between gates and states. In this work, we propose POPQORN (Propagated-output Quantified Robustness for RNNs), a general algorithm to quantify robustness of RNNs, including vanilla RNNs, LSTMs, and GRUs. We demonstrate its effectiveness on different network architectures and show that the robustness quantification on individual steps can lead to new insights.

paragraphs: Assessing adversarial robustness requires more than observing whether a particular attack succeeds. A certified lower bound on the smallest adversarial perturbation provides a guaranteed bound on how much input change is needed. This paper addresses that form of robustness quantification for recurrent networks, where methods developed for feed-forward architectures do not directly settle the problem.

Recurrent models introduce inputs at multiple time steps and, in architectures such as LSTMs and GRUs, interactions between gates and states. POPQORN is a general algorithm designed to handle robustness quantification for vanilla recurrent networks as well as these gated architectures. Its contribution extends the range of network structures for which such quantification can be performed.

The authors demonstrate effectiveness across different architectures and show that examining robustness at individual time steps can reveal additional insights. This allows the analysis to distinguish positions in a sequence rather than reporting only an undifferentiated network-level assessment. The certified quantity remains a lower bound on the minimum adversarial perturbation, rather than an assertion that the exact minimum has been found.
summary.tldr: POPQORN quantifies certified robustness for recurrent networks, including LSTMs and GRUs, and supports analysis of individual time steps.

title: POPQORN: Quantifying Robustness of Recurrent Neural Networks

abstract: In min-min optimization or max-min optimization, one has to compute the gradient of a function defined as a minimum. In most cases, the minimum has no closed-form, and an approximation is obtained via an iterative algorithm. There are two usual ways of estimating the gradient of the function: using either an analytic formula obtained by assuming exactness of the approximation, or automatic differentiation through the algorithm. In this paper, we study the asymptotic error made by these estimators as a function of the optimization error. We find that the error of the automatic estimator is close to the square of the error of the analytic estimator, reflecting a super-efficiency phenomenon. The convergence of the automatic estimator greatly depends on the convergence of the Jacobian of the algorithm. We analyze it for gradient descent and stochastic gradient descent and derive convergence rates for the estimators in these cases. Our analysis is backed by numerical experiments on toy problems and on Wasserstein barycenter computation. Finally, we discuss the computational complexity of these estimators and give practical guidelines to chose between them.

paragraphs: Some optimization problems require differentiating a function whose value is itself obtained by minimizing another function. When that inner minimum has no closed form, an iterative algorithm approximates it. The paper compares two ways to estimate the outer gradient: using an analytic formula that treats the approximation as exact, or differentiating through the iterative algorithm.

The analysis relates gradient-estimation error to the remaining optimization error. Asymptotically, the automatic-differentiation estimator has error close to the square of the analytic estimator's error. This is the reported super-efficiency phenomenon: improving the approximate inner solution can yield a substantially more accurate gradient when differentiation follows the computation that produced it.

That advantage depends strongly on convergence of the algorithm's Jacobian, which describes the sensitivity of its outputs. The authors analyze gradient descent and stochastic gradient descent and derive estimator convergence rates. Numerical experiments on toy problems and Wasserstein barycenters support the analysis. They also examine computational complexity and give guidance for choosing between the two estimators.
summary.tldr: Differentiating through an approximate minimization algorithm can yield asymptotically much smaller gradient error, with behavior tied to Jacobian convergence.

title: Super-efficiency of automatic differentiation for functions defined as a minimum

abstract: We consider off-policy evaluation (OPE), which evaluates the performance of a new policy from observed data collected from previous experiments, without requiring the execution of the new policy. This finds important applications in areas with high execution cost or safety concerns, such as medical diagnosis, recommendation systems and robotics. In practice, due to the limited information from off-policy data, it is highly desirable to construct rigorous confidence intervals, not just point estimation, for the policy performance. In this work, we propose a new variational framework which reduces the problem of calculating tight confidence bounds in OPE into an optimization problem on a feasible set that catches the true state-action value function with high probability. The feasible set is constructed by leveraging statistical properties of a recently proposed kernel Bellman loss (Feng et al., 2019). We design an efficient computational approach for calculating our bounds, and extend it to perform post-hoc diagnosis and correction for existing estimators. Empirical results show that our method yields tight confidence intervals in different settings.

paragraphs: Off-policy evaluation asks how a new decision policy would perform using data gathered under earlier policies. This is valuable when trying the new policy directly would be expensive or raise safety concerns. Because historical data provides limited information about the new policy, a single performance estimate can conceal substantial uncertainty. The paper focuses on producing rigorous confidence intervals instead.

The authors turn confidence-bound calculation into an optimization problem over candidate state-action value functions. These functions describe the value of taking an action in a particular state. Their feasible set is constructed to contain the true value function with high probability, using statistical properties of a kernel Bellman loss. Optimizing over that set produces bounds on policy performance.

The paper provides an efficient computational method for obtaining these bounds and extends it to diagnose and correct existing estimators after they have been computed. Experiments report tight confidence intervals across different settings. The contribution connects uncertainty about value functions to explicit uncertainty about policy performance, making the evaluation more informative than a point estimate alone.
summary.tldr: A kernel-based optimization framework produces confidence bounds for off-policy evaluation and supports diagnosis and correction of existing estimators.

title: Accountable Off-Policy Evaluation With Kernel Bellman Statistics

abstract: Label smoothing is commonly used in training deep learning models, wherein one-hot training labels are mixed with uniform label vectors. Empirically, smoothing has been shown to improve both predictive performance and model calibration. In this paper, we study whether label smoothing is also effective as a means of coping with label noise. While label smoothing apparently amplifies this problem — being equivalent to injecting symmetric noise to the labels — we show how it relates to a general family of loss-correction techniques from the label noise literature. Building on this connection, we show that label smoothing is competitive with loss-correction under label noise. Further, we show that when distilling models from noisy data, label smoothing of the teacher is beneficial; this is in contrast to recent findings for noise-free problems, and sheds further light on settings where label smoothing is beneficial.

paragraphs: Label smoothing replaces a completely concentrated training target with a mixture of that target and a uniform label distribution. It is known to help prediction and calibration empirically, but its role when training labels are already noisy is less obvious. Because smoothing is equivalent to adding symmetric label noise, it can appear to aggravate the problem.

The paper investigates this apparent tension by relating label smoothing to a broader family of loss-correction methods developed for noisy labels. That connection supplies a different way to understand what smoothing does to the learning objective. Building on it, the authors show that smoothing is competitive with loss correction under label noise.

They also study distillation from noisy data, where a student learns from a teacher model. Smoothing the teacher's labels is beneficial in this setting, contrasting with earlier findings for noise-free problems. The result makes the data's noise conditions central to interpreting smoothing's usefulness, rather than treating findings from clean-label distillation as universally applicable.
summary.tldr: Label smoothing connects to noise-corrected losses and can help both noisy-label learning and distillation from noisy data.

title: Does label smoothing mitigate label noise?

abstract: Tasks in multi-task learning often correlate, conflict, or even compete with each other. As a result, a single solution that is optimal for all tasks rarely exists. Recent papers introduced the concept of Pareto optimality to this field and directly cast multi-task learning as multi-objective optimization problems, but solutions returned by existing methods are typically finite, sparse, and discrete. We present a novel, efficient method that generates locally continuous Pareto sets and Pareto fronts, which opens up the possibility of continuous analysis of Pareto optimal solutions in machine learning problems. We scale up theoretical results in multi-objective optimization to modern machine learning problems by proposing a sample-based sparse linear system, for which standard Hessian-free solvers in machine learning can be applied. We compare our method to the state-of-the-art algorithms and demonstrate its usage of analyzing local Pareto sets on various multi-task classification and regression problems. The experimental results confirm that our algorithm reveals the primary directions in local Pareto sets for trade-off balancing, finds more solutions with different trade-offs efficiently, and scales well to tasks with millions of parameters.

paragraphs: Multi-task learning often involves competing objectives, so one model rarely optimizes every task simultaneously. Pareto analysis studies trade-offs where improving one objective requires giving ground on another. Existing methods typically return a sparse collection of separate solutions, making it difficult to examine how nearby trade-offs connect.

This paper proposes a method for generating locally continuous Pareto sets and their corresponding objective trade-offs, or Pareto fronts. To make multi-objective theory practical at modern model sizes, the authors formulate a sample-based sparse linear system. Standard Hessian-free solvers can then be applied, providing a computational route to exploring nearby solutions.

Experiments on multi-task classification and regression show that the method identifies principal directions within local Pareto sets, efficiently discovers additional trade-offs, and scales to tasks with millions of parameters. Its value is in making local trade-off structure available for analysis and balancing. The stated scope is local continuous exploration, rather than a claim to recover every possible trade-off across the entire optimization landscape.
summary.tldr: A scalable method explores continuous local Pareto trade-offs between tasks instead of returning only isolated solutions.

title: Efficient Continuous Pareto Exploration in Multi-Task Learning

abstract: Learning from demonstrations can be challenging when the quality of demonstrations is diverse, and even more so when the quality is unknown and there is no additional information to estimate the quality. We propose a new method for imitation learning in such scenarios. We show that simple quality-estimation approaches might fail due to compounding error, and fix this issue by jointly estimating both the quality and reward using a variational approach. Our method is easy to implement within reinforcement-learning frameworks and also achieves state-of-the-art performance on continuous-control benchmarks.Our work enables scalable and data-efficient imitation learning under more realistic settings than before.

Our method is easy to implement within reinforcement-learning frameworks and also achieves state-of-the-art performance on continuous-control benchmarks.Our work enables scalable and data-efficient imitation learning under more realistic settings than before.

paragraphs: Imitation learning becomes difficult when demonstrations vary in quality. The problem is harder when those quality differences are unknown and no additional information is available to assess them. This paper develops a method specifically for learning from demonstrations in that setting.

The authors show that simple approaches to estimating demonstration quality can fail because errors compound. Their solution jointly estimates quality and reward through a variational approach. Treating these quantities together addresses the interaction between judging the examples and learning what behavior should be encouraged, rather than relying on a simple quality estimate as a separate starting point.

The method can be implemented within reinforcement learning frameworks and achieves state-of-the-art performance on the reported continuous-control benchmarks. The authors present it as enabling scalable, data-efficient imitation learning under more realistic demonstration conditions. The significance is that useful learning need not start with uniformly strong demonstrations or known quality labels; the proposed procedure learns quality information alongside the reward in the studied setting.
summary.tldr: Joint variational estimation of demonstration quality and reward improves imitation learning when examples have mixed, unknown quality.

title: Variational Imitation Learning with Diverse-quality Demonstrations

abstract: In face recognition, designing margin-based (\emph{e.g.}, angular, additive, additive angular margins) softmax loss functions plays an important role to learn discriminative features. However, these hand-crafted heuristic methods may be sub-optimal because they require much effort to explore the large design space. Recently, an AutoML for loss function search method AM-LFS has been derived, which leverages reinforcement learning to search loss functions during the training process. But its search space is complex and unstable that hindering its superiority. In this paper, we first analyze that the key to enhance the feature discrimination is actually \textbf{how to reduce the softmax probability}. We then design a unified formulation for the current margin-based softmax losses. Accordingly, we define a novel search space and develop a reward-guided search method to automatically obtain the best candidate. Experimental results on a variety of face recognition benchmarks have demonstrated the effectiveness of our method over the state-of-the-art alternatives.

paragraphs: Face recognition depends on learning features that distinguish identities. Margin-based softmax losses are an important tool for this, but manually designing them requires exploring many possibilities. The paper also identifies a difficulty with an existing automated loss-search approach: its complicated and unstable search space can hinder the benefit of automatic search.

The authors analyze how reducing softmax probability relates to improving feature discrimination. Using that analysis, they construct a unified formulation for existing margin-based softmax losses. This formulation becomes the basis for a new search space. A reward-guided search method then automatically selects the best candidate within the search, connecting the design of candidate losses to the paper's analysis.

Experiments on multiple face recognition benchmarks show the method's effectiveness relative to state-of-the-art alternatives. The contribution lies in organizing the loss-design problem before automating the search. The results indicate that a search space informed by a common formulation of margin losses can produce useful objectives for learning discriminative face representations.
summary.tldr: The paper unifies margin-based softmax losses and uses reward-guided search to select effective face recognition objectives.

title: Loss Function Search for Face Recognition

abstract: To collect large scale annotated data, it is inevitable to introduce label noise, i.e., incorrect class labels. To be robust against label noise, many successful methods rely on the noisy classifiers (i.e., models trained on the noisy training data) to determine whether a label is trustworthy. However, it remains unknown why this heuristic works well in practice. In this paper, we provide the first theoretical explanation for these methods. We prove that the prediction of a noisy classifier can indeed be a good indicator of whether the label of a training data is clean. Based on the theoretical result, we propose a novel algorithm that corrects the labels based on the noisy classifier prediction. The corrected labels are consistent with the true Bayesian optimal classifier with high probability. We incorporate our label correction algorithm into the training of deep neural networks and train models that achieve superior testing performance on multiple public datasets.

paragraphs: Large annotated datasets can contain incorrect class labels. Many methods try to detect these errors using predictions from a model trained on the same noisy data. That strategy raises a basic question: why should a model exposed to incorrect labels still provide useful evidence about which labels are trustworthy? This paper supplies a theoretical explanation.

The authors prove that predictions from a noisy classifier can be a good indicator of whether a training label is clean. They use this result to design an algorithm that corrects labels according to the classifier's predictions. The corrected labels agree with the true Bayesian optimal classifier with high probability, giving the correction procedure a probabilistic theoretical foundation.

The correction algorithm is incorporated into deep neural network training. Models trained this way achieve superior test performance on multiple public datasets in the reported experiments. The contribution connects a practical heuristic to an analyzed correction rule: predictions learned from imperfect supervision can still guide improvements to that supervision. Its high-probability result does not assert that every corrected label is always correct.
summary.tldr: The paper theoretically motivates using noisy classifiers to correct labels and reports improved deep-network test performance.

title: Error-Bounded Correction of Noisy Labels

abstract: Hindsight allows reinforcement learning agents to leverage new observations to make inferences about earlier states and transitions. In this paper, we exploit the idea of hindsight and introduce posterior value functions. Posterior value functions are computed by inferring the posterior distribution over hidden components of the state in previous timesteps and can be used to construct novel unbiased baselines for policy gradient methods. Importantly, we prove that these baselines reduce (and never increase) the variance of policy gradient estimators compared to traditional state value functions. While the posterior value function is motivated by partial observability, we extend these results to arbitrary stochastic MDPs by showing that hindsight-capable agents can model stochasticity in the environment as a special case of partial observability. Finally, we introduce a pair of methods for learning posterior value functions and prove their convergence.

paragraphs: Later observations can reveal information about what was happening earlier in a reinforcement learning episode. This paper uses that hindsight to construct posterior value functions. They are computed by inferring a probability distribution over hidden components of earlier states, allowing subsequent evidence to refine the agent's assessment of past situations.

The authors use these value functions to build baselines for policy gradient methods. Such baselines help control the variability of gradient estimates. The proposed baselines are unbiased, and the paper proves that their variance is no greater than that obtained with traditional state-value baselines. This is a formal comparison of estimator variance.

Although partial observability motivates the construction, the results extend to arbitrary stochastic Markov decision processes. The authors show that hindsight-capable agents can treat environmental randomness as a special form of hidden information. They also propose two methods for learning posterior value functions and prove their convergence, connecting the theoretical baseline construction to learnable quantities.
summary.tldr: Posterior value functions use hindsight to build unbiased policy-gradient baselines whose variance never exceeds that of traditional state-value baselines.

title: Posterior Value Functions: Hindsight Baselines for Policy Gradient Methods

abstract: Sequential data with serial correlation and an unknown, unstructured, and dynamic background is ubiquitous in neuroscience, psychology, and econometrics. Inferring serial correlation for such data is a fundamental challenge in statistics. We propose a Total Variation (TV) constrained least square estimator coupled with hypothesis tests to infer the serial correlation in the presence of unknown and unstructured dynamic background. The TV constraint on the dynamic background encourages a piecewise constant structure, which can approximate a wide range of dynamic backgrounds. The tuning parameter is selected via the Ljung-Box test to control the bias-variance trade-off. We establish a non-asymptotic upper bound for the estimation error through variational inequalities. We also derive a lower error bound via Fano’s method and show the proposed method is near-optimal. Numerical simulation and a real study in psychology demonstrate the excellent performance of our proposed method compared with the state-of-the-art.

paragraphs: Sequential measurements can contain both dependence across time and a background that changes in an unknown way. Distinguishing these components is a statistical challenge: apparent temporal structure must be assessed while accounting for the moving background. This paper develops an estimator and associated hypothesis tests for inferring serial correlation in that setting.

The estimator uses least squares with a total variation constraint on the background. That constraint encourages a piecewise constant description, which can approximate a broad range of changing backgrounds. The tuning parameter is selected using the Ljung-Box test to manage the bias-variance tradeoff, connecting the amount of background flexibility to the inference procedure.

The authors establish a finite-sample upper bound on estimation error using variational inequalities. They also derive a lower error bound through Fano’s method and show that their estimator is near-optimal. Simulations and a psychology study demonstrate strong performance relative to state-of-the-art methods. Together, the bounds and experiments support treating unknown background variation explicitly when estimating dependence in sequential observations.
summary.tldr: A total-variation-constrained estimator infers serial correlation amid changing backgrounds, with near-optimal error guarantees and supporting experiments.

title: Inferring serial correlation with dynamic backgrounds

abstract: Estimating the difficulty of a dataset typically involves comparing state-of-the-art models to humans; the bigger the performance gap, the harder the dataset is said to be. However, this comparison provides little understanding of how difficult each instance in a given distribution is, or what attributes make the dataset difficult for a given model. To address these questions, we frame dataset difficulty—w.r.t. a model $\mathcal{V}$—as the lack of $\mathcal{V}$-usable information (Xu et al., 2019), where a lower value indicates a more difficult dataset for $\mathcal{V}$. We further introduce pointwise $\mathcal{V}$-information (PVI) for measuring the difficulty of individual instances w.r.t. a given distribution. While standard evaluation metrics typically only compare different models for the same dataset, $\mathcal{V}$-usable information and PVI also permit the converse: for a given model $\mathcal{V}$, we can compare different datasets, as well as different instances/slices of the same dataset. Furthermore, our framework allows for the interpretability of different input attributes via transformations of the input, which we use to discover annotation artefacts in widely-used NLP benchmarks.

That comparison says little about which examples are difficult for a particular model or which input attributes cause difficulty. This paper treats difficulty as relative to a model's ability to extract usable information from a data distribution.

The framework uses V-usable information: lower usable information means greater difficulty for the specified model V. It also introduces pointwise V-information, or PVI, to assess individual examples relative to a given distribution. These measures make the model and distribution part of the difficulty assessment instead of assigning an unqualified difficulty label.

This perspective supports comparisons across datasets for a fixed model, as well as comparisons among examples or slices within a dataset. The authors also transform inputs to investigate the contribution of different attributes, using the framework to uncover annotation artifacts in widely used language benchmarks. The contribution links dataset-level evaluation with example-level analysis and provides a way to investigate what information a model can actually use.
summary.tldr: V-usable information and its pointwise counterpart measure dataset and example difficulty relative to a model, enabling comparisons and analysis of input attributes.

title: Understanding Dataset Difficulty with $\mathcal{V}$-Usable Information

abstract: We propose a novel theoretical framework of analysis for Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs). We reveal a fundamental flaw of previous analyses which, by incorrectly modeling GANs’ training scheme, are subject to ill-defined discriminator gradients. We overcome this issue which impedes a principled study of GAN training, solving it within our framework by taking into account the discriminator’s architecture. To this end, we leverage the theory of infinite-width neural networks for the discriminator via its Neural Tangent Kernel. We characterize the trained discriminator for a wide range of losses and establish general differentiability properties of the network. From this, we derive new insights about the convergence of the generated distribution, advancing our understanding of GANs’ training dynamics. We empirically corroborate these results via an analysis toolkit based on our framework, unveiling intuitions that are consistent with GAN practice.

paragraphs: A generative adversarial network learns through an interaction between a generator and a discriminator. This paper argues that previous theoretical analyses sometimes model that interaction incorrectly, leaving the discriminator gradients mathematically ill-defined. Because those gradients are central to understanding training, this is a problem with the foundation of the analysis.

The authors build a framework that explicitly accounts for the discriminator’s architecture. They use the neural tangent kernel associated with an infinite-width discriminator to describe its behavior during learning. Within this framework, they characterize the trained discriminator for a broad range of loss functions and establish differentiability properties that make its gradients well-defined.

These results support new conclusions about how the generated distribution converges and how GAN training evolves. The authors also develop an analysis toolkit and use experiments to corroborate their theoretical findings. The contribution is a more principled way to study training dynamics, with empirical observations that agree with practical GAN behavior; it is not a claim that every GAN training procedure converges.
summary.tldr: An architecture-aware neural tangent kernel framework resolves ill-defined discriminator gradients in previous GAN analyses and yields insights into training dynamics.

title: A Neural Tangent Kernel Perspective of GANs

abstract: PAC-Bayesian error bounds provide a theoretical guarantee on the generalization abilities of meta-learning from training tasks to unseen tasks. However, it is still unclear how tight PAC-Bayesian bounds we can achieve for meta-learning. In this work, we propose a general PAC-Bayesian framework to cope with single-task learning and meta-learning uniformly. With this framework, we generalize the two tightest PAC-Bayesian bounds (i.e., kl-bound and Catoni-bound) from single-task learning to standard meta-learning, resulting in fast convergence rates for PAC-Bayesian meta-learners. By minimizing the derived two bounds, we develop two meta-learning algorithms for classification problems with deep neural networks. For regression problems, by setting Gibbs optimal posterior for each training task, we obtain the closed-form formula of the minimizer of our Catoni-bound, leading to an efficient Gibbs meta-learning algorithm. Although minimizing our kl-bound can not yield a closed-form solution, we show that it can be extended for analyzing the more challenging meta-learning setting where samples from different training tasks exhibit interdependencies. Experiments empirically show that our proposed meta-learning algorithms achieve competitive results with respect to latest works.

paragraphs: Meta-learning uses experience across training tasks to support learning on unseen tasks. PAC-Bayesian bounds provide theoretical guarantees for this transfer, but how tight those guarantees can be remains an important question. The paper develops a common framework for analyzing both ordinary single-task learning and meta-learning.

Within that framework, the authors extend the kl-bound and Catoni-bound to standard meta-learning and obtain fast convergence rates. Minimizing the resulting bounds produces two algorithms for classification with deep neural networks. The kl-bound lacks such a closed-form minimizer, but its analysis can extend to tasks whose samples are interdependent. Experiments report competitive performance against recent methods, complementing the contribution of tighter theory and bound-driven algorithm design.
summary.tldr: A unified PAC-Bayesian framework yields fast-rate meta-learning guarantees and algorithms built by minimizing those bounds.

title: Fast-Rate PAC-Bayesian Generalization Bounds for Meta-Learning

abstract: We study two model selection settings in stochastic linear bandits (LB). In the first setting, which we refer to as feature selection, the expected reward of the LB problem is in the linear span of at least one of $M$ feature maps (models). In the second setting, the reward parameter of the LB problem is arbitrarily selected from $M$ models represented as (possibly) overlapping balls in $\mathbb R^d$. However, the agent only has access to misspecified models, i.e., estimates of the centers and radii of the balls. We refer to this setting as parameter selection. For each setting, we develop and analyze a computationally efficient algorithm that is based on a reduction from bandits to full-information problems. This allows us to obtain regret bounds that are not worse (up to a $\sqrt{\log M}$ factor) than the case where the true model is known. This is the best reported dependence on the number of models $M$ in these settings. Finally, we empirically show the effectiveness of our algorithms using synthetic and real-world experiments.

paragraphs: A stochastic linear bandit learner must choose actions while learning how their features relate to reward. This paper adds uncertainty about the appropriate model itself. It considers two forms of model selection and asks how much additional regret arises compared with knowing the correct model in advance.

In feature selection, at least one of several candidate feature maps can express the expected reward linearly. In parameter selection, the reward parameter belongs to one of several possibly overlapping balls in parameter space. The learner has only imperfect estimates of those balls’ centers and radii. For each setting, the authors develop a computationally efficient algorithm by reducing the bandit problem to a full-information problem.

Their regret bounds are no worse than the known-model case up to a square-root-logarithmic factor in the number of candidate models. The authors report this as the best dependence on model count then available for these settings. Experiments with synthetic and real-world data support the algorithms’ effectiveness, complementing the theoretical account of the cost of model uncertainty.
summary.tldr: Efficient linear-bandit algorithms select features or parameter models with only a square-root-logarithmic regret factor in the number of candidates.

title: Feature and Parameter Selection in Stochastic Linear Bandits

abstract: Neural network ensembles, such as Bayesian neural networks (BNNs), have shown success in the areas of uncertainty estimation and robustness. However, a crucial challenge prohibits their use in practice. BNNs require a large number of predictions to produce reliable results, leading to a significant increase in computational cost. To alleviate this issue, we propose spatial smoothing, a method that ensembles neighboring feature map points of convolutional neural networks. By simply adding a few blur layers to the models, we empirically show that spatial smoothing improves accuracy, uncertainty estimation, and robustness of BNNs across a whole range of ensemble sizes. In particular, BNNs incorporating spatial smoothing achieve high predictive performance merely with a handful of ensembles. Moreover, this method also can be applied to canonical deterministic neural networks to improve the performances. A number of evidences suggest that the improvements can be attributed to the stabilized feature maps and the smoothing of the loss landscape. In addition, we provide a fundamental explanation for prior works {—} namely, global average pooling, pre-activation, and ReLU6 {—} by addressing them as special cases of spatial smoothing. These not only enhance accuracy, but also improve uncertainty estimation and robustness by making the loss landscape smoother in the same manner as spatial smoothing. The code is available at https://github.com/xxxnell/spatial-smoothing.

paragraphs: Combining multiple neural-network predictions can improve uncertainty estimates and robustness, but reliable Bayesian neural-network predictions may require many evaluations. This paper explores a cheaper complementary operation inside convolutional networks: combining nearby locations in their feature maps. The authors implement this spatial smoothing by inserting a few blur layers.

Experiments show improvements in accuracy, uncertainty estimation, and robustness across a range of ensemble sizes. With smoothing, Bayesian networks achieve strong predictive performance using only a handful of ensemble members. The method also improves conventional deterministic networks, so its reported usefulness extends beyond models that explicitly combine multiple predictions.

The authors present evidence suggesting that steadier feature maps and a smoother loss landscape help explain these gains. They also interpret global average pooling, pre-activation, and ReLU6 as special cases of spatial smoothing, offering a common explanation for their benefits. The broader contribution is an empirical and conceptual connection between local feature averaging and advantages usually associated with ensembles.
summary.tldr: Adding blur layers to convolutional networks empirically improves accuracy, uncertainty estimates, and robustness through spatial feature smoothing.

title: Blurs Behave Like Ensembles: Spatial Smoothings to Improve Accuracy, Uncertainty, and Robustness

abstract: Meta learning automatically infers an inductive bias, that includes the hyperparameter of the baselearning algorithm, by observing data from a finite number of related tasks. This paper studies PAC-Bayes bounds on meta generalization gap. The meta-generalization gap comprises two sources of generalization gaps: the environmentlevel and task-level gaps resulting from observation of a finite number of tasks and data samples per task, respectively. In this paper, by upper bounding arbitrary convex functions, which link the expected and empirical losses at the environment and also per-task levels, we obtain new PAC-Bayes bounds. Using these bounds, we develop new PAC-Bayes meta-learning algorithms. Numerical examples demonstrate the merits of the proposed novel bounds and algorithm in comparison to prior PAC-Bayes bounds for meta-learning

paragraphs: Meta-learning uses experience from related tasks to learn an inductive bias, including hyperparameters for the learning algorithm applied within each task. A central question is how well that learned bias transfers beyond the observed data. This paper studies that question through PAC-Bayes bounds on the meta-generalization gap.

The analysis separates two sources of uncertainty. Observing only a finite number of tasks creates an environment-level gap, while observing only a finite number of examples within each task creates a task-level gap. The authors derive new bounds by upper bounding convex functions that connect empirical losses with expected losses at both levels. This provides a common mathematical route for handling the two gaps together.

The bounds also serve as the basis for new meta-learning algorithms, connecting the theoretical analysis to a training procedure. Numerical examples demonstrate advantages over earlier PAC-Bayes bounds and algorithms for meta-learning. These findings support the usefulness of the proposed formulation in the examined examples, alongside its contribution to understanding how limited task and sample counts affect generalization.
summary.tldr: A unified PAC-Bayes analysis accounts for limited tasks and limited examples per task, yielding new meta-learning bounds and algorithms.

title: A Unified View on PAC-Bayes Bounds for Meta-Learning

abstract: We propose a metric— Projection Norm —to predict a model’s performance on out-of-distribution (OOD) data without access to ground truth labels. Projection Norm first uses model predictions to pseudo-label test samples and then trains a new model on the pseudo-labels. The more the new model’s parameters differ from an in-distribution model, the greater the predicted OOD error. Empirically, our approach outperforms existing methods on both image and text classification tasks and across different network architectures. Theoretically, we connect our approach to a bound on the test error for overparameterized linear models. Furthermore, we find that Projection Norm is the only approach that achieves non-trivial detection performance on adversarial examples. Our code is available at \url{https://github.com/yaodongyu/ProjNorm}.

paragraphs: When a model encounters a new data distribution, its original accuracy may no longer describe its performance. Measuring the new error directly normally requires correct labels. This paper introduces Projection Norm, a metric intended to predict out-of-distribution error using test samples without access to their ground-truth labels.

The method first uses model predictions as provisional labels for the test samples. It trains a new model on those pseudo-labels and compares the new model’s parameters with those of an in-distribution model. A larger parameter difference corresponds to a larger predicted error. This turns the effect of training on the new samples into a signal about expected performance.

Experiments across image and text classification and different architectures show improvements over existing methods. The authors also connect Projection Norm to a test-error bound for overparameterized linear models. In their adversarial-example evaluation, it is the only compared approach with non-trivial detection performance. The theory and experiments provide complementary support, with the formal connection specifically established for the linear model setting.
summary.tldr: Projection Norm predicts error on unlabeled shifted data by measuring parameter differences after training a model on pseudo-labeled test samples.

title: Predicting Out-of-Distribution Error with the Projection Norm

abstract: The prevalence and importance of algorithmic two-sided marketplaces has drawn attention to the issue of fairness in such settings. Algorithmic decisions are used in assigning students to schools, users to advertisers, and applicants to job interviews. These decisions should heed the preferences of individuals, and simultaneously be fair with respect to their merits (synonymous with fit, future performance, or need). Merits conditioned on observable features are always uncertain , a fact that is exacerbated by the widespread use of machine learning algorithms to infer merit from the observables. As our key contribution, we carefully axiomatize a notion of individual fairness in the two-sided marketplace setting which respects the uncertainty in the merits; indeed, it simultaneously recognizes uncertainty as the primary potential cause of unfairness and an approach to address it. We design a linear programming framework to find fair utility-maximizing distributions over allocations, and we show that the linear program is robust to perturbations in the estimated parameters of the uncertain merit distributions, a key property in combining the approach with machine learning techniques.

paragraphs: Matching systems assign people to opportunities, such as students to schools or applicants to interviews. Such decisions need to account for individual preferences and relevant merit, which may mean fit, need, or future performance. The difficulty is that merit inferred from observable information remains uncertain, including when machine learning supplies the estimates.

This paper formalizes individual fairness for two-sided marketplaces while explicitly respecting that uncertainty. Its formulation treats uncertainty as both a possible source of unfairness and something that can help address it. The authors then develop a linear programming framework for finding distributions over allocations that maximize utility subject to their fairness requirements.

Working with distributions means the framework chooses how allocations should be randomized, rather than only selecting one fixed assignment. The authors also show robustness to perturbations in the estimated parameters of merit distributions. This property matters when the framework uses machine learning estimates: the proposed optimization accounts for uncertainty, and its robustness result addresses sensitivity to errors in the parameters used to describe that uncertainty.
summary.tldr: The paper formalizes fairness under uncertain merit and optimizes randomized allocations with robustness to perturbations in estimated distribution parameters.

title: Fairness in Matching under Uncertainty

abstract: We consider the task of evaluating policies of algorithmic resource allocation through randomized controlled trials (RCTs). Such policies are tasked with optimizing the utilization of limited intervention resources, with the goal of maximizing the benefits derived. Evaluation of such allocation policies through RCTs proves difficult, notwithstanding the scale of the trial, because the individuals’ outcomes are inextricably interlinked through resource constraints controlling the policy decisions. Our key contribution is to present a new estimator leveraging our proposed novel concept, that involves retrospective reshuffling of participants across experimental arms at the end of an RCT. We identify conditions under which such reassignments are permissible and can be leveraged to construct counterfactual trials, whose outcomes can be accurately ascertained, for free. We prove theoretically that such an estimator is more accurate than common estimators based on sample means – we show that it returns an unbiased estimate and simultaneously reduces variance. We demonstrate the value of our approach through empirical experiments on synthetic, semisynthetic as well as real case study data and show improved estimation accuracy across the board.

paragraphs: Resource-allocation policies decide how to distribute a limited supply of interventions. Evaluating them through randomized trials is difficult because resource constraints link participants’ outcomes through the policy’s decisions. Increasing the trial size alone does not remove this interdependence, so conventional comparisons of experimental-arm averages leave an important estimation challenge.

The paper introduces an estimator based on retrospectively reshuffling participants between trial arms. The authors identify conditions under which these reassignments are permissible and the outcomes of the resulting counterfactual trials can be determined accurately without running new experiments. The reshuffling is therefore a way to extract additional information from an already completed trial.

Theoretical results show that the estimator remains unbiased while reducing variance compared with common sample-mean estimators. Experiments using synthetic data, semisynthetic data, and real case-study data report improved estimation accuracy throughout. The key qualification is that the counterfactual reassignments must satisfy the identified conditions; arbitrary reshuffling is not justified. Within that framework, the method improves policy evaluation by reusing the structure of existing trial evidence.
summary.tldr: Permissible retrospective participant reshuffling yields an unbiased, lower-variance estimator for randomized trials of resource-allocation policies.

title: Improved Policy Evaluation for Randomized Trials of Algorithmic Resource Allocation

abstract: Policies often fail at test-time due to distribution shifts —changes in the state and reward that occur when an end user deploys the policy in environments different from those seen in training. Data augmentation can help models be more robust to such shifts by varying specific concepts in the state, e.g. object color, that are task-irrelevant and should not impact desired actions. However, designers training the agent don’t often know which concepts are irrelevant a priori . We propose a human-in-the-loop framework to leverage feedback from the end user to quickly identify and augment task-irrelevant visual state concepts. Our framework generates counterfactual demonstrations that allow users to quickly isolate shifted state concepts and identify if they should not impact the desired task, and can therefore be augmented using existing actions. We present experiments validating our full pipeline on discrete and continuous control tasks with real human users. Our method better enables users to (1) understand agent failure, (2) improve sample efficiency of demonstrations required for finetuning, and (3) adapt the agent to their desired reward.

paragraphs: A policy can fail after deployment because its environment differs from the one used in training. Some visual differences, such as object color, may be irrelevant to the desired action. Augmenting those features can improve robustness, but a model designer may not know in advance which features an end user's task should ignore.

This paper places the user inside the adaptation process. Its framework generates counterfactual demonstrations that help users isolate changed visual concepts and judge whether those changes should affect the task. When a concept is identified as irrelevant, the system can vary it while retaining existing actions, turning feedback into additional material for fine-tuning.

Experiments with real users cover both discrete and continuous control tasks. The authors report that the full pipeline helps users understand failures, use demonstrations more efficiently during fine-tuning, and adapt the agent to their desired reward. The approach matters because it ties augmentation decisions to the user's understanding of the task, supplying information that may have been unavailable during original training.
summary.tldr: User feedback on counterfactual demonstrations guides visual augmentation and helps adapt policies to deployment changes.

title: Diagnosis, Feedback, Adaptation: A Human-in-the-Loop Framework for Test-Time Policy Adaptation

abstract: We present AIRS: A utomatic I ntrinsic R eward S haping that intelligently and adaptively provides high-quality intrinsic rewards to enhance exploration in reinforcement learning (RL). More specifically, AIRS selects shaping function from a predefined set based on the estimated task return in real-time, providing reliable exploration incentives and alleviating the biased objective problem. Moreover, we develop an intrinsic reward toolkit to provide efficient and reliable implementations of diverse intrinsic reward approaches. We test AIRS on various tasks of MiniGrid, Procgen, and DeepMind Control Suite. Extensive simulation demonstrates that AIRS can outperform the benchmarking schemes and achieve superior performance with simple architecture.

paragraphs: Intrinsic rewards give reinforcement learning agents additional incentives to explore. The difficulty is making those incentives useful for the actual task: an exploration bonus can change what the agent is encouraged to optimize. This paper introduces AIRS, a method that adapts reward shaping during learning to provide exploration incentives while alleviating that biased-objective problem.

AIRS selects a shaping function from a predefined collection, using an estimate of task return available during training. Its central choice is therefore which available exploration incentive to apply as learning proceeds. Connecting that selection to estimated task performance makes the shaping mechanism responsive to the task, rather than leaving the same incentive fixed throughout training.

The work also supplies an intrinsic-reward toolkit with implementations of multiple approaches. The authors evaluate AIRS on tasks from MiniGrid, Procgen, and the DeepMind Control Suite. Their simulations show that AIRS can outperform the benchmark schemes with a simple architecture. These findings support adaptive selection among existing shaping functions as a useful mechanism for improving exploration.
summary.tldr: AIRS adapts exploration rewards using estimated task return and outperforms benchmark schemes in simulation.

title: Automatic Intrinsic Reward Shaping for Exploration in Deep Reinforcement Learning

abstract: We aim to address Multi-Task Learning (MTL) with a large number of tasks by Multi-Task Grouping (MTG). Given $N$ tasks, we propose to simultaneously identify the best task groups from $2^N$ candidates and train the model weights simultaneously in one-shot, with the high-order task-affinity fully exploited. This is distinct from the pioneering methods which sequentially identify the groups and train the model weights, where the group identification often relies on heuristics. As a result, our method not only improves the training efficiency, but also mitigates the objective bias introduced by the sequential procedures that potentially leads to a suboptimal solution. Specifically, we formulate MTG as a fully differentiable pruning problem on an adaptive network architecture determined by an unknown Categorical distribution. To categorize $N$ tasks into $K$ groups (represented by $K$ encoder branches), we initially set up $KN$ task heads, where each branch connects to all $N$ task heads to exploit the high-order task-affinity. Then, we gradually prune the $KN$ heads down to $N$ by learning a relaxed differentiable Categorical distribution, ensuring that each task is exclusively and uniquely categorized into only one branch. Extensive experiments on CelebA and Taskonomy datasets with detailed ablations show the promising performance and efficiency of our method. The codes are available at https://github.com/ethanygao/DMTG.
