paragraphs: When many tasks are learned together, choosing which ones should share a model becomes a substantial optimization problem. Earlier grouping methods choose task groups and train model weights in separate stages, often using heuristics for grouping. DMTG jointly learns the grouping and the weights, aiming to improve efficiency and reduce the objective mismatch introduced by sequential decisions.

The method expresses grouping as differentiable pruning of an adaptive network. For N tasks and K groups, it starts with K encoder branches, each connected to all N task heads. A learned, relaxed categorical distribution gradually removes connections until only N heads remain, assigning each task to exactly one branch.

Initially connecting every branch to every task allows the method to exploit relationships involving multiple tasks together. Grouping decisions can then evolve alongside the model being trained, instead of being fixed beforehand. Experiments on CelebA and Taskonomy, including ablation studies, show promising performance and efficiency for this joint approach to organizing many tasks.
summary.tldr: DMTG jointly learns task groups and model weights by differentiably pruning a network into one branch assignment per task.

title: DMTG: One-Shot Differentiable Multi-Task Grouping

abstract: Spiking neural networks (SNNs) are promising brain-inspired energy-efficient models. Compared to conventional deep Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs), SNNs exhibit superior efficiency and capability to process temporal information. However, it remains a challenge to train SNNs due to their undifferentiable spiking mechanism. The surrogate gradients method is commonly used to train SNNs, but often comes with an accuracy disadvantage over ANNs counterpart. We link the degraded accuracy to the vanishing of gradient on the temporal dimension through the analytical and experimental study of the training process of Leaky Integrate-and-Fire (LIF) Neuron-based SNNs. Moreover, we propose the Complementary Leaky Integrate-and-Fire (CLIF) Neuron. CLIF creates extra paths to facilitate the backpropagation in computing temporal gradient while keeping binary output. CLIF is hyperparameter-free and features broad applicability. Extensive experiments on a variety of datasets demonstrate CLIF’s clear performance advantage over other neuron models. Furthermore, the CLIF’s performance even slightly surpasses superior ANNs with identical network structure and training conditions. The code is available at https://github.com/HuuYuLong/Complementary-LIF.

paragraphs: Spiking neural networks process information through discrete spikes and offer promise for energy-efficient temporal processing. Their discrete outputs also make training difficult because the spiking operation is not differentiable. Surrogate gradients provide a way to train these networks, but their accuracy often remains below that of conventional artificial neural networks.

This paper investigates that gap in networks built from leaky integrate-and-fire neurons. Analytical and experimental studies connect degraded accuracy to gradients fading as they propagate through time. The proposed complementary leaky integrate-and-fire neuron, CLIF, adds paths that help temporal gradients travel during backpropagation while preserving binary outputs. The neuron design is also described as hyperparameter-free.

Experiments across several datasets show a clear performance advantage over other neuron models. Under matched network structures and training conditions, CLIF even slightly exceeds the performance of strong conventional neural networks in the reported evaluations. The contribution links a specific training difficulty to a neuron-level modification, showing that improving temporal gradient flow can substantially narrow the accuracy gap.
summary.tldr: CLIF adds temporal gradient paths to spiking neurons, improving reported accuracy while retaining binary outputs.

title: CLIF: Complementary Leaky Integrate-and-Fire Neuron for Spiking Neural Networks

abstract: Known learning rules tend to fall near one of two extremes: single-pass associative learning with low complexity and capacity, and multi-pass iterative learning with high complexity and capacity. In this work we investigate the mathematical feasibility of learning rules that are both single-pass and achieve the theoretical upper bound on capacity. We consider a fairly broad family of learning rules we call “span rules,” which include known rules such as Hebbian learning, perceptron learning, and backpropagation as special cases. To our knowledge, previous work has not determined whether single-pass, full-capacity span rules exist, even in the most fundamental case of a linear threshold neuron with binary input vectors, which is the focus of this study. We derive a necessary condition for the existence of such learning rules, which takes the form of a linear program, and show that the linear program is infeasible. This establishes an impossibility result that span rules can not be both single-pass and full-capacity.

paragraphs: Learning rules often trade computational simplicity against storage capacity. Some associative rules learn in one pass but have limited capacity, while iterative methods can achieve higher capacity through repeated passes. This paper asks whether a rule can combine single-pass learning with the theoretical maximum capacity in a basic neuron model.

The setting is a linear threshold neuron with binary input vectors. The authors study a broad family called span rules, which includes Hebbian learning, perceptron learning, and backpropagation as special cases. They derive a necessary condition that any single-pass, full-capacity span rule would have to satisfy, expressed as the feasibility of a linear program.

They then show that this linear program is infeasible. Because the condition is necessary, its failure establishes that no rule in the studied family can have both properties in this setting. The result therefore identifies a mathematical boundary for learning-rule design. Its scope is the specified span-rule family and neuron setting, where the desired combination is impossible rather than merely difficult to achieve with existing algorithms.
summary.tldr: Span rules cannot combine single-pass learning with full theoretical capacity for the studied binary-input threshold neuron.

title: On the Feasibility of Single-Pass Full-Capacity Learning in Linear Threshold Neurons with Binary Input Vectors

abstract: With the incorporation of the UNet architecture, diffusion probabilistic models have become a dominant force in image generation tasks. One key design in UNet is the skip connections between the encoder and decoder blocks. Although skip connections have been shown to improve training stability and model performance, we point out that such shortcuts can be a limiting factor for the complexity of the transformation. As the sampling steps decrease, the generation process and the role of the UNet get closer to the push-forward transformations from Gaussian distribution to the target, posing a challenge for the network’s complexity. To address this challenge, we propose Skip-Tuning, a simple yet surprisingly effective training-free tuning method on the skip connections. For instance, our method can achieve 100% FID improvement for pretrained EDM on ImageNet 64 with only 19 NFEs (1.75), breaking the limit of ODE samplers regardless of sampling steps. Surprisingly, the improvement persists when we increase the number of sampling steps and can even surpass the best result from EDM-2 (1.58) with only 39 NFEs (1.57). Comprehensive exploratory experiments are conducted to shed light on the surprising effectiveness of our Skip-Tuning. We observe that while Skip-Tuning increases the score-matching losses in the pixel space, the losses in the feature space are reduced, particularly at intermediate noise levels, which coincide with the most effective range accounting for image quality improvement.

paragraphs: Diffusion models built with UNets use skip connections to pass information between encoder and decoder blocks. These shortcuts help training, but the paper argues they can also limit transformation complexity. That matters especially when generation uses fewer sampling steps, requiring the network to perform a more demanding transformation from noise toward the image distribution.

Skip-Tuning adjusts those connections without additional training. The authors report an FID of 1.75 for pretrained EDM on ImageNet 64 using 19 network function evaluations. Improvements persist with more sampling steps: at 39 evaluations, the reported FID is 1.57, slightly better than the cited best EDM-2 result of 1.58.

Those levels also correspond to the range contributing most effectively to image-quality improvements. The observations suggest that better sampling quality can accompany worse pixel-space loss, making the representation used to assess prediction errors relevant to understanding the tuning effect.
summary.tldr: Training-free tuning of UNet skip connections improves diffusion image generation, with gains associated with lower feature-space prediction losses.

title: The Surprising Effectiveness of Skip-Tuning in Diffusion Sampling

abstract: Estimating the uncertainty of a model’s prediction on a test point is a crucial part of ensuring reliability and calibration under distribution shifts.A minimum description length approach to this problem uses the predictive normalized maximum likelihood (pNML) distribution, which considers every possible label for a data point, and decreases confidence in a prediction if other labels are also consistent with the model and training data. In this work we propose IF-COMP, a scalable and efficient approximation of the pNML distribution that linearizes the model with a temperature-scaled Boltzmann influence function. IF-COMP can be used to produce well-calibrated predictions on test points as well as measure complexity in both labelled and unlabelled settings. We experimentally validate IF-COMP on uncertainty calibration, mislabel detection, and OOD detection tasks, where it consistently matches or beats strong baseline methods.

paragraphs: A model's confidence should reflect whether alternative labels remain plausible given its training data. Predictive normalized maximum likelihood, or pNML, approaches uncertainty by considering every possible label for a test point. When several labels remain consistent with the model and data, the resulting prediction becomes less confident.

The paper introduces IF-COMP as a scalable, efficient approximation to this distribution. It linearizes the model using a temperature-scaled Boltzmann influence function. This provides a computational route to the pNML approach while supporting both calibrated predictions and measurements of data complexity. The complexity measurements apply in settings with labels and in settings without them.

The authors evaluate IF-COMP on uncertainty calibration, detecting incorrect labels, and identifying out-of-distribution data. Across these experiments, it consistently matches or exceeds strong baseline methods. The results connect one approximation method to several reliability tasks: assessing prediction confidence, finding questionable annotations, and recognizing unfamiliar inputs. Its significance lies in making a label-alternative view of uncertainty usable at greater computational scale.
summary.tldr: IF-COMP efficiently approximates a distribution that considers alternative labels, supporting uncertainty calibration, mislabel detection, and out-of-distribution detection.

title: Measuring Stochastic Data Complexity with Boltzmann Influence Functions

abstract: Models trained on ultrasound images from one institution typically experience a decline in effectiveness when transferred directly to other institutions. Moreover, unlike natural images, dense and overlapped structures exist in fetus ultrasound images, making the detection of structures more challenging. Thus, to tackle this problem, we propose a new Unsupervised Domain Adaptation (UDA) method named ToMo-UDA for fetus structure detection, which consists of the Topology Knowledge Transfer (TKT) and the Morphology Knowledge Transfer (MKT) module. The TKT leverages prior knowledge of the medical anatomy of fetal as topological information, reconstructing and aligning anatomy features across source and target domains. Then, the MKT formulates a more consistent and independent morphological representation for each substructure of an organ. To evaluate the proposed ToMo-UDA for ultrasound fetal anatomical structure detection, we introduce FUSH$^2$, a new Fetal UltraSound benchmark, comprises Heart and Head images collected from Two health centers, with 16 annotated regions. Our experiments show that utilizing topological and morphological anatomy information in ToMo-UDA can greatly improve organ structure detection. This expands the potential for structure detection tasks in medical image analysis.

paragraphs: Ultrasound detection models often lose effectiveness when moved between institutions. Fetal ultrasound adds another difficulty: anatomical structures can be dense and overlapping. ToMo-UDA addresses this transfer problem by incorporating anatomical relationships and structural shape information into unsupervised domain adaptation.

The method has two components. Topology Knowledge Transfer uses prior anatomical knowledge to reconstruct and align anatomy features across source and target domains. Morphology Knowledge Transfer develops more consistent, independent representations for the individual substructures of an organ. Together, these components address both relationships among structures and how each structure is represented.

The authors also introduce FUSH², a benchmark containing fetal heart and head ultrasound images from two health centers, with 16 annotated regions. Their experiments show substantial improvements in organ-structure detection from using topological and morphological anatomy information. The findings support anatomy-informed adaptation for this detection setting, connecting prior structural knowledge with the practical challenge of transferring models across institutions.
summary.tldr: ToMo-UDA uses anatomical relationships and morphology to improve fetal ultrasound structure detection across institutions.

title: Unsupervised Domain Adaptation for Anatomical Structure Detection in Ultrasound Images

abstract: Discovering reliable and informative relationships among brain regions from functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) signals is essential in phenotypic predictions in neuroscience. Most of the current methods fail to accurately characterize those interactions because they only focus on pairwise connections and overlook the high-order relationships of brain regions. We propose that these high-order relationships should be maximally informative and minimally redundant (MIMR). However, identifying such high-order relationships is challenging and under-explored due to the exponential search space and the absence of a tractable objective. In response to this gap, we propose a novel method named HyBRiD, which aims to extract MIMR high-order relationships from fMRI data. HyBRiD employs a Constructor to identify hyperedge structures, and a Weighter to compute a weight for each hyperedge, which avoids searching in exponential space. HyBRiD achieves the MIMR objective through an innovative information bottleneck framework named multi-head drop-bottleneck with theoretical guarantees. Our comprehensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our model. Our model outperforms the state-of-the-art predictive model by an average of 11.2%, regarding the quality of hyperedges measured by CPM, a standard protocol for studying brain connections.

paragraphs: Predicting phenotypes from fMRI depends on identifying informative relationships among brain regions. Pairwise connections can miss relationships involving larger groups. The paper proposes seeking group relationships that provide as much useful information as possible while repeating as little information as possible, a principle the authors call maximally informative and minimally redundant.

HyBRiD represents these relationships using hyperedges, which can connect multiple brain regions at once. A Constructor identifies hyperedge structures, and a Weighter assigns their weights. This design avoids searching the full exponential collection of possible group relationships. A multi-head drop-bottleneck framework supplies a tractable route to the information objective, together with theoretical guarantees.

Experiments support the effectiveness of the resulting relationships. The authors report an average 11.2% improvement over the state-of-the-art predictive model in hyperedge quality measured through the CPM protocol. This finding concerns the informativeness of learned brain connections under that evaluation. The approach makes higher-order relationship discovery computationally manageable while explicitly accounting for redundant information among the relationships it learns.
summary.tldr: HyBRiD learns informative, minimally redundant groups of brain-region relationships from fMRI without exhaustively searching all possible groups.

title: Learning High-Order Relationships of Brain Regions

abstract: Asynchronous action coordination presents a pervasive challenge in Multi-Agent Systems (MAS), which can be represented as a Stackelberg game (SG). However, the scalability of existing Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) methods based on SG is severely restricted by network architectures or environmental settings. To address this issue, we propose the Stackelberg Decision Transformer (STEER). It efficiently manages decision-making processes by incorporating the hierarchical decision structure of SG, the modeling capability of autoregressive sequence models, and the exploratory learning methodology of MARL. Our approach exhibits broad applicability across diverse task types and environmental configurations in MAS. Experimental results demonstrate both the convergence of our method towards Stackelberg equilibrium strategies and its superiority over strong baselines in complex scenarios.

paragraphs: In a multi-agent system, agents may need to coordinate actions taken at different times. The paper represents this asynchronous coordination through a Stackelberg game, which supplies a hierarchical decision structure. It argues that existing reinforcement-learning approaches built around this structure face scalability restrictions arising from their network architectures or environmental settings.

The proposed Stackelberg Decision Transformer, called STEER, combines three elements: the game’s hierarchy, autoregressive sequence modeling, and exploratory multi-agent reinforcement learning. Sequence modeling provides a way to represent decisions in order, while the hierarchy organizes how those decisions relate. The reinforcement-learning component brings exploration into the process of learning coordinated behavior.

The authors report applicability across varied task types and environmental configurations. In complex experimental scenarios, STEER outperforms strong baselines and shows convergence toward Stackelberg equilibrium strategies. That convergence is an experimental finding in the supplied account. The broader contribution is an architecture that brings ordered decision modeling and hierarchical game structure together to handle asynchronous coordination, addressing the scalability problems that motivate the work.
summary.tldr: STEER combines Stackelberg game structure, autoregressive modeling, and reinforcement learning to improve asynchronous coordination among agents.

title: Sequential Asynchronous Action Coordination in Multi-Agent Systems: A Stackelberg Decision Transformer Approach

abstract: We consider a learning augmented framework for NP-hard permutation problems. The algorithm has access to predictions telling, given a pair $u,v$ of elements, whether $u$ is before $v$ or not in an optimal solution. Building on the work of Braverman and Mossel (SODA 2008), we show that for a class of optimization problems including scheduling, network design and other graph permutation problems, these predictions allow to solve them in polynomial time with high probability, provided that predictions are true with probability at least $1/2+\epsilon$. Moreover, this can be achieved with a parsimonious access to the predictions.
originalAbstract: We consider a learning augmented framework for NP-hard permutation problems. The algorithm has access to predictions telling, given a pair $u,v$ of elements, whether $u$ is before $v$ or not in an optimal solution. Building on the work of Braverman and Mossel (SODA 2008), we show that for a class of optimization problems including scheduling, network design and other graph permutation problems, these predictions allow to solve them in polynomial time with high probability, provided that predictions are true with probability at least $1/2+\epsilon$. Moreover, this can be achieved with a parsimonious access to the predictions.

paragraphs: Permutation optimization problems seek an ordering of elements that optimizes an objective, and many are NP-hard. This paper studies what becomes possible when an algorithm receives predictions about the ordering in an optimal solution. Each prediction answers a local question: whether one specified element comes before another.

For a class of problems including scheduling, network design, and other graph permutation problems, the authors show that these predictions enable polynomial-time solutions with high probability. The stated condition is that predictions are correct with probability at least one-half plus epsilon. Thus, the result depends on access to predictions with an advantage over random pairwise guesses.

The algorithms also use predictions parsimoniously, making the amount of predictive information accessed part of the contribution. The result shows how limited, imperfect ordering guidance can change computational possibilities for the studied class. Its scope remains the learning-augmented setting: the high-probability polynomial-time guarantee relies on the supplied prediction model and its stated accuracy condition.
summary.tldr: For a class of NP-hard ordering problems, sufficiently accurate pairwise predictions enable polynomial-time solutions with high probability.

title: Polynomial Time Learning Augmented Algorithms for NP-hard Permutation Problems

abstract: Multimodal data is a precious asset enabling a variety of downstream tasks in machine learning. However, real-world data collected across different modalities is often not paired, which is a significant challenge to learn a joint distribution. A prominent approach to address the modality coupling problem is Minimum Entropy Coupling (MEC), which seeks to minimize the joint Entropy, while satisfying constraints on the marginals. Existing approaches to the MEC problem focus on finite, discrete distributions, limiting their application for cases involving continuous data. In this work, we propose a novel method to solve the continuous MEC problem, using well-known generative diffusion models that learn to approximate and minimize the joint Entropy through a cooperative scheme, while satisfying a relaxed version of the marginal constraints. We empirically demonstrate that our method, DDMEC, is general and can be easily used to address challenging tasks, including unsupervised single-cell multi-omics data alignment and unpaired image translation, outperforming specialized methods.

paragraphs: Data from different modalities often arrives without examples being matched across them. Learning a joint distribution then requires deciding how the separate collections should relate. Minimum Entropy Coupling approaches this by seeking a joint distribution with low entropy while retaining the specified distribution of each modality, known as its marginal.

Existing methods largely handle finite, discrete distributions. This paper introduces DDMEC for continuous data, using generative diffusion models in a cooperative training scheme. The models learn to approximate and reduce joint entropy while satisfying a relaxed form of the marginal constraints. The relaxation is part of the proposed formulation, so the method's matching objective allows flexibility in preserving the individual distributions.

The authors evaluate DDMEC on unsupervised alignment of single-cell multi-omics data and on unpaired image translation. They report that it outperforms specialized methods on these challenging applications. The significance is that one continuous coupling approach can support substantially different kinds of unpaired data, extending the reach of minimum-entropy matching beyond its established discrete setting.
summary.tldr: DDMEC uses cooperating diffusion models to match continuous unpaired data through low joint entropy and relaxed marginal constraints.

title: Learning to Match Unpaired Data with Minimum Entropy Coupling

abstract: To avoid myopic behavior, multi-step lookahead Bayesian optimization (BO) algorithms consider the sequential nature of BO and have demonstrated promising results in recent years. However, owing to the curse of dimensionality, most of these methods make significant approximations or suffer scalability issues. This paper presents a novel reinforcement learning (RL)-based framework for multi-step lookahead BO in high-dimensional black-box optimization problems. The proposed method enhances the scalability and decision-making quality of multi-step lookahead BO by efficiently solving the sequential dynamic program of the BO process in a near-optimal manner using RL. We first introduce an Attention-DeepSets encoder to represent the state of knowledge to the RL agent and subsequently propose a multi-task, fine-tuning procedure based on end-to-end (encoder-RL) on-policy learning. We evaluate the proposed method, EARL-BO (Encoder Augmented RL for BO), on synthetic benchmark functions and hyperparameter tuning problems, finding significantly improved performance compared to existing multi-step lookahead and high-dimensional BO methods.

paragraphs: Bayesian optimization can choose evaluations by considering how they affect several future decisions. This lookahead helps avoid shortsighted search, but becomes difficult as the number of input dimensions grows. Existing approaches often need substantial approximations or encounter scaling problems when reasoning over possible sequences of evaluations.

EARL-BO uses reinforcement learning to address the sequential decision problem underlying multi-step Bayesian optimization. An Attention-DeepSets encoder represents the current state of knowledge for the learning agent. The framework also includes a multi-task fine-tuning procedure that trains the encoder and reinforcement-learning component together through on-policy learning. The authors describe this as efficiently solving the sequential dynamic program in a near-optimal manner.

Evaluations on synthetic benchmark functions and hyperparameter-tuning problems show significantly better performance than the compared multi-step lookahead and high-dimensional Bayesian optimization methods. The approach matters because it makes representation learning and sequential decision-making part of the same optimization framework. Its reported gains support using a learned decision process to improve the scalability and quality of lookahead search.
summary.tldr: EARL-BO combines a learned knowledge encoder with reinforcement learning to improve multi-step Bayesian optimization in high dimensions.

title: EARL-BO: Reinforcement Learning for Multi-Step Lookahead, High-Dimensional Bayesian Optimization

abstract: Spatial conditioning control offers a powerful way to guide diffusion-based generative models. Yet, most implementations (e.g., ControlNet) rely on ad-hoc heuristics to choose which network blocks to control — an approach that varies unpredictably with different tasks. To address this gap, we propose FlexControl, a novel framework that equips all diffusion blocks with control signals during training and employs a trainable gating mechanism to dynamically select which control signal to activate at each denoising step. By introducing a computation-aware loss, we can encourage the control signal to activate only when it benefits the generation quality. By eliminating manual control unit selection, FlexControl enhances adaptability across diverse tasks and streamlines the design pipeline with computation-aware training loss in an end-to-end training manner. Through comprehensive experiments on both UNet and DiT architectures on different control methods, we show that our method can upgrade existing controllable generative models in certain key aspects of interest. As evidenced by both quantitative and qualitative evaluations, FlexControl preserves or enhances image fidelity while also reducing computational overhead by selectively activating the most relevant blocks to control. These results underscore the potential of a flexible, data-driven approach for controlled diffusion and open new avenues for efficient generative model design. The code will soon be available at https://github.com/Daryu-Fan/FlexControl.

paragraphs: Spatial control helps guide diffusion-based image generation, but existing implementations often rely on manually chosen rules for deciding which network blocks receive control. Those choices can behave unpredictably across tasks. FlexControl turns block selection into a learned decision, allowing the pattern of control to change during the denoising process.

During training, every diffusion block is equipped with control signals. A trainable gating mechanism selects which signals to activate at each denoising step. A computation-aware loss encourages activation when it benefits generation quality, making computational cost part of the training objective. This provides an end-to-end way to learn where control is useful instead of requiring manual selection of control units.

Experiments cover both UNet and DiT architectures and different control methods. Quantitative and qualitative evaluations show that selective activation can preserve or improve image fidelity while reducing computational overhead. The authors describe improvements in particular aspects of existing controllable generators, supporting learned routing as a flexible way to balance control quality and computational demands across the tested settings.
summary.tldr: FlexControl learns which diffusion blocks need spatial control at each denoising step, preserving or improving image quality with less computation.

title: FlexControl: Computation-Aware Conditional Control with Differentiable Router for Text-to-Image Generation

abstract: Out-of-distribution (OOD) detection and OOD generalization are widely studied in Deep Neural Networks (DNNs), yet their relationship remains poorly understood. We empirically show that the degree of Neural Collapse (NC) in a network layer is inversely related with these objectives: stronger NC improves OOD detection but degrades generalization, while weaker NC enhances generalization at the cost of detection. This trade-off suggests that a single feature space cannot simultaneously achieve both tasks. To address this, we develop a theoretical framework linking NC to OOD detection and generalization. We show that entropy regularization mitigates NC to improve generalization, while a fixed Simplex ETF projector enforces NC for better detection. Based on these insights, we propose a method to control NC at different DNN layers. In experiments, our method excels at both tasks across OOD datasets and DNN architectures.

paragraphs: This paper examines a tension between recognizing unfamiliar inputs and generalizing successfully to them. The authors empirically connect both objectives to the degree of neural collapse in a network layer. Stronger collapse improves out-of-distribution detection in their study, but weakens generalization; reducing collapse reverses that pattern. Their findings suggest that asking one feature space to serve both objectives creates a trade-off.

The authors develop a theoretical framework relating neural collapse to these two outcomes. They identify two ways to influence it: entropy regularization reduces collapse to support generalization, while a fixed Simplex ETF projector promotes collapse to support detection. These mechanisms give the model explicit controls over a property associated with competing objectives.

The resulting method controls neural collapse at different network layers, allowing different representations to support different needs. Experiments across out-of-distribution datasets and network architectures show strong performance on both tasks. The contribution is therefore a layer-specific approach to managing the observed tension, supported by theoretical analysis and empirical evaluation.
summary.tldr: Controlling neural collapse at different network layers helps reconcile unfamiliar-input detection with generalization.

title: Controlling Neural Collapse Enhances Out-of-Distribution Detection and Transfer Learning

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in complex reasoning tasks. However, existing approaches mainly rely on imitation learning and struggle to achieve effective test-time scaling. While reinforcement learning (RL) holds promise for enabling self-exploration, recent attempts yield modest improvements in complex reasoning. In this paper, we present T1 to scale RL by encouraging exploration and understand inference scaling. We first initialize the LLM using synthesized chain-of-thought data that integrates trial-and-error and self-verification. To scale RL training, we promote increased sampling diversity through over-sampling. We demonstrate that T1 with open LLMs as its base exhibits inference scaling behavior and achieves superior performance on challenging math reasoning benchmarks. More importantly, we present a simple strategy to examine inference scaling, where increased inference budgets directly lead to T1’s better performance without any additional verification. The model weights and training data are publicly available at https://github.com/THUDM/T1.

paragraphs: T1 investigates how reinforcement learning can improve language model reasoning and make additional inference computation useful. The paper argues that imitation-focused approaches struggle to scale effectively at test time, while previous reinforcement learning attempts have produced only modest improvements on difficult reasoning. Its approach emphasizes exploration during learning and examines the resulting inference behavior.

Training begins with synthesized reasoning traces that include trial and error as well as self-verification. The subsequent reinforcement learning stage uses over-sampling to encourage greater sampling diversity. These choices aim to expose the model to varied reasoning attempts and ways of checking them, rather than depending entirely on reproducing a fixed set of demonstrations.

Using open language models as starting points, T1 demonstrates inference scaling and superior performance on challenging mathematical reasoning benchmarks. The authors also introduce a simple strategy for studying that scaling: increasing the inference budget improves T1's performance without additional verification. The reported finding links the training approach to a useful deployment property, where more computation at inference can translate directly into better reasoning results.
summary.tldr: T1 encourages diverse reinforcement learning exploration and shows improved math reasoning as inference budgets increase without additional verification.

title: T1: Advancing Language Model Reasoning through Reinforcement Learning and Inference Scaling

abstract: A key challenge in Domain Generalization (DG) is preventing overfitting to source domains, which can be mitigated by finding flatter minima in the loss landscape. In this work, we propose Quantization-aware Training for Domain Generalization (QT-DoG) and demonstrate that weight quantization effectively leads to flatter minima in the loss landscape, thereby enhancing domain generalization. Unlike traditional quantization methods focused on model compression, QT-DoG exploits quantization as an implicit regularizer by inducing noise in model weights, guiding the optimization process toward flatter minima that are less sensitive to perturbations and overfitting. We provide both an analytical perspective and empirical evidence demonstrating that quantization inherently encourages flatter minima, leading to better generalization across domains. Moreover, with the benefit of reducing the model size through quantization, we demonstrate that an ensemble of multiple quantized models further yields superior accuracy than the state-of-the-art DG approaches with no computational or memory overheads. Code is released at: https://saqibjaved1.github.io/QT_DoG/.

paragraphs: Domain generalization asks a model to work beyond the domains represented in its training data. Overfitting to those source domains is a central obstacle. QT-DoG uses quantization-aware training to address that obstacle, treating reduced weight precision as a source of regularization as well as a way to shrink models.

The proposed explanation is that quantization introduces noise into model weights and steers optimization toward flatter minima. In such regions, small weight perturbations have less effect on the loss. The paper provides an analytical perspective and empirical evidence linking weight quantization to this flatter geometry and to improved generalization across domains.

The authors also use the smaller size of quantized models to build an ensemble. They report that combining multiple quantized models surpasses state-of-the-art domain-generalization approaches without additional computational or memory overhead in their comparison. The findings give quantization two connected roles: shaping the training dynamics of individual models and making it possible to combine several compact models within the reported resource budget.
summary.tldr: QT-DoG uses weight quantization as regularization to encourage flatter minima and improve domain generalization, including through compact-model ensembles.

title: QT-DoG: Quantization-Aware Training for Domain Generalization

abstract: Shock waves caused by earthquakes can be devastating. Generating realistic earthquake-caused ground motion waveforms help reducing losses in lives and properties, yet generative models for the task tend to generate subpar waveforms. We present High-fidelity Earthquake Groundmotion Generation System (HEGGS) and demonstrate its superior performance using earthquakes from North American, East Asian, and European regions. HEGGS exploits the intrinsic characteristics of earthquake dataset and learns the waveforms using an end-to-end differentiable generator containing conditional latent diffusion model and hi-fidelity waveform construction model. We show the learning efficiency of HEGGS by training it on a single GPU machine and validate its performance using earthquake databases from North America, East Asia, and Europe, using diverse criteria from waveform generation tasks and seismology. Once trained, HEGGS can generate three dimensional E-N-Z seismic waveforms with accurate P/S phase arrivals, envelope correlation, signal-to-noise ratio, GMPE analysis, frequency content analysis, and section plot analysis.

paragraphs: Realistic synthetic earthquake waveforms can help efforts to reduce earthquake losses, but generating convincing ground motion remains challenging. This paper introduces HEGGS, a system that learns to generate three-component seismic waveforms. Its design combines a conditional latent diffusion model with a model that constructs high-fidelity waveforms.

The complete generator is differentiable end to end and uses characteristics of earthquake data in its learning process. The authors demonstrate that it can be trained on a single-GPU machine. They assess it using earthquake databases from North America, East Asia, and Europe, combining evaluation criteria from waveform generation with criteria relevant to seismology.

The reported outputs accurately reproduce several important waveform properties, including P- and S-wave arrival timing, envelope correlation, signal-to-noise ratio, and frequency content. The evaluation also includes ground-motion prediction equation analysis and section plots. These findings support the system’s ability to reproduce multiple aspects of seismic signals rather than relying on just one measure of waveform quality. The contribution concerns synthesizing ground motion, with superior performance reported in the studied regional data.
summary.tldr: HEGGS combines latent diffusion and waveform construction to generate realistic three-component earthquake signals with single-GPU training.

title: Broadband Ground Motion Synthesis by Diffusion Model with Minimal Condition

abstract: Transformers with linear recurrent modeling offer linear-time training and constant-memory inference. Despite their demonstrated efficiency and performance, pretraining such non-standard architectures from scratch remains costly and risky. The linearization of large language models (LLMs) transforms pretrained standard models into linear recurrent structures, enabling more efficient deployment. However, current linearization methods typically introduce additional feature map modules that require extensive fine-tuning and overlook the gating mechanisms used in state-of-the-art linear recurrent models. To address these issues, this paper presents Liger, short for Linearizing LLMs to gated recurrent structures. Liger is a novel approach for converting pretrained LLMs into gated linear recurrent models without adding extra parameters. It repurposes the pretrained key matrix weights to construct diverse gating mechanisms, facilitating the formation of various gated recurrent structures while avoiding the need to train additional components from scratch. Using lightweight fine-tuning with Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA), Liger restores the performance of the linearized gated recurrent models to match that of the original LLMs. Additionally, we introduce Liger Attention, an intra-layer hybrid attention mechanism, which significantly recovers 93% of the Transformer-based LLM performance at 0.02% pre-training tokens during the linearization process, achieving competitive results across multiple benchmarks, as validated on models ranging from 1B to 8B parameters.

paragraphs: Linear recurrent language models offer linear-time training and constant-memory inference, but training a new architecture from scratch is costly. Liger instead converts pretrained language models into gated linear recurrent structures. It addresses two issues in existing conversion methods: extra feature-map modules that need extensive fine-tuning and insufficient use of gating mechanisms.

Liger reuses pretrained key-matrix weights to create gates, allowing different recurrent structures without adding parameters for new components. Lightweight LoRA fine-tuning then restores the converted models' performance to match the original language models, according to the reported results. Reusing existing weights makes the conversion itself central to the efficiency strategy.

The authors additionally introduce Liger Attention, an attention mechanism that combines approaches within a layer. They report recovery of 93% of Transformer-model performance using tokens amounting to 0.02% of pretraining volume during conversion. Evaluations cover models from one billion to eight billion parameters and show competitive results across multiple benchmarks. Together, the contributions support adapting existing language models for more efficient recurrent deployment.
summary.tldr: Liger reuses pretrained weights to convert language models into gated recurrent structures and recovers performance through lightweight adaptation.

title: Liger: Linearizing Large Language Models to Gated Recurrent Structures

abstract: Unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) for semantic segmentation aims to transfer knowledge from a labeled source domain to an unlabeled target domain. Despite the effectiveness of self-training techniques in UDA, they struggle to learn each class in a balanced manner due to inherent class imbalance and distribution shift in both data and label space between domains. To address this issue, we propose Balanced Learning for Domain Adaptation (BLDA), a novel approach to directly assess and alleviate class bias without requiring prior knowledge about the distribution shift. First, we identify over-predicted and under-predicted classes by analyzing the distribution of predicted logits. Subsequently, we introduce a post-hoc approach to align the logits distributions across different classes using shared anchor distributions. To further consider the network’s need to generate unbiased pseudo-labels during self-training, we estimate logits distributions online and incorporate logits correction terms into the loss function. Moreover, we leverage the resulting cumulative density as domain-shared structural knowledge to connect the source and target domains. Extensive experiments on two standard UDA semantic segmentation benchmarks demonstrate that BLDA consistently improves performance, especially for under-predicted classes, when integrated into various existing methods.

paragraphs: Semantic segmentation assigns a category to each image pixel. This paper studies transferring that ability from labeled source images to a target domain without labels. Self-training can help, but unequal class frequencies and differences between domains can cause the model to predict some classes too often and others too rarely. Those biases also affect the labels it generates for its own training.

Balanced Learning for Domain Adaptation measures this imbalance through distributions of logits, the scores a model produces before converting them into predictions. It identifies over-predicted and under-predicted classes, then aligns their score distributions to shared reference distributions. During self-training, it also estimates these distributions online and adds corrections to the training loss. The resulting cumulative distributions provide structural information shared between source and target domains.

The method does not require advance knowledge of the distribution shift. Across two standard benchmarks, adding it to various existing methods consistently improves segmentation performance, with particularly useful gains for under-predicted classes.
summary.tldr: BLDA corrects class prediction biases during domain adaptation, improving segmentation especially for under-predicted classes.

title: Balanced Learning for Domain Adaptive Semantic Segmentation

abstract: Recent progress in Meta-Black-Box-Optimization (MetaBBO) has demonstrated that using RL to learn a meta-level policy for dynamic algorithm configuration (DAC) over an optimization task distribution could significantly enhance the performance of the low-level BBO algorithm. However, the online learning paradigms in existing works makes the efficiency of MetaBBO problematic. To address this, we propose an offline learning-based MetaBBO framework in this paper, termed Q-Mamba, to attain both effectiveness and efficiency in MetaBBO. Specifically, we first transform DAC task into long-sequence decision process. This allows us further introduce an effective Q-function decomposition mechanism to reduce the learning difficulty within the intricate algorithm configuration space. Under this setting, we propose three novel designs to meta-learn DAC policy from offline data: we first propose a novel collection strategy for constructing offline DAC experiences dataset with balanced exploration and exploitation. We then establish a decomposition-based Q-loss that incorporates conservative Q-learning to promote stable offline learning from the offline dataset. To further improve the offline learning efficiency, we equip our work with a Mamba architecture which helps long-sequence learning effectiveness and efficiency by selective state model and hardware-aware parallel scan respectively. Through extensive benchmarking, we observe that Q-Mamba achieves competitive or even superior performance to prior online/offline baselines, while significantly improving the training efficiency of existing online baselines. We provide sourcecodes of Q-Mamba https://github.com/MetaEvo/Q-Mamba.

paragraphs: Meta-black-box optimization learns how to configure an optimization algorithm as it works on a task. Reinforcement learning can improve these configuration decisions across a distribution of tasks, but existing online training approaches can be inefficient. Q-Mamba learns the configuration policy from previously collected experience, aiming to retain effectiveness while reducing training cost.

Its data collection strategy balances exploration and exploitation. A decomposition-based loss incorporates conservative Q-learning to promote stable learning from the fixed dataset, linking the policy-training objective to the offline setting.

Q-Mamba also uses a Mamba architecture, combining a selective state model for long sequences with a hardware-aware parallel scan for efficient computation. Benchmarking finds performance competitive with or superior to prior online and offline baselines, alongside substantially better training efficiency than existing online baselines. The contribution joins dataset construction, value learning, and sequence modeling into one offline configuration framework.
summary.tldr: Q-Mamba learns optimizer-configuration policies from offline experience, combining decomposed Q-learning and sequence modeling to improve training efficiency.

title: Meta-Black-Box-Optimization through Offline Q-function Learning

abstract: Real-world time series are often governed by complex nonlinear dynamics. Understanding these underlying dynamics is crucial for precise future prediction. While deep learning has achieved major success in time series forecasting, many existing approaches do not explicitly model the dynamics. To bridge this gap, we introduce DeepEDM, a framework that integrates nonlinear dynamical systems modeling with deep neural networks. Inspired by empirical dynamic modeling (EDM) and rooted in Takens’ theorem, DeepEDM presents a novel deep model that learns a latent space from time-delayed embeddings, and employs kernel regression to approximate the underlying dynamics, while leveraging efficient implementation of softmax attention and allowing for accurate prediction of future time steps. To evaluate our method, we conduct comprehensive experiments on synthetic data of nonlinear dynamical systems as well as real-world time series across domains. Our results show that DeepEDM is robust to input noise, and outperforms state-of-the-art methods in forecasting accuracy. Our code is available at: https://abrarmajeedi.github.io/deep_edm.

paragraphs: Many real-world time series reflect nonlinear dynamics, yet successful deep forecasting systems do not always model those dynamics explicitly. DeepEDM combines a dynamical-systems approach with a neural network, aiming to connect the representation used for prediction with the process governing how the series evolves.

The framework is inspired by empirical dynamic modeling and grounded in Takens’ theorem. It starts from time-delayed embeddings, which assemble observations from different times, and learns a latent representation of them. Kernel regression then approximates the underlying dynamics in that representation. An efficient softmax-attention implementation supports this computation and prediction of future time steps.

The authors evaluate DeepEDM on synthetic nonlinear dynamical systems and real-world time series from multiple domains. They report robustness to input noise and better forecasting accuracy than state-of-the-art methods in their experiments. The results support combining learned representations with explicit modeling of temporal dynamics. The contribution is the integration of these components into a forecasting framework, rather than relying on a neural representation alone to capture the evolution implicitly.
summary.tldr: DeepEDM combines learned time-delay representations with nonlinear dynamics modeling to improve forecasting accuracy and robustness to input noise.

title: LETS Forecast: Learning Embedology for Time Series Forecasting

abstract: Learning a latent dynamics model provides a task-agnostic representation of an agent’s understanding of its environment. Leveraging this knowledge for model-based reinforcement learning (RL) holds the potential to improve sample efficiency over model-free methods by learning from imagined rollouts. Furthermore, because the latent space serves as input to behavior models, the informative representations learned by the world model facilitate efficient learning of desired skills. Most existing methods rely on holistic representations of the environment’s state. In contrast, humans reason about objects and their interactions, predicting how actions will affect specific parts of their surroundings. Inspired by this, we propose Slot-Attention for Object-centric Latent Dynamics (SOLD), a novel model-based RL algorithm that learns object-centric dynamics models in an unsupervised manner from pixel inputs. We demonstrate that the structured latent space not only improves model interpretability but also provides a valuable input space for behavior models to reason over. Our results show that SOLD outperforms DreamerV3 and TD-MPC2 - state-of-the-art model-based RL algorithms - across a range of multi-object manipulation environments that require both relational reasoning and dexterous control. Videos and code are available at https:// slot-latent-dynamics.github.io.

paragraphs: Model-based reinforcement learning learns a representation of the environment and predicts how it changes. Such a world model can support learning through imagined rollouts, while its representation also becomes input to the agent’s behavior model. SOLD studies the value of organizing that representation around objects and their interactions.

The method uses slot attention to learn object-centric latent dynamics from pixels without supervision. Instead of encoding the whole scene only as a holistic state, its structured latent space represents the environment in an object-focused way. The authors show that this improves model interpretability and gives behavior models a useful space for relational reasoning.

Across multi-object manipulation environments requiring both relational reasoning and dexterous control, SOLD outperforms DreamerV3 and TD-MPC2 in the reported results. These comparisons support the usefulness of object-centric dynamics for the evaluated control tasks. The broader motivation is that a world model’s internal organization matters twice: for predicting environmental changes and for providing information that helps the agent learn how to act.
summary.tldr: SOLD learns object-centric world models from pixels and outperforms DreamerV3 and TD-MPC2 on evaluated relational manipulation tasks.

title: SOLD: Slot Object-Centric Latent Dynamics Models for Relational Manipulation Learning from Pixels

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are empowering decision-making in several applications, including tool or API usage and answering multiple-choice questions (MCQs). However, incorrect outputs pose significant risks in high-stakes domains like healthcare and finance. To quantify LLM uncertainty and thereby mitigate these risks, recent works employ conformal prediction (CP), a model- and distribution-agnostic framework that uses LLM outputs to generate a prediction set containing the true answer with high probability. Leveraging CP, we propose conformal revision of questions (CROQ), which revises the question by narrowing down the available choices to those in the prediction set and asking the LLM the revised question. We expect LLMs to be more accurate on revised questions with fewer choices. Furthermore, we expect CROQ to be effective when the prediction sets from CP are small. Commonly used logit scores often lead to large sets, diminishing CROQ’s effectiveness. To overcome this, we propose CP-OPT, an optimization framework to learn scores that minimize set sizes while maintaining coverage. Our extensive experiments on MMLU, ToolAlpaca, and TruthfulQA datasets with multiple LLMs show that CROQ improves accuracy over the standard inference, with more pronounced gains when paired with CP-OPT.

However, incorrect outputs pose significant risks in high-stakes domains like healthcare and finance. To quantify LLM uncertainty and thereby mitigate these risks, recent works employ conformal prediction (CP), a model- and distribution-agnostic framework that uses LLM outputs to generate a prediction set containing the true answer with high probability. We expect LLMs to be more accurate on revised questions with fewer choices. Furthermore, we expect CROQ to be effective when the prediction sets from CP are small. Commonly used logit scores often lead to large sets, diminishing CROQ’s effectiveness. To overcome this, we propose CP-OPT, an optimization framework to learn scores that minimize set sizes while maintaining coverage. Our extensive experiments on MMLU, ToolAlpaca, and TruthfulQA datasets with multiple LLMs show that CROQ improves accuracy over the standard inference, with more pronounced gains when paired with CP-OPT.

paragraphs: When a language model chooses an answer or a tool, uncertainty can be represented by a set of plausible choices. Conformal prediction constructs such a set with high-probability coverage of the true answer. This paper uses that set to revise the decision problem presented to the model.

Conformal revision of questions, or CROQ, removes choices outside the prediction set and asks the model the narrowed question. The motivation is that fewer alternatives may improve accuracy. Since large prediction sets leave little to prune, the authors also introduce CP-OPT, which learns scores designed to reduce set size while maintaining coverage.

Experiments on MMLU, ToolAlpaca, and TruthfulQA with multiple language models show that CROQ improves accuracy over standard inference, with larger gains when combined with CP-OPT. The results connect uncertainty estimation to a practical inference procedure. Coverage concerns the retained answer set, while the observed accuracy gains concern the model's subsequent choice from that set; they are related but distinct outcomes.
summary.tldr: CROQ improves tested LLM decisions by re-asking questions with conformal prediction sets, especially when CP-OPT learns smaller sets while maintaining coverage.

title: Prune ’n Predict: Optimizing LLM Decision-making with Conformal Prediction

abstract: Wasserstein Distributionally Robust Optimization (WDRO) is a principled framework for robust estimation under distributional uncertainty. However, its standard formulation can be overly conservative, particularly in small-sample regimes. We propose a novel knowledge-guided WDRO (KG-WDRO) framework for transfer learning, which adaptively incorporates multiple sources of external knowledge to improve generalization accuracy. Our method constructs smaller Wasserstein ambiguity sets by controlling the transportation along directions informed by the source knowledge. This strategy can alleviate perturbations on the predictive projection of the covariates and protect against information loss. Theoretically, we establish the equivalence between our WDRO formulation and the knowledge-guided shrinkage estimation based on collinear similarity, ensuring tractability and geometrizing the feasible set. This also reveals a novel and general interpretation for recent shrinkage-based transfer learning approaches from the perspective of distributional robustness. In addition, our framework can adjust for scaling differences in the regression models between the source and target and accommodates general types of regularization such as lasso and ridge. Extensive simulations demonstrate the superior performance and adaptivity of KG-WDRO in enhancing small-sample transfer learning.

title: Knowledge-Guided Wasserstein Distributionally Robust Optimization

abstract: Modern scientific discovery increasingly relies on high-performance computing for complex modeling and simulation. A key challenge in improving parallel program performance is efficiently mapping tasks to processors and data to memory, a process dictated by intricate, low-level system code known as mappers. Developing high-performance mappers demands days of manual tuning, posing a significant barrier for domain scientists without systems expertise. We introduce a framework that automates mapper development with generative optimization, leveraging richer feedback beyond scalar performance metrics. Our approach features the Agent-System Interface, which includes a Domain-Specific Language (DSL) to abstract away the low-level complexity of system code and define a structured search space, as well as AutoGuide, a mechanism that interprets raw execution output into actionable feedback. Unlike traditional reinforcement learning methods such as OpenTuner, which rely solely on scalar feedback, our method finds superior mappers in far fewer iterations. With just 10 iterations, it outperforms OpenTuner even after 1000 iterations, achieving $3.8\times$ faster performance. Our approach finds mappers that surpass expert-written mappers by up to $1.34\times$ speedup across nine benchmarks while reducing tuning time from days to minutes.

paragraphs: Parallel programs depend on mappers that decide where tasks execute and where data resides in memory. These decisions can strongly affect performance, but writing effective mappers requires detailed systems knowledge and extensive tuning. This paper develops a framework that automates mapper development through generative optimization.

The framework's Agent-System Interface has two main components. A domain-specific language hides low-level coding complexity and defines a structured space of possible mappers. AutoGuide turns raw execution output into feedback that the optimizer can act on. Together, they let the optimizer use richer evidence about execution than a single performance score provides.

Across nine benchmarks, it also exceeds expert-written mappers by up to 1.34 times and reduces tuning time from days to minutes. These findings show the value of designing both the optimizer's programming interface and its feedback, making mapper search substantially more effective in the evaluated workloads.
summary.tldr: A structured mapper language and actionable execution feedback help LLM optimizers improve parallel-program performance with far fewer tuning iterations.

title: Improving Parallel Program Performance with LLM Optimizers via Agent-System Interfaces

abstract: Drag-based editing within pretrained diffusion model provides a precise and flexible way to manipulate foreground objects. Traditional methods optimize the input feature obtained from DDIM inversion directly, adjusting them iteratively to guide handle points towards target locations. However, these approaches often suffer from limited accuracy due to the low representation ability of the feature in motion supervision, as well as inefficiencies caused by the large search space required for point tracking. To address these limitations, we present DragLoRA, a novel framework that integrates LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) adapters into the drag-based editing pipeline. To enhance the training of LoRA adapters, we introduce an additional denoising score distillation loss which regularizes the online model by aligning its output with that of the original model. Additionally, we improve the consistency of motion supervision by adapting the input features using the updated LoRA, giving a more stable and accurate input feature for subsequent operations. Building on this, we design an adaptive optimization scheme that dynamically toggles between two modes, prioritizing efficiency without compromising precision. Extensive experiments demonstrate that DragLoRA significantly enhances the control precision and computational efficiency for drag-based image editing. The Codes of DragLoRA are available at: https://github.com/Sylvie-X/DragLoRA.

paragraphs: Drag-based image editing lets a user move selected points on an object toward desired locations. Existing diffusion-based methods repeatedly adjust an input feature representation and track those points. The paper identifies two obstacles: the representation may inadequately support motion supervision, and searching for the moving points can consume substantial computation.

DragLoRA introduces low-rank adaptation modules into this editing process and optimizes them online. An additional denoising score distillation loss keeps the adapted model’s output aligned with the original model. The updated adapters also reshape the input features, providing more stable and accurate representations for the subsequent motion-supervision steps.

The framework adds an adaptive optimization scheme that switches between two modes to improve efficiency while preserving precision. Experiments report significant gains in both editing control and computational efficiency. The central contribution is to connect model adaptation with feature adjustment during an edit, so that the representation used to guide movement can improve alongside the editing process itself.
summary.tldr: DragLoRA adapts a diffusion model during drag-based editing to improve movement precision and computational efficiency.

title: DragLoRA: Online Optimization of LoRA Adapters for Drag-based Image Editing in Diffusion Model

abstract: In this paper, we derive refined generalization bounds for the Deep Ritz Method (DRM) and Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs). For the DRM, we focus on two prototype elliptic partial differential equations (PDEs): Poisson equation and static Schrödinger equation on the $d$-dimensional unit hypercube with the Neumann boundary condition. Furthermore, sharper generalization bounds are derived based on the localization techniques under the assumptions that the exact solutions of the PDEs lie in the Barron spaces or the general Sobolev spaces. For the PINNs, we investigate the general linear second order elliptic PDEs with Dirichlet boundary condition using the local Rademacher complexity in the multi-task learning setting. Finally, we discuss the generalization error in the setting of over-parameterization when solutions of PDEs belong to Barron space.

paragraphs: This paper sharpens theoretical guarantees for two neural approaches to solving partial differential equations: the Deep Ritz Method and physics-informed neural networks. Generalization analysis concerns how well learning from sampled information controls error beyond those samples. The contribution is a more refined mathematical treatment for specified classes of elliptic equations.

For the Deep Ritz Method, the authors study the Poisson and static Schrödinger equations on a d-dimensional unit hypercube with Neumann boundary conditions. They use localization techniques to obtain sharper bounds, assuming the exact solutions belong to Barron spaces or general Sobolev spaces. These solution-space assumptions define the scope of the analysis.

For physics-informed neural networks, the paper considers general linear second-order elliptic equations with Dirichlet boundary conditions. It uses local Rademacher complexity in a multi-task learning formulation to analyze generalization. The authors additionally discuss over-parameterized models when solutions belong to Barron space. The results strengthen error analysis for these neural solvers under the stated equation, boundary, and solution assumptions.
summary.tldr: The paper derives sharper generalization bounds for neural PDE solvers under specified boundary conditions and assumptions about solution spaces.

title: Refined generalization analysis of the Deep Ritz Method and Physics-Informed Neural Networks

abstract: Cross-domain few-shot learning (CDFSL) aims to transfer knowledge from a data-sufficient source domain to data-scarce target domains. Although Vision Transformer (ViT) has shown superior capability in many vision tasks, its transferability against huge domain gaps in CDFSL is still under-explored. In this paper, we find an intriguing phenomenon: during the source-domain training, prompt tuning, as a common way to train ViT, could be harmful for the generalization of ViT in target domains, but setting them to random noises (i.e., random registers) could consistently improve target-domain performance. We then delve into this phenomenon for an interpretation. We find that learnable prompts capture domain information during the training on the source dataset, which views irrelevant visual patterns as vital cues for recognition. This can be viewed as a kind of overfitting and increases the sharpness of the loss landscapes. In contrast, random registers are essentially a novel way of perturbing attention for the sharpness-aware minimization, which helps the model find a flattened minimum in loss landscapes, increasing the transferability. Based on this phenomenon and interpretation, we further propose a simple but effective approach for CDFSL to enhance the perturbation on attention maps by adding random registers on the semantic regions of image tokens, improving the effectiveness and efficiency of random registers. Extensive experiments on four benchmarks validate our rationale and state-of-the-art performance. Codes and models are available at https://github.com/shuaiyi308/REAP.

paragraphs: Cross-domain few-shot learning transfers knowledge from a well-supplied source domain to target domains with few examples. The authors find that training vision transformers with learnable prompts on the source domain can hurt target-domain generalization. Replacing those prompts with random noise, called random registers, consistently improves target performance in their study.

Their analysis suggests that learned prompts capture source-domain information and encourage reliance on visual patterns that are irrelevant elsewhere. They connect this overfitting to sharper loss landscapes. Random registers instead perturb attention, functioning as a form of sharpness-aware minimization that helps the model reach flatter minima and improves transferability.

Building on this interpretation, the authors place random registers on semantic regions of image tokens to strengthen useful attention perturbations. This improves the effectiveness and efficiency of the approach. Experiments on four benchmarks support the explanation and report state-of-the-art performance. The paper’s key insight is that the way additional tokens disturb attention can be beneficial for transfer, even when those tokens do not learn source-specific content.
summary.tldr: Random register tokens perturb vision-transformer attention and improve cross-domain few-shot transfer in the reported experiments.

title: Random Registers for Cross-Domain Few-Shot Learning

abstract: Medical large language models (LLMs) research often makes bold claims, from encoding clinical knowledge to reasoning like a physician. These claims are usually backed by evaluation on competitive benchmarks—a tradition inherited from mainstream machine learning. But how do we separate real progress from a leaderboard flex? Medical LLM benchmarks, much like those in other fields, are arbitrarily constructed using medical licensing exam questions. For these benchmarks to truly measure progress, they must accurately capture the real-world tasks they aim to represent. In this position paper, we argue that medical LLM benchmarks should—and indeed can—be empirically evaluated for their construct validity. In the psychological testing literature, “construct validity” refers to the ability of a test to measure an underlying “construct”, that is the actual conceptual target of evaluation. By drawing an analogy between LLM benchmarks and psychological tests, we explain how frameworks from this field can provide empirical foundations for validating benchmarks. To put these ideas into practice, we use real-world clinical data in proof-of-concept experiments to evaluate popular medical LLM benchmarks and report significant gaps in their construct validity. Finally, we outline a vision for a new ecosystem of medical LLM evaluation centered around the creation of valid benchmarks.

paragraphs: This paper asks whether medical language-model benchmarks actually measure the abilities claimed on their behalf. Strong results on licensing-exam questions often support statements about clinical knowledge or physician-like reasoning. The authors argue that such interpretations need empirical validation connecting benchmark performance to the real-world capability the benchmark is intended to represent.

They use the idea of construct validity from psychological testing. A construct is the underlying conceptual target of a test, and construct validity concerns whether the test measures that target. Drawing an analogy between psychological tests and language-model benchmarks provides a framework for investigating this relationship instead of assuming it from a benchmark's medical subject matter.

The authors conduct proof-of-concept experiments using real clinical data and report significant construct-validity gaps in popular medical benchmarks. They then propose an evaluation ecosystem centered on developing valid benchmarks. The findings challenge the interpretation of existing scores and support treating benchmark validation as an empirical task in its own right, alongside evaluating the models that take those tests.
summary.tldr: The paper finds construct-validity gaps in popular medical LLM benchmarks and argues that their connection to intended clinical abilities should be tested empirically.

title: Position: Medical Large Language Model Benchmarks Should Prioritize Construct Validity

abstract: Frontier language models are deployed as black-box services, where model weights cannot be modified and customization is limited to prompting. We introduce Advisor Models, a method to train small open-weight models to generate dynamic, per-instance natural language advice that improves the capabilities of black-box frontier models. Advisor Models improve GPT-5.2’s performance on RuleArena (Taxes) by 27.4%, reduce Gemini 3 Pro’s steps taken in SWE agent tasks by 24.6%, and outperform static prompt optimizers in personalizing GPT-5 to user preferences (85-100% vs. 40-60%). We also find that advisors are transferable: an advisor trained with a low-cost student model still transfers improvements to a frontier model. Moreover, Advisor Models are robust: we observe no degradation on other benchmarks than the pipeline is trained on. Our method shows how to perform parametric optimization for black-box frontier models in a practical and cost-effective way.

paragraphs: Customizing a language model served through an API is difficult when its weights cannot be changed. Advisor Models move the trainable component outside that service: a small open-weight model learns to produce natural-language advice for each individual request. The frontier model then receives that advice through its available prompting interface.

Because advice changes with the instance, the method can tailor guidance to the problem or user preference at hand. The authors report a 27.4% performance improvement for GPT-5.2 on RuleArena’s Taxes task and 24.6% fewer steps for Gemini 3 Pro on software engineering agent tasks. These findings suggest that training a separate advice generator can provide practical customization for black-box models, including when training directly against the final model would be costly.
summary.tldr: Small trainable advisor models generate request-specific advice that improves black-box language models across several evaluated tasks.

title: How to Train Your Advisor: Steering Black-Box LLMs with Advisor Models

abstract: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) has emerged as a promising paradigm for Continual Learning. It independently updates its low-rank factors ($A$ and $B$), creating a composite update to the full weight matrix through their interaction. To prevent catastrophic forgetting, this update should remain orthogonal to the task-specific subspace that contains previously learned knowledge. However, we identify that this composite update systematically violates this orthogonality, reintroducing interference and undermining stability. Furthermore, naively enforcing this orthogonality compromises plasticity, disrupting the delicate stability-plasticity trade-off. To resolve these issues, we propose Janus-LoRA, a framework that restores this balance through two novel components. Specifically, we first introduce Gradient Rectification, a closed-form solution that mathematically decouples LoRA’s factor updates, enforcing orthogonality against the historical knowledge subspace identified by an efficient Online Estimation. Next, to enhance plasticity, we introduce a Decoupled Margin Loss that promotes feature-level separation by pushing new feature representations away from old ones, thus creating distinct, low-interference regions for new learning. Comprehensive experiments on challenging benchmarks demonstrate that by harmonizing parameter-level orthogonality with feature-level separation, Janus-LoRA achieves a superior balance and establishes new state-of-the-art performance.

paragraphs: Continual learning must accommodate new tasks while preserving previously learned knowledge. With LoRA, two low-rank factors interact to produce a full weight update. The paper identifies a problem in that interaction: independently updating the factors can make the combined update violate orthogonality to the subspace representing earlier knowledge, reintroducing interference.

Janus-LoRA addresses this with Gradient Rectification, a closed-form procedure that mathematically decouples the factor updates. It enforces orthogonality against a historical knowledge subspace maintained through efficient online estimation.
