A Decoupled Margin Loss adds feature-level separation by pushing new representations away from old ones. This creates distinct regions for new learning with less interference. Experiments on challenging benchmarks report state-of-the-art performance and a stronger balance between retaining knowledge and acquiring new capabilities. The central contribution is coordinating constraints on parameter changes with separation in the learned feature space.
summary.tldr: Janus-LoRA combines corrected low-rank updates with feature separation to balance knowledge retention and new learning.

title: JANUS-LORA: A Balanced Low-Rank Adaptation for Continual Learning

abstract: Spectroscopy infers the internal structure of physical systems by measuring their response to perturbations. We apply this principle to neural networks: perturbing the data distribution by upweighting a token $y$ in context $x$, we measure the model’s response via susceptibilities $\chi_{xy}$, which are covariances between component-level observables and the perturbation computed over a localized Gibbs posterior via stochastic gradient Langevin dynamics (SGLD). Theoretically, we show that susceptibilities decompose as a sum over modes of the data distribution, explaining why tokens that follow their contexts “for similar reasons” cluster together in susceptibility space. Empirically, we apply this methodology to Pythia-14M, developing a conductance-based clustering algorithm that identifies 510 interpretable clusters ranging from grammatical patterns to code structure to mathematical notation. Comparing to sparse autoencoders, 50% of our clusters match SAE features, validating that both methods recover similar structure.

paragraphs: Spectroscopy studies internal structure by observing how a system responds to perturbations. This paper applies that idea to language models by increasing the weight of a particular token in a particular context and measuring the response. The resulting susceptibilities describe how component-level observables covary with that perturbation.

The measurements are computed over a localized Gibbs posterior using stochastic gradient Langevin dynamics. The authors theoretically show that susceptibilities decompose into a sum over modes of the data distribution. This explains why context-token pairs supported by similar underlying reasons can cluster together according to their response patterns, providing a route from controlled perturbations to interpretable structure.

Applied to Pythia-14M, the method uses a conductance-based clustering algorithm to identify 510 interpretable clusters. These cover grammatical patterns, code structure, and mathematical notation. Half of the clusters match features from sparse autoencoders, supporting the claim that the two approaches recover some similar structure. The result offers a response-based perspective on interpretation, with empirical evidence from the particular language model studied.
summary.tldr: Measuring language-model responses to data perturbations reveals interpretable token-context clusters, half of which match sparse-autoencoder features in Pythia-14M.

title: Towards Spectroscopy: Susceptibility Clusters in Language Models

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) with extended context windows enable powerful applications but impose significant memory overhead, as caching all key-value (KV) states scales linearly with sequence length and batch size. Existing cache eviction methods address this by exploiting attention sparsity, yet they typically rank tokens heuristically using accumulated attention weights without considering their true impact on attention outputs. We propose Optimal Brain Cache (OBCache), a principled framework that formulates cache eviction as a layer-wise structured pruning problem. Building upon the Optimal Brain Damage (OBD) theory, OBCache quantifies token saliency by measuring the perturbation in attention outputs induced by pruning tokens, with closed-form scores derived for isolated keys, isolated values, and joint key-value pairs. Our scores account not only for attention weights but also for information from value states and attention outputs, thereby enhancing existing eviction strategies with output-aware signals. Experiments on LLaMA and Qwen models demonstrate that replacing the heuristic scores in existing works, which estimate token saliency across different query positions, with OBCache’s output-aware scores consistently improves long-context accuracy. Code is available at https://github.com/DreamSoul-AI/OBCache.

Our scores account not only for attention weights but also for information from value states and attention outputs, thereby enhancing existing eviction strategies with output-aware signals. Experiments on LLaMA and Qwen models demonstrate that replacing the heuristic scores in existing works, which estimate token saliency across different query positions, with OBCache’s output-aware scores consistently improves long-context accuracy. paragraphs: Language models retain key and value states from earlier tokens so they can reuse them during inference. This cache grows with sequence length and batch size, making long contexts memory-intensive. Many eviction methods rank tokens using accumulated attention weights, but those weights alone do not measure how much removing a token changes the attention output.

OBCache treats cache eviction as structured pruning within each layer. Drawing on Optimal Brain Damage theory, it derives closed-form importance scores based on the output perturbation caused by removing isolated keys, isolated values, or complete key-value pairs. These scores include information from value states and attention outputs as well as attention weights.

Experiments on LLaMA and Qwen models replace heuristic scores inside existing eviction strategies with OBCache's output-aware scores. The substitutions consistently improve long-context accuracy in the reported evaluations. The contribution is therefore an improved basis for deciding what to retain: it estimates the effect of pruning on the computation being preserved, allowing existing cache-management approaches to make better-informed eviction decisions.
summary.tldr: OBCache improves KV-cache eviction by scoring tokens through their effect on attention outputs, yielding better long-context accuracy in LLaMA and Qwen experiments.

title: OBCache: Optimal Brain KV Cache Pruning for Efficient Long-Context LLM Inference

abstract: Extended chain-of-thought reasoning can degrade performance on deterministic state-tracking tasks, not solely because of preference biases but, on the evidence we present, because of information-theoretic limits in the capacity of decoder-only attention. We present: (1) an Attention Bottleneck analysis providing evidence that total state-tracking capacity in bits is bounded in terms of head count, head dimension, and context length under stated modeling assumptions, and that total capacity is not the binding constraint; (2) a context-dependent error model with a depth-dependent quadratic term in the error exponent; (3) the State-Space Jaccard metric measuring state drift; and (4) a Deterministic Horizon $d^* \in [19, 31]$ (at $\alpha = 0.5$) marking the depth at which unaided accuracy crosses 50%. Across twelve models and eight task domains (including SWE-Bench, WebArena, and SQL-Multi), tool-integrated reasoning reaches 76–94% accuracy versus 17–42% for neural chain-of-thought on PermutationProbe. Fine-tuning on optimal-length traces yields $<$3 percentage-point improvement, supporting an architectural ceiling.

paragraphs: Longer reasoning traces can make deterministic state tracking worse. This paper presents evidence that the problem extends beyond preference biases to limits associated with decoder-only attention. Its analysis bounds state-tracking capacity using attention-head count, head dimension, and context length under stated modeling assumptions, while finding that total capacity is not the binding constraint.

The authors introduce a context-dependent error model with a quadratic depth term in the error exponent, plus a State-Space Jaccard metric for tracking state drift. They identify a deterministic horizon between depths 19 and 31 at alpha equal to 0.5, where unaided accuracy crosses the 50% threshold. This gives a concrete characterization of performance deterioration within their analysis.

The study spans twelve models and eight task domains. On PermutationProbe, tool-integrated reasoning reaches 76–94% accuracy compared with 17–42% for neural chain-of-thought. Fine-tuning on optimal-length traces improves performance by less than three percentage points. These results support the authors' architectural-ceiling interpretation and the value of tool delegation, while the capacity argument remains tied to its modeling assumptions.
summary.tldr: The paper finds depth-dependent failures in deterministic state tracking and evidence that tool delegation can outperform extended unaided reasoning.

title: The Deterministic Horizon: When Extended Reasoning Fails and Tool Delegation Becomes Necessary

abstract: Personality traits have long been studied as predictors of human behavior. Recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) suggest similar patterns may emerge in artificial systems, with advanced LLMs displaying consistent behavioral tendencies resembling human traits like agreeableness and self-regulation. Understanding these patterns is crucial, yet prior work primarily relied on simplified self-reports and heuristic prompting, with little behavioral validation. In this study, we systematically characterize LLM personality across three dimensions: (1) the dynamic emergence and evolution of trait profiles throughout training stages; (2) the predictive validity of self-reported traits in behavioral tasks; and (3) the impact of targeted interventions, such as persona injection, on both self-reports and behavior. Our findings reveal that instructional alignment (e.g., RLHF, instruction tuning) significantly stabilizes trait expression and strengthens trait correlations in ways that mirror human data. However, these self-reported traits do not reliably predict behavior, and observed associations often diverge from human patterns. While persona injection successfully steers self-reports in the intended direction, it exerts little or inconsistent effect on actual behavior. By distinguishing surface-level trait expression from behavioral consistency, our findings challenge assumptions about LLM personality and underscore the need for deeper evaluation in alignment and interpretability.

paragraphs: A language model can describe itself as agreeable or self-controlled without behaving consistently with that description. This paper investigates that distinction by examining personality-like traits across training stages, testing whether self-reports predict behavior, and measuring how targeted interventions affect both. It extends evaluation beyond questionnaires and persona prompts to behavioral validation.

The study finds that instruction tuning and other instructional alignment, including RLHF, make trait expression more stable and strengthen correlations among traits in ways resembling human data. Yet the resulting self-reports do not reliably predict performance in behavioral tasks. When associations do appear, they often differ from the patterns observed in humans.

Persona injection presents a similar split: it moves reported traits in the intended direction but has little or inconsistent influence on actual behavior. These findings distinguish stable personality language from dependable behavioral tendencies. They challenge the use of self-reported traits as a sufficient basis for interpreting model behavior and support evaluating behavioral consistency directly when studying alignment and interpretability.
summary.tldr: LLM personality self-reports can become stable and respond to persona prompts without reliably predicting or changing actual behavior.

title: The Personality Illusion: Revealing Dissociation Between Self-Reports & Behavior in LLMs

abstract: We propose 3DGS$^2$-TR, a second-order optimizer for accelerating the scene training problem in 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS). Unlike existing second-order approaches that rely on explicit or dense curvature representations, such as 3DGS-LM (Höllein et al., 2025) or 3DGS2 (Lan et al., 2025), our method approximates curvature using only the diagonal of the Hessian matrix, estimated efficiently via Hutchinson’s method. Our approach is fully matrix-free and has the same complexity as ADAM (Kingma, 2024), $O(n)$ in both computation and memory costs. To ensure stable optimization in the presence of strong nonlinearity in the 3DGS rasterization process, we introduce a parameter-wise trust-region technique based on the squared Hellinger distance, regularizing updates to Gaussian parameters. Under identical parameter initialization and without densification, 3DGS$^2$-TR is able to achieve better reconstruction quality on standard datasets, using 50% fewer training iterations compared to ADAM, while incurring less than 1GB of peak GPU memory overhead (17% more than ADAM and 85% less than 3DGS-LM), enabling scalability to very large scenes and potentially to distributed training settings.

paragraphs: Training a scene with 3D Gaussian Splatting involves adjusting Gaussian parameters through a strongly nonlinear rendering process. This paper introduces an optimizer that uses curvature information to guide those adjustments while keeping computation and memory linear in the number of parameters. Its aim is to make second-order optimization practical for large scenes.

The method estimates only the diagonal of the Hessian using Hutchinson’s method, avoiding explicit or dense curvature matrices. It combines this approximation with a separate trust region for each parameter, based on squared Hellinger distance. These trust regions regularize Gaussian updates to support stable optimization despite the rendering process’s nonlinearity.

With identical initialization and no densification, the method achieves better reconstruction quality than ADAM using 50% fewer iterations on standard datasets. Reported peak GPU memory overhead is below 1GB: 17% above ADAM and 85% below 3DGS-LM. These findings support large-scene scalability; extension to distributed training is presented as a possibility.
summary.tldr: A matrix-free curvature approximation and parameter-wise trust regions improve 3D Gaussian Splatting training with linear computation and memory costs.

title: 3DGS$^2$-TR: Scalable Second-Order Trust-Region Method for 3D Gaussian Splatting

abstract: Large-scale Set Cover Problems (SCP) with millions of variables and complex cost structures require high-quality solutions within seconds, yet remain beyond the reach of exact solvers and pose severe generalization challenges for neural methods. Such problems necessitate decomposition into bounded subproblems; however, when the induced subproblem topology differs from that observed during training, existing neural approaches often fail to transfer reliably. We introduce Generative Large Neighborhood Search (GLNS), which reframes neighborhood selection as generation using a discrete diffusion model. Our key insight is that the diffusion denoising trajectory exposes variables exhibiting high prediction instability across timesteps and identifies regions where local repair yields downstream improvement. GLNS exploits this trajectory-level signal to construct high-impact neighborhoods via a localized, bounded-complexity generative sampling procedure, enabling robust neighborhood selection without retraining. As a result, GLNS transfers effectively across cost regimes and instance scales within SCP. Under tight and equal wall-clock budgets, GLNS consistently outperforms established neural baselines and achieves competitive performance with state-of-the-art MIP solvers. These results demonstrate trajectory-guided generation as a scalable framework for large-scale SCP and suggest potential relevance to other constrained optimization settings.

paragraphs: Large set cover problems can contain millions of variables, making rapid optimization difficult. Breaking them into bounded subproblems helps control computation, but learned methods can struggle when those subproblems have structures unlike their training examples. Generative Large Neighborhood Search addresses the choice of which part of a solution should undergo local repair.

The method uses a discrete diffusion model to generate neighborhoods. Its key signal comes from the denoising trajectory: variables whose predictions change substantially across steps identify regions where repair can lead to further improvements. A localized sampling procedure uses this instability signal to construct influential neighborhoods while bounding computational complexity, supporting neighborhood selection without retraining.

The reported experiments show transfer across cost structures and instance scales within set cover. Under equally tight wall-clock budgets, the method consistently beats established neural baselines and performs competitively with leading mixed-integer programming solvers. These results support trajectory-guided neighborhood selection for large set cover problems; the authors also suggest possible relevance to other constrained optimization tasks.
summary.tldr: GLNS uses instability along diffusion denoising trajectories to select promising regions for scalable local repair in set cover optimization.

title: Generative Large Neighborhood Search: Scalable Set Cover Optimization via Discrete Diffusion

abstract: While heavy-tailed synaptic weight distributions are pervasive in biological neural networks, their computational role—particularly in relation to generalization—remains poorly understood. To address this, we develop a novel optimal-transport-based optimization algorithm that incorporates key biological constraints, including Dale’s principle and heavy-tailed synaptic statistics, to train recurrent neural networks (RNNs) on a wide range of cognitive tasks. We show that these biologically constrained, heavy-tailed RNNs exhibit substantially improved generalization, which we further characterize within a PAC-Bayes framework. Our theoretical analysis and numerical experiments reveal two complementary mechanisms underlying this generalization enhancement. Topologically, heavy-tailed connectivity induces an effectively low-rank structure, which in turn yields low-dimensional neural dynamics. Geometrically, heavy-tailed connectivity intrinsically shapes task variable representations to lie near a linear manifold, thereby improving generalization for a linear readout strategy. Together, these results identify heavy-tailed connectivity as a biologically grounded intrinsic mechanism that promotes low-rank structure and favorable representational geometry, leading to improved generalization in flexible cognitive tasks.

paragraphs: Biological neural networks commonly have heavy-tailed distributions of synaptic weights, but the computational significance of that pattern is unclear. This paper investigates its relationship to generalization in recurrent neural networks trained on cognitive tasks. The authors introduce an optimization algorithm based on optimal transport that incorporates heavy-tailed weight statistics together with biological constraints, including Dale’s principle.

Their theoretical analysis and numerical experiments identify two complementary explanations for the gains. First, heavy-tailed connectivity produces an effectively low-rank network structure and correspondingly low-dimensional neural dynamics. Second, it organizes representations of task variables near a linear manifold. That geometry makes the representations more favorable for a linear readout to generalize.

The constrained networks show substantially improved generalization across the studied cognitive tasks, with the behavior further characterized through a PAC-Bayes analysis. The contribution therefore goes beyond reporting a benefit from biological realism: it connects the weight distribution to both the dimensionality of network activity and the geometry of learned representations, offering mechanisms for the observed improvements.
summary.tldr: Biologically constrained recurrent networks with heavy-tailed weights generalize better through low-dimensional dynamics and representations suited to linear readouts.

title: Biologically Plausible Heavy-Tailed Connectivity Enhances Generalization on Cognitive Tasks in Recurrent Neural Networks

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are enabling reasoning over 2D and 3D structures, yet existing methods remain modality-specific and typically compress structural inputs through sequence-based tokenization or fixed-length query connectors. Such architectures either omit the geometric grounding requisite for mitigating structural hallucinations, or impose inflexible modality fusion bottlenecks that concurrently over-compress and suboptimally allocate structural tokens, thereby impeding the realization of generalized all-atom reasoning. We introduce Cuttlefish, a unified multimodal LLM that grounds language reasoning in geometric cues while scaling modality tokens with structural complexity. First, Scaling-Aware Patching leverages an instruction-conditioned gating mechanism to generate variable-size patches over structural graphs, adaptively scaling the query token budget with structural complexity to mitigate fixed-length connector bottlenecks. Second, Geometry Grounding Adapter refines these adaptive tokens via cross-attention to modality embeddings and injects the resulting modality tokens into the LLM, exposing explicit geometric cues to reduce structural hallucination. Experiments across interdisciplinary all-atom benchmarks demonstrate that Cuttlefish achieves superior performance in heterogeneous structure-grounded reasoning. Code: github.com/zihao-jing/Cuttlefish.

paragraphs: Reasoning about two- and three-dimensional structures requires more than translating them into a fixed sequence of language-model inputs. Existing connectors can lose geometric information or allocate too few tokens to complex structures. Cuttlefish addresses these problems by adapting the structural token budget and explicitly supplying geometric cues.

Its Scaling-Aware Patching component uses an instruction-conditioned gate to form variable-size patches over structural graphs. The query-token budget changes with structural complexity, making the representation responsive to the input. A Geometry Grounding Adapter then refines these tokens through cross-attention to modality embeddings and passes them into the language model.

Together, these components aim to reduce structural hallucinations while avoiding the bottleneck of a fixed-length connector. Experiments across interdisciplinary all-atom benchmarks report superior performance on heterogeneous structure-grounded reasoning. The contribution is a unified mechanism for combining language with structural information: token allocation responds to complexity, while geometric refinement supplies the information needed to ground the resulting reasoning.
summary.tldr: Cuttlefish adapts structural token budgets to input complexity and injects geometric cues to improve structure-grounded language-model reasoning.

title: Scaling-Aware Adapter for Structure-Grounded LLM Reasoning

abstract: Recent work has identified a counterintuitive phenomenon termed "Hyperfitting”, where fine-tuning Large Language Models (LLMs) to near-zero training loss on small datasets surprisingly enhances open-ended generation quality and mitigates repetition in greedy decoding. While effective, the underlying mechanism remains poorly understood, with the extremely low-entropy output distributions suggesting a potential equivalence to simple temperature scaling. In this work, we demonstrate that this phenomenon is fundamentally distinct from distribution sharpening; entropy-matched control experiments reveal that temperature scaling fails to replicate the diversity gains of hyperfitting. Furthermore, we falsify the hypothesis of static vocabulary reweighting, showing through ablation studies that hyperfitting relies on a dynamic, context-dependent rank reordering mechanism. Layer-wise analysis localizes this effect to a "Terminal Expansion” in the final transformer block, where a substantial geometric expansion of the feature space ($\Delta \mathrm{Dim} \approx +80.8$) facilitates the promotion of deep-tail tokens. Additionally, we introduce Late-Stage LoRA, a targeted fine-tuning strategy that updates only the final 5 layers, yielding robust generation with minimal parameter updates.

paragraphs: Hyperfitting describes a surprising observation: fine-tuning a language model until its loss on a small training set is nearly zero can improve open-ended generation and reduce repetition during greedy decoding. Because the resulting output distributions are highly concentrated, this paper investigates whether the effect is simply equivalent to changing the sampling temperature.

Experiments that match output entropy show that temperature scaling does not reproduce hyperfitting’s diversity gains. Ablations also reject an explanation based on fixed changes to vocabulary preferences. Instead, the reported mechanism changes token rankings according to context. Layer-wise analysis locates this behavior in the final transformer block, where an expansion of the feature representation, measured at approximately 80.8 additional dimensions, helps promote tokens from deep in the probability tail.

The authors translate this analysis into Late-Stage LoRA, which updates only the final five layers. They report robust generation with few parameter updates. The findings connect hyperfitting’s benefits to context-dependent changes in late model representations, providing a basis for concentrating adaptation near the output.
summary.tldr: Hyperfitting improves generation through context-dependent token reordering associated with late-layer geometric expansion, rather than temperature-like sharpening.

title: Beyond Temperature: Hyperfitting as a Late-Stage Geometric Expansion

abstract: While Large Language Models (LLMs) possess strong reasoning capabilities, enabling them to learn continuously from experience without parametric retraining remains an open challenge. Existing Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) approaches typically treat memory as a static or append-only corpus, leading to "memory saturation," where accumulating noise and redundant information degrade performance over time. To address this, we propose an Experience Library Optimization framework that treats the agent’s external memory, which we call the experience library, as a learnable parameter under an explicit capacity budget. We introduce Textual Stochastic Gradient Descent (TSGD), a discrete optimization algorithm that refines this library via failure-driven Add, Edit, and Delete operations. TSGD estimates "textual gradients" through self-reflection and uses a dual-verification mechanism to ensure generalization, which prevents overfitting to local errors. Empirical results on MATH and AIME benchmarks show that TSGD achieves state-of-the-art performance, improving accuracy by up to $18.7%$ over zero-shot baselines and substantially outperforming static RAG, while keeping a compact memory footprint (compressing hundreds of experiences into $\approx 30$ high-utility rules).

paragraphs: An agent can retain experience outside its model weights, but a memory that only grows may accumulate noise and repeated information. This paper treats external memory as something to optimize within an explicit capacity budget. The aim is continued learning from experience without retraining the language model’s parameters.

Textual Stochastic Gradient Descent updates an experience library through Add, Edit, and Delete operations triggered by failures. Self-reflection produces textual guidance for these changes, playing the role of a gradient in a discrete editing process. A dual-verification mechanism checks proposed updates for generalization and guards against fitting the library too closely to individual local errors.

On MATH and AIME, the authors report state-of-the-art performance, accuracy improvements of up to 18.7% over zero-shot baselines, and substantial gains over static retrieval-augmented generation. Hundreds of experiences are compressed into approximately 30 useful rules. The result illustrates the value of revising and removing memories as well as adding them: a small, actively maintained library can preserve useful experience without continual accumulation.
summary.tldr: TSGD improves reasoning by continually adding, editing, and deleting external-memory rules within a fixed capacity budget.

title: Textual Stochastic Gradient Descent: Discrete Optimization of External Memory for Reasoning Language Agents

abstract: To overcome the computational burden of traditional computational fluid dynamics (CFD), graph neural network-based (GNN) learned simulators have attracted growing interest because they naturally operate on CFD meshes. However, classical GNNs only exchange information between neighbouring nodes, limiting flow prediction accuracy. While graph rewiring can improve information propagation, existing methods are mostly designed for generic graphs, and PIORF relies on long-range connections for fluid simulation. In this work, we show that simply connecting all 2-hop nodes can already achieve competitive performance with PIORF, raising questions about the necessity of distant rewiring. Motivated by fluid transport principles, we propose Flow Alignment Rewiring (FLARE), a simple and efficient local rewiring method that connects 2-hop nodes only when their relative direction aligns with the input flow direction. Hence, FLARE is a physics-informed local rewiring method, different from PIORF and well-aligned with fluid physics. Extensive numerical experiments on flows over a cylinder, single-, and tandem-airfoil under different flow conditions and deep network architectures demonstrate that FLARE outperforms PIORF and various 2-hop rewiring approaches by a significant margin.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks can predict fluid behavior directly on simulation meshes, but ordinary message passing only exchanges information between neighboring nodes. Adding connections can improve propagation. This paper first finds that connecting all nodes two graph steps apart already performs competitively with PIORF, a fluid-simulation method using long-range connections.

That observation motivates Flow Alignment Rewiring, or FLARE. It considers these same nearby two-hop connections but keeps them only when their relative direction aligns with the input flow direction. The connection rule therefore incorporates a fluid-transport principle into the graph structure, selecting local information routes according to the flow being modeled.

Numerical experiments cover flows around a cylinder, a single airfoil, and tandem airfoils under different flow conditions and with deep network architectures. FLARE significantly outperforms PIORF and several other two-hop rewiring approaches in these tests. The findings support flow-aligned local connectivity as an effective design choice, while the initial comparison questions whether distant connections are needed to achieve competitive prediction.
summary.tldr: FLARE improves graph-based fluid simulation by adding nearby connections only when they align with the input flow direction.

title: Graph Rewiring based on Flow Alignment for Improving Fluid Simulation

abstract: Reinforcement Learning (RL) post-training alignment for language models is effective, but also costly and unstable in practice, owing to its complicated training process. To address this, we propose a training-free inference method to sample directly from the optimal RL policy. The transition probability applied to Masked Language Modeling (MLM) consists of a reference policy model and an energy term. Based on this, our algorithm, Energy-Guided Test-Time Scaling (ETS), estimates the key energy term via online Monte Carlo, with a provable convergence rate. Moreover, to ensure practical efficiency, ETS leverages modern acceleration frameworks alongside tailored importance sampling estimators, substantially reducing inference latency while provably preserving sampling quality. Experiments on MLM (including autoregressive models and diffusion language models) across reasoning, coding, and science benchmarks show that our ETS consistently improves generation quality, validating its effectiveness and design. The code is available at https://github.com/sheriyuo/ETS.

The code is available at https://github.com/sheriyuo/ETS.

paragraphs: ETS explores whether the benefits targeted by reinforcement learning alignment can be obtained during generation without running an additional training process. Its starting point is a formulation of masked language modeling transitions that combines a reference policy with an energy term. That term provides the adjustment needed to target the optimal reinforcement learning policy.

Because the energy term must be estimated, ETS uses online Monte Carlo computation and establishes a convergence rate for the estimate. The method therefore moves work into inference: generation is guided by an estimated quantity rather than by newly trained model parameters. The theoretical convergence result supports this estimation-based route to the target policy.

To make that computation more practical, the authors combine acceleration frameworks with tailored importance sampling estimators. They report substantially lower inference latency while proving preservation of sampling quality. Experiments cover autoregressive and diffusion language models on reasoning, coding, and science benchmarks, with consistent improvements in generation quality. The findings support inference-time computation as a useful route to alignment without post-training.
summary.tldr: ETS uses inference-time energy estimation to target an optimal reinforcement learning policy without additional training.

title: ETS: Energy-Guided Test-Time Scaling for Training-Free RL Alignment

abstract: Disease screening is critical for early detection and timely intervention in clinical practice. However, most current screening models for medical images suffer from limited interpretability and suboptimal performance. They often lack effective mechanisms to reference historical cases or provide transparent reasoning pathways. To address these challenges, we introduce EviScreen, an evidential reasoning framework for disease screening that leverages region-level evidence from historical cases. The proposed EviScreen offers retrospection interpretability through regional evidence retrieved from dual knowledge banks. Using this evidential mechanism, the subsequent evidence-aware reasoning module makes predictions using both the current case and evidence from historical cases, thereby enhancing disease screening performance. Furthermore, rather than relying on post-hoc saliency maps, EviScreen enhances localization interpretability by leveraging abnormality maps derived from contrastive retrieval. Our method achieves superior performance on our carefully established benchmarks for real-world disease screening, yielding notably higher specificity at clinical-level recall. Code is publicly available at https://github.com/DopamineLcy/EviScreen.
originalAbstract: Disease screening is critical for early detection and timely intervention in clinical practice. However, most current screening models for medical images suffer from limited interpretability and suboptimal performance. They often lack effective mechanisms to reference historical cases or provide transparent reasoning pathways. To address these challenges, we introduce EviScreen, an evidential reasoning framework for disease screening that leverages region-level evidence from historical cases. The proposed EviScreen offers retrospection interpretability through regional evidence retrieved from dual knowledge banks. Using this evidential mechanism, the subsequent evidence-aware reasoning module makes predictions using both the current case and evidence from historical cases, thereby enhancing disease screening performance. Furthermore, rather than relying on post-hoc saliency maps, EviScreen enhances localization interpretability by leveraging abnormality maps derived from contrastive retrieval. Our method achieves superior performance on our carefully established benchmarks for real-world disease screening, yielding notably higher specificity at clinical-level recall. Code is publicly available at https://github.com/DopamineLcy/EviScreen.

paragraphs: Medical image screening models can produce predictions without clearly connecting them to relevant prior cases or showing where abnormalities are supported. EviScreen addresses both issues by making regional evidence from historical cases part of the prediction process. Its aim is to improve screening performance while giving users more interpretable evidence.

The framework retrieves region-level information from two knowledge banks. An evidence-aware reasoning module then combines the current case with that historical evidence to make its prediction. This creates a retrospective explanation: a prediction can be understood through the retrieved regions that informed it. The method also derives abnormality maps through contrastive retrieval, providing a localization mechanism within its evidential approach.

On the authors' benchmarks for real-world disease screening, EviScreen achieves superior performance, including higher specificity at clinically relevant recall. In practical terms, that result means better rejection of negative cases while retaining the reported level of disease detection. The two forms of interpretability serve complementary purposes: historical regions expose supporting comparisons, while abnormality maps indicate where relevant evidence appears in the image.
summary.tldr: EviScreen uses regional evidence from historical cases to improve screening specificity and make predictions and abnormality locations more interpretable.

title: Evidential Reasoning Advances Interpretable Real-World Disease Screening

abstract: Training-free test-time adaptation (TTA) for vision-language models (VLMs) can improve zero-shot classification under mild shifts, but often degrades under severe style/environment variation. We identify two shared failure modes in training-free pipelines: (i) retrieval confounding, where feature similarity is dominated by nuisance/style variation and corrupts retrieval evidence; and (ii) environment-biased priors, where VLM logits exhibit environment-dependent centered shifts that distort gating and prior-like terms. Therefore, we propose D$^2$O, a training-free debiasing operator that outputs three inference-time objects: a retrieval-oriented content feature for semantic matching, a style-aware routing coordinate for bias tracking, and debiased logits for corrected priors. D$^2$O composes plug-and-play with retrieval-based and closed-form Gaussian adapters in online and transductive settings. We further provide operator-to-decision guarantees: finite-difference covariance recovers a nuisance-sensitive subspace, routing-based EMA controls centered-logit template estimates, and these errors yield bounded pairwise score perturbations, leading to a margin-based condition for label invariance. Extensive experiments show that D$^2$O achieves its clearest gains under style/environment-dominant shifts, with broader gains elsewhere. Code is available at https://github.com/MAiTL-Group/D2O.

paragraphs: Vision–language classifiers can adapt during inference without retraining, yet these methods may deteriorate when image style or environment changes substantially. The paper separates two causes. Style can dominate feature similarity and retrieve misleading evidence, while environment-dependent shifts in model scores can distort the quantities used as priors or to route decisions.

D²O addresses both through three outputs: a content feature for semantic retrieval, a style-aware coordinate for tracking bias, and corrected classification scores. These outputs can be inserted into retrieval-based adapters and closed-form Gaussian adapters. The framework supports both online adaptation and transductive settings, making the correction usable within multiple existing adaptation pipelines.

The theoretical analysis connects errors in identifying nuisance directions and estimating score shifts to bounded changes in pairwise decision scores. It then gives a margin-based condition under which the predicted label remains unchanged. This is a conditional guarantee. Experiments show the clearest improvements when shifts are dominated by style or environment, together with broader gains in other evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: D²O corrects style-confounded retrieval and environment-biased scores to improve training-free adaptation of vision–language classifiers.

title: D$^2$O: A Dual Debiasing Operator for Training-Free Test-Time Adaptation of Vision–Language Models

abstract: Large language models can memorize information that must be removed—ranging from copyright-sensitive content (e.g., book chapters) to personally identifiable information (e.g., income)—to ensure responsible and compliant behavior. Unlearning has emerged as an efficient alternative to full retraining, aiming to remove specific knowledge. However, users may still expect model to leverage the removed information when it is re-introduced in the prompt. Existing evaluations of unlearning methods focus on (1) the extent of forgetting of the target knowledge (forget set) and (2) performance preservation on the retain set (i.e., utility), but overlook this critical usability dimension. Through a systematic evaluation of six state-of-the-art unlearning methods, we show that they consistently degrade such contextual utility—the model’s ability to use forgotten knowledge when it is provided in context. To address this, we augment unlearning objectives with a plug-in term that explicitly preserves contextual utility. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our approach restores contextual utility to near original levels while still maintaining effective forgetting and retain-set utility.

paragraphs: Removing memorized information from a language model creates a subtle usability requirement. The model should forget the targeted knowledge, yet users may still want it to work with that information when they explicitly provide it in a prompt. The paper calls this latter ability contextual utility.

Standard unlearning evaluations measure forgetting and preservation of performance on information that should remain. The authors add the contextual-use dimension and systematically evaluate six state-of-the-art methods. They find that these methods consistently damage the ability to use forgotten material when it is supplied again, exposing a cost that the usual evaluation misses.

To address that problem, the authors add a plug-in term to unlearning objectives that explicitly preserves contextual utility. Experiments show recovery to near the original level of contextual performance while maintaining effective forgetting and retain-set utility. The findings distinguish access to memorized knowledge from the ability to process supplied information, and show that unlearning objectives can account for both.
summary.tldr: An added unlearning objective preserves a model’s ability to use explicitly supplied information while still forgetting its memorized version.

title: Forget to Know, Remember to Use: Context-Aware Unlearning for Large Language Models

abstract: Cooperative reasoning under incomplete information remains complex for both humans and multi-agent AI, requiring agents to transcend individual logic in favor of recursive Theory-of-Mind (ToM) and strategic coordination. To investigate these challenges, we conduct a large-scale evaluation of 17 state-of-the-art LLMs (4B–600B+) on Hanabi card game across 2–5 players. To examine their limitations, we analyze the impact of context engineering and scaffold robustness, ranging from minimal prompts (Watson setting) to Bayesian-motivated scaffolding (Sherlock setting) and multi-turn working memory (Mycroft setting). Our findings reveal that: (1) top-performing models can autonomously track game states via internal working memory, although not reliably, and (2) cross-play performance scales smoothly with model capability. However, even the best models (scoring $\approx$ 15/25) trail specialist human experts ($>$ 20/25). We introduce and release two novel datasets: HanabiLogs (1,520 annotated trajectories) and HanabiRewards (560 games with dense move-level utilities). By fine-tuning a 4B open-weight model (Qwen3-Instruct) on our datasets, we achieve performance gains of up to 156%, bringing performance to within 3 points of a strong proprietary reasoning model (o4-mini) and surpassing the best non-reasoning model (GPT-4.1) by 52%. Crucially, our HanabiRewards RL-finetuned model further generalizes beyond Hanabi, improving performance on a cooperative group-guessing benchmark by 11 percentage points, temporal reasoning on EventQA by 6.4 points, instruction-following on IFBench by 1.7 Pass@10, and matching AIME 2025 mathematical reasoning Pass@10. Code and datasets are available at https://app.primeintellect.ai/dashboard/environments/mahesh-ramesh/hanabi.

paragraphs: Hanabi tests cooperation when players must coordinate with incomplete information and reason about what others know. This paper evaluates 17 language models, ranging from 4B to more than 600B parameters, in games with two to five players. It compares minimal prompting, Bayesian-motivated scaffolding, and multi-turn working memory.

The strongest models sometimes track game state through internal working memory, but do so unreliably. Performance when playing with other models improves smoothly with model capability. Even the best models score around 15 out of 25, below specialist human experts scoring above 20. The authors release annotated trajectories and games with detailed move-level utilities to support further training.

These results show transfer beyond Hanabi in the evaluated tasks.
summary.tldr: LLMs show incomplete cooperative reasoning in Hanabi, while targeted training substantially improves a small model and transfers to several other tasks.

title: Sparks of Cooperative Reasoning: LLMs as Strategic Hanabi Agents

abstract: This article initiates the study of a basic question about model pruning. Given a vector s of importance scores assigned to model components, how many of the scored components could be discarded without sacrificing performance? We propose Effective Model Pruning (EMP), which derives the desired sparsity directly from the score distribution using the notion of effective sample size from particle filtering, also known as the inverse Simpson index. Rather than prescribe a pruning criterion, EMP supplies a universal adaptive threshold derived from the distribution of the score $s$ over the model components: EMP maps $s$ to a number $N_{eff} = N_{eff} (s)$, called the effective sample size. The $N - N_{eff}$ lowest scoring components are discarded. A tight lower bound on the preserved mass fraction seff (the sum of retained normalized scores) in terms of $N_{eff}$ is derived. This process yields models with a provable upper bound on the loss change relative to the original dense model. Numerical experiments are performed demonstrating this phenomenon across a variety of network architectures including MLPs, CNNs, Transformers, LLMs, and KAN. It is also shown that EMP addresses a rich set of pruning criteria such as weight magnitude, attention score, KAN importance score, and even feature-level signals such as image pixels.

paragraphs: Pruning methods assign importance scores to model components, but those scores do not automatically specify how many components to remove. Effective Model Pruning addresses that second decision. It uses the distribution of existing scores to determine an adaptive pruning amount, making it applicable to several different ways of measuring importance.

The method borrows effective sample size, also known as the inverse Simpson index, from particle filtering. It converts a vector of scores into an effective component count, N_eff, then removes the N minus N_eff components with the lowest scores. Conceptually, the distribution reveals whether importance is spread broadly across components or concentrated in a smaller subset.

The authors derive a tight lower bound on the fraction of normalized score mass retained and establish an upper bound on the change in loss relative to the dense model. Such a bound controls possible loss change rather than asserting that it is always zero. Experiments cover architectures including MLPs, CNNs, Transformers, LLMs, and KANs, with importance signals ranging from weights and attention scores to image pixels.
summary.tldr: Effective Model Pruning derives how much to prune from importance-score distributions and provides bounds on retained score mass and loss change.

title: Effective Model Pruning : Measuring the Redundancy of Model Components

abstract: Generative Flow Networks (GFlowNets) enable fine-tuning large language models to approximate reward-proportional posteriors, but they remain prone to mode collapse, manifesting as prefix collapse and length bias. We attribute this to two factors: (i) weak credit assignment to early prefixes, and (ii) biased replay that induces a shifted, non-representative training flow distribution. We propose Rooted absorbed prefix Trajectory Balance (RapTB), an objective that anchors subtrajectory supervision at the root and propagates terminal rewards to intermediate prefixes via absorbed suffix-based backups, providing dense prefix-level learning signals. To mitigate replay-induced distribution shift, we further introduce SubM, a submodular replay refresh strategy that promotes both high reward and diversity. Empirically, on tasks such as molecule generation with LLM using SMILES strings, RapTB combined with SubM consistently improves optimization performance and molecular diversity while preserving high validity. The code is released on https://github.com/ComDec/ChemGFN.

paragraphs: GFlowNets can train language models to sample outputs according to reward, but their diversity can collapse through shared prefixes or biased output lengths. This paper attributes those problems partly to weak feedback for early prefixes and partly to an unrepresentative replay distribution. It addresses both learning signals and data reuse.

Rooted absorbed prefix Trajectory Balance anchors subtrajectory supervision at the root and carries terminal reward back to intermediate prefixes through suffix-based backups. This supplies denser credit assignment. A companion submodular replay strategy, SubM, refreshes examples to retain both high reward and diversity.

In tasks including SMILES-based molecular generation, the combined method improves optimization and molecular diversity while maintaining high validity. The contribution is a coordinated objective and replay design for reward-proportional generation. The abstract does not establish complete elimination of mode collapse or translate molecular validity into demonstrated biological effectiveness.
summary.tldr: RapTB and submodular replay improve prefix credit assignment and sampling diversity in GFlowNet language-model training.

title: Rooted Absorbed Prefix Trajectory Balance with Submodular Replay for GFlowNet Training

abstract: Continual Offline Reinforcement Learning (CORL) enables building long-term autonomous agents from static datasets. However, it faces heterogeneity in environment dynamics, reward functions, and behavior policies across tasks. Combined with the inherent distribution shift in offline learning, this requires agents to selectively reuse shared knowledge during transfer while isolating task-specific features. The flat knowledge sharing mechanisms employed by existing methods struggle to capture such distinctions, limiting cross-task generalization. To address this, we propose Hierarchical Task-Aware Composition (HTAC), which balances plasticity and stability through dual-level task encoding and soft composition mechanisms. HTAC comprises four modules: (1) a Hierarchical Semantic Task Representation that decomposes tasks into domain-level and task-level embeddings; (2) a Dual-level Expert Network that creates domain and task experts on demand for parameter-efficient knowledge isolation; (3) an Adaptive Knowledge Composition module that integrates historical expert outputs via attention mechanisms for knowledge reuse; (4) Task Adapters that preserve historical routing weights to prevent forgetting. Experiments on Offline Continual World show that HTAC outperforms existing baselines, demonstrating better knowledge reuse and transfer capabilities.

paragraphs: Continual offline reinforcement learning trains an agent across tasks using previously collected datasets. Tasks can differ in their dynamics, rewards, and the behavior that produced the data. Reusing everything indiscriminately can mix incompatible knowledge, while keeping everything separate limits transfer. HTAC addresses the need to share useful knowledge while preserving task-specific distinctions.

The method represents tasks at two levels: a broader domain embedding and a more specific task embedding. It creates domain and task experts as needed, allowing knowledge to be isolated with parameter efficiency in mind. An attention-based composition module combines historical experts’ outputs, while task adapters retain past routing weights to help prevent forgetting.

This hierarchy gives knowledge reuse more structure than a single flat sharing mechanism. Shared domain information and task-specific information can contribute differently as new tasks arrive. Experiments on Offline Continual World show that HTAC outperforms existing baselines, with better reuse and transfer. The reported results support its approach to balancing adaptation to new tasks with preservation of previously learned behavior.
summary.tldr: HTAC organizes reusable knowledge into domain and task experts to improve continual learning from offline reinforcement-learning datasets.

title: HTAC: Hierarchical Task-Aware Composition for Continual Offline Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Recent success of large reasoning models (such as OpenAI o1 and DeepSeek R1) have spurred a resurgence of interest in reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards (RLVR). However, progress is still largely driven by RL algorithm design, while data scheduling – the data-side decisions that determine what the model trains on over time – is critical but remains underexplored. Therefore, data scheduling becomes the focus of this paper, including how to curate data for supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and how to select prompts and collect rollouts for reinforcement learning (RL). We introduce a pipeline with careful designs on data scheduling, consisting of hardness-prioritized SFT and two-stage RL. Specifically, we first fine-tune the base model on supervision data that is curated to prioritize difficulty based on both arena learning and classification. Then, we introduce two-stage RL where a decreased max sequence length during rollout is used in the first stage to expand entropy and reduce repetition, and a large number rollouts per prompt and curriculum design are adopted in the second stage to encourage exploration for challenging problems. We implement this pipeline on Qwen2.5-32B and an internal 389B MoE model, and evaluate them on a wide range of benchmarks including challenging LeetCode and Codeforces weekly contests. The results not only indicate the effectiveness and scalability of our pipeline but also demonstrate our model achieve sota of 32B models in competitive code generation.

paragraphs: DRIVE studies how training data should be scheduled for competitive code generation with verifiable rewards. Its focus includes which examples to use for supervised fine-tuning, which prompts to select during reinforcement learning, and how to collect generated attempts. These decisions determine what challenges the model encounters as its abilities develop.

The pipeline begins with supervised data curated to prioritize difficulty using arena learning and classification. Reinforcement learning then proceeds in two stages. The first reduces the maximum rollout sequence length to increase entropy and reduce repetition. The second uses many rollouts per prompt together with a curriculum, encouraging exploration on challenging problems. Different stages therefore use different data-generation settings to support the intended learning behavior.

The authors implement DRIVE on Qwen2.5-32B and an internal 389-billion-parameter mixture-of-experts model. Evaluations include difficult LeetCode and Codeforces weekly contests. They report effective scaling and leading competitive-code performance among 32-billion-parameter models, supporting data scheduling as a consequential part of reasoning-model training alongside the reinforcement learning algorithm itself.
summary.tldr: DRIVE improves competitive code generation through difficulty-prioritized supervision and a two-stage reinforcement learning data schedule.

title: DRIVE: Best Data Scheduling Practices for Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Reward in Competitive Code Generation

abstract: In this paper we describe a new method to reduce the complexity of support vector machines by reducing the number of necessary support vectors included in their solutions. The reduction process iteratively selects two nearest support vectors belonging to the same class and replaces them by a newly constructed vector. Through the analysis of relation between vectors in the input and feature spaces, we present the construction of new vectors that requires to ﬁnd the unique maximum point of a one-variable function on the interval (0, 1), not to minimize a function of many variables with local minimums in former reduced set methods. Experimental results on real life datasets show that the proposed method is eﬀective in reducing number of support vectors and preserving machine’s generalization performance.

The reduction process iteratively selects two nearest support vectors belonging to the same class and replaces them by a newly constructed vector. Through the analysis of relation between vectors in the input and feature spaces, we present the construction of new vectors that requires to ﬁnd the unique maximum point of a one-variable function on the interval (0, 1), not to minimize a function of many variables with local minimums in former reduced set methods. Experimental results on real life datasets show that the proposed method is eﬀective in reducing number of support vectors and preserving machine’s generalization performance.

paragraphs: A support vector machine represents its solution using a collection of support vectors. This paper proposes simplifying that representation by reducing how many vectors it needs. The aim is to retain the machine’s ability to generalize while replacing a more elaborate solution with a smaller one.

The reduction proceeds iteratively. At each step, the method selects two nearest support vectors from the same class and replaces them with a newly constructed vector. The construction uses an analysis of the relationship between vectors in the original input space and their representations in feature space. This makes the replacement a specific mathematical operation rather than simply discarding one member of the pair.

The resulting construction requires finding the unique maximum of a function of one variable within the interval from zero to one. The authors contrast this with earlier reduced-set methods that minimize functions of many variables with local minima. Experiments on real datasets show that the method reduces support-vector counts while preserving generalization performance in the evaluated cases.
summary.tldr: Iteratively merging nearby support vectors from the same class simplifies SVMs while preserving generalization in the reported experiments.

title: An efficient method for simplifying support vector machines

abstract: Empirical evidence suggests that hashing is an effective strategy for dimensionality reduction and practical nonparametric estimation. In this paper we provide exponential tail bounds for feature hashing and show that the interaction between random subspaces is negligible with high probability. We demonstrate the feasibility of this approach with experimental results for a new use case --- multitask learning with hundreds of thousands of tasks.

In this paper we provide exponential tail bounds for feature hashing and show that the interaction between random subspaces is negligible with high probability. We demonstrate the feasibility of this approach with experimental results for a new use case --- multitask learning with hundreds of thousands of tasks.

paragraphs: Hashing had already shown empirical promise as a way to reduce dimensionality and support practical nonparametric estimation. This paper strengthens that motivation with theoretical analysis and explores an unusually large multitask learning application. Its focus is on whether a compact hashed representation can remain useful when learning involves very many tasks.

The authors establish exponential tail bounds for feature hashing. These bounds provide probabilistic control over the deviations covered by their analysis. They also show that interactions between random subspaces are negligible with high probability. That qualification matters: the result describes a probabilistic guarantee, rather than claiming that interactions disappear in every possible instance.

Experiments demonstrate feasibility for multitask learning with hundreds of thousands of tasks. This gives a concrete application to the analysis by showing that hashing can support learning at that scale. Together, the theoretical results and experiments connect a practical dimensionality-reduction technique to guarantees about its behavior and evidence of its usefulness for very large collections of learning tasks.
summary.tldr: Feature hashing receives probabilistic guarantees and an experimental demonstration involving hundreds of thousands of learning tasks.

title: Feature hashing for large scale multitask learning

abstract: We consider multiarmed bandit problems where the expected reward is unimodal over partially ordered arms. In particular, the arms may belong to a continuous interval or correspond to vertices in a graph, where the graph structure represents similarity in rewards. The unimodality assumption has an important advantage: we can determine if a given arm is optimal by sampling the possible directions around it. This property allows us to quickly and efficiently find the optimal arm and detect abrupt changes in the reward distributions. For the case of bandits on graphs, we incur a regret proportional to the maximal degree and the diameter of the graph, instead of the total number of vertices.

paragraphs: This paper studies multiarmed bandit problems whose expected rewards have a unimodal structure over partially ordered choices. The choices may lie on a continuous interval or form the vertices of a graph. In the graph setting, connections represent similarities in reward, giving the learner structural information about how alternatives relate.

The unimodality assumption makes local exploration particularly useful. By sampling the possible directions around a choice, the learner can determine whether that choice is optimal. The authors use this property to find the optimal arm efficiently and to detect abrupt changes in reward distributions. These benefits rely on the stated reward structure.

For graph-based problems, the reported regret is proportional to the graph's maximum degree and diameter instead of its total number of vertices. This changes which aspects of the problem govern the bound: local connectivity and graph extent take the place of the sheer number of choices. The result shows how an informative structure among arms can guide both exploration and adaptation.
summary.tldr: Unimodal reward structure enables efficient local exploration, with graph-bandit regret depending on maximum degree and diameter rather than vertex count.

title: Unimodal Bandits

abstract: Glorot et al. (2011) have successfully used Stacked Denoising Autoencoders (SDAs) (Vincent et al., 2008) to learn new representations for domain adaptation, resulting in record accuracy levels on well-known benchmark datasets for sentiment analysis. The representations are learned by reconstructing input data from partial corruption. In this paper, we introduce a variation, marginalized SDA (mSDA). In contrast to the original SDA, mSDA requires no training through back-propagation as we explicitly marginalize out the feature corruption and solve for the parameters in closed form. mSDA learns representations that lead to comparable accuracy levels, but can be implemented in only 20 lines of MATLAB and reduces the computation time on large data sets from several days to mere minutes.
originalAbstract: Glorot et al. (2011) have successfully used Stacked Denoising Autoencoders (SDAs) (Vincent et al., 2008) to learn new representations for domain adaptation, resulting in record accuracy levels on well-known benchmark datasets for sentiment analysis. paragraphs: Denoising autoencoders learn representations by reconstructing inputs after some of their information has been corrupted. Stacking these models had produced strong sentiment-analysis results for domain adaptation, where a representation must remain useful across domains. This paper seeks to retain that benefit while greatly reducing the cost of learning the representation.

The proposed marginalized stacked denoising autoencoder explicitly averages out the feature corruption and solves for its parameters in closed form. It therefore avoids training through backpropagation. The central change is computational: the corruption remains part of the learning formulation, but its effect is handled analytically instead of requiring the original training procedure.

The authors report comparable accuracy to the original approach while reducing computation on large datasets from several days to minutes. They also describe an implementation requiring only twenty lines of MATLAB. These findings make the method significant as a simpler and faster way to obtain useful domain-adaptation representations, preserving the reported accuracy level while substantially lowering the practical cost of training.
summary.tldr: Marginalizing feature corruption enables closed-form denoising autoencoder training, retaining comparable accuracy while reducing reported training time from days to minutes.

title: Marginalized Denoising Autoencoders for Domain Adaptation

abstract: Online learning algorithms are designed to learn even when their input is generated by an adversary. The widely-accepted formal definition of an online algorithm's ability to learn is the game-theoretic notion of regret. We argue that the standard definition of regret becomes inadequate if the adversary is allowed to adapt to the online algorithm's actions. We define the alternative notion of pol- icy regret, which attempts to provide a more meaningful way to measure an online algorithm's performance against adaptive adversaries. Focusing on the online bandit setting, we show that no bandit algorithm can guarantee a sublinear policy regret against an adaptive adversary with unbounded memory. On the other hand, if the adversary's memory is unbounded, we present a general technique that converts any bandit algorithm with a sublinear regret bound into an algorithm with a sublinear policy regret bound. We extend this result to other variants of regret, such as switching regret, internal regret, and swap regret.

We argue that the standard definition of regret becomes inadequate if the adversary is allowed to adapt to the online algorithm's actions. Focusing on the online bandit setting, we show that no bandit algorithm can guarantee a sublinear policy regret against an adaptive adversary with unbounded memory. paragraphs: Online learning often evaluates performance through regret, a comparison against alternative actions. This paper argues that the standard comparison becomes inadequate when an adversary can adapt to the learner's actions. It introduces policy regret as an alternative intended to measure performance more meaningfully when the environment responds to what the learner does.

In the bandit setting, the authors prove that no algorithm can guarantee sublinear policy regret against an adaptive adversary with unbounded memory. Sublinear growth would make policy regret per round diminish over time, so this impossibility result places a fundamental constraint on the desired learning guarantee.

The abstract also reports a conversion from algorithms with sublinear regret to algorithms with sublinear policy regret, with extensions to switching, internal, and swap regret. However, it labels the adversary's memory as unbounded in this positive statement too, conflicting with the preceding impossibility result. The supplied evidence therefore supports describing the proposed conversion, but does not establish a coherent memory condition under which its guarantee holds.
summary.tldr: The paper introduces policy regret for adaptive adversaries and proves an impossibility result, while its abstract gives conflicting memory conditions for a positive conversion result.

title: Online Bandit Learning against an Adaptive Adversary: from Regret to Policy Regret

abstract: Can one parallelize complex exploration–exploitation tradeoffs? As an example, consider the problem of optimal high-throughput experimental design, where we wish to sequentially design batches of experiments in order to simultaneously learn a surrogate function mapping stimulus to response, as well as identifying the maximum of the function. We formalize the task as a multi-armed bandit problem, where the unknown payoff function is sampled from a Gaussian process (GP), and instead of a single arm, in each round we pull a batch of several arms in parallel. We develop GP-BUCB, a principled algorithm for choosing batches, based on the GP-UCB algorithm for sequential GP optimization. We prove that, perhaps surprisingly, the cumulative regret of the parallel algorithm, compared to the sequential approach, only increases by a constant factor independent of the batch size B, for any fixed B. Our results provide rigorous theoretical support for exploiting parallelism in Bayesian global optimization. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on two real-world applications.

We formalize the task as a multi-armed bandit problem, where the unknown payoff function is sampled from a Gaussian process (GP), and instead of a single arm, in each round we pull a batch of several arms in parallel. We develop GP-BUCB, a principled algorithm for choosing batches, based on the GP-UCB algorithm for sequential GP optimization. We prove that, perhaps surprisingly, the cumulative regret of the parallel algorithm, compared to the sequential approach, only increases by a constant factor independent of the batch size B, for any fixed B. Our results provide rigorous theoretical support for exploiting parallelism in Bayesian global optimization. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on two real-world applications.

paragraphs: Experimental design can require learning an unknown response function while also finding inputs that produce high responses. Sequential optimization chooses one experiment at a time, using its result to guide the next choice. High-throughput settings instead run several experiments together, creating a need to balance exploration and exploitation across a whole batch.

The paper models the unknown payoff function as a sample from a Gaussian process and allows several arms to be selected in parallel each round. Its GP-BUCB algorithm extends sequential GP-UCB to this batch setting. The algorithm supplies a principled way to choose simultaneous evaluations when their outcomes are not yet available.

The authors prove that, for any fixed batch size B, cumulative regret increases over the sequential approach by only a constant factor independent of B. This provides theoretical support for parallel Bayesian global optimization without requiring the regret penalty to grow with the fixed batch size. Demonstrations on two real-world applications also support the effectiveness of the proposed batch-selection approach.
summary.tldr: GP-BUCB chooses parallel evaluation batches with a cumulative-regret increase bounded by a constant independent of batch size, for any fixed batch size.

title: Parallelizing Exploration-Exploitation Tradeoffs with Gaussian Process Bandit Optimization

abstract: We propose Coactive Learning as a model of interaction between a learning system and a human user, where both have the common goal of providing results of maximum utility to the user. At each step, the system (e.g. search engine) receives a context (e.g. query) and predicts an object (e.g. ranking). The user responds by correcting the system if necessary, providing a slightly improved – but not necessarily optimal – object as feedback. We argue that such feedback can be inferred from observable user behavior, specifically clicks in web search. Evaluating predictions by their cardinal utility to the user, we propose efficient learning algorithms that have O(1/sqrt{T}) average regret, even though the learning algorithm never observes cardinal utility values. We demonstrate the applicability of our model and learning algorithms on a movie recommendation task, as well as ranking for web search.

At each step, the system (e.g. search engine) receives a context (e.g. query) and predicts an object (e.g. ranking). The user responds by correcting the system if necessary, providing a slightly improved – but not necessarily optimal – object as feedback. We argue that such feedback can be inferred from observable user behavior, specifically clicks in web search. Evaluating predictions by their cardinal utility to the user, we propose efficient learning algorithms that have O(1/sqrt{T}) average regret, even though the learning algorithm never observes cardinal utility values. We demonstrate the applicability of our model and learning algorithms on a movie recommendation task, as well as ranking for web search.

paragraphs: Coactive Learning models an interaction in which a system and its user share the goal of producing useful results. The system receives a context, such as a query, and proposes an object, such as a ranking. The user can respond with an improvement that need not be the best possible answer.

This feedback model allows learning from partial corrections instead of requiring an optimal target at every step. The authors argue that such improvements can be inferred from observable behavior, including search clicks. Their algorithms evaluate performance in terms of the user's numerical utility even though those utility values are never directly observed by the learner.

The proposed efficient algorithms achieve O(1/sqrt(T)) average regret. This gives a quantitative statement about how average regret decreases with interaction under the learning model. Demonstrations on movie recommendation and web search ranking show its applicability. The contribution links a relatively modest feedback requirement—an improved result—to learning guarantees and practical tasks involving structured outputs.
summary.tldr: Coactive Learning learns from user-provided improvements without observing utility values and achieves O(1/sqrt(T)) average regret.

title: Online Structured Prediction via Coactive Learning
